title: Integrating 6 psychology frameworks in supernemawashi — 1 framework = 1 file parallel agents
description:
Introduction

supernemawashi's nemawashi-analyze skill stopped holding the profile as a single monolithic file and moved to 1 framework = 1 file × 1 parallel agent. Six psychology frameworks (defense mechanisms / Thomas-Kilmann / Transactional Analysis / Core Motivators / Cognitive Biases / Attachment Style) are each analyzed independently by an agent running in parallel. Here's why, and how I implemented it.

The first supernemawashi (v1.x) wrote the profile to a single markdown file (profile.md). The psychological analysis was one section inside it. That causes problems:

  • "I want to add one new framework" means rewriting the structure inside the monolithic file
  • Every re-run of analyze wipes and overwrites all the other frameworks' analyses too
  • The independent signals (facts) per framework get mixed, and you lose track of which judgment came from which evidence
  • Even if you want to parallelize, you get write contention on the one file

1 framework = 1 file × 1 agent

Decompose the profile per framework.

PROFILE_DIR/<person-name>/
├── profile.md                          ← slim index (Core Pattern + summary table only)
├── facts.jsonl                          ← facts (collect's output)
└── frameworks/
    ├── defense-mechanisms.md            ← per-framework classification + evidence + DO/DON'T
    ├── thomas-kilmann-tki.md
    ├── transactional-analysis-ta.md
    ├── core-motivators.md
    ├── cognitive-biases.md
    └── attachment-style.md

Each framework file is fully independent. Updating one doesn't touch the other five.

Make the framework registry the single source of truth

The frameworks' slug / display name / tier have one table as the source of truth:

Slug Display name Tier
defense-mechanisms Defense Mechanisms 1
thomas-kilmann-tki Conflict Mode (TKI) 1
transactional-analysis-ta Ego States (TA) 1
core-motivators Core Motivators 1
cognitive-biases Cognitive Biases 1
attachment-style Attachment Style 2

Tier 1 = analyzed by default; Tier 2 = analyzed only when signal density is sufficient (if thin, surfaced explicitly as a Data Gap). Steps to add a new framework:

  1. Add a row to the registry table
  2. Create frameworks/<slug>.md following the contract
  3. Update the situation→framework priority mapping in nemawashi-reply (if needed)
  4. Confirm the registry matches the actual files with scripts/check-frameworks.sh

Because a script detects drift between the registry and the real files, you can't break things by adding only one side.

Parallel agent dispatch

nemawashi-analyze's flow:

[1] Read the shared inputs (profile.md + facts.jsonl)
        ↓
[2] Dispatch one agent per framework in the registry, in parallel
    ┌─ agent: defense-mechanisms     ──┐
    ├─ agent: thomas-kilmann-tki     ──┤
    ├─ agent: transactional-analysis ──┤  run in parallel
    ├─ agent: core-motivators        ──┤
    ├─ agent: cognitive-biases       ──┤
    └─ agent: attachment-style       ──┘
        ↓ wait for all agents to finish
[3] Synthesis pass (synchronous)
    - Update profile.md's Framework Summary table
    - Re-derive the Core Pattern

Each agent only reads facts.jsonl and writes its own framework's frameworks/<slug>.md. It shares no state with the other agents. The synthesis pass only aggregates results — it doesn't re-analyze.

What goes in a framework file

Each frameworks/<slug>.md follows the same contract:

---
framework: Defense Mechanisms
tier: 1
output_label: Defense Mechanisms
---

# Defense Mechanisms

## Purpose
(what this framework reveals)

## Classification Guidance
(how to extract signals from facts)

## Reference Table
(mechanism / definition / observable signals / DO / DON'T)

## Rule Generation
(classification → situation-indexed rules)

## Signal Tags
(the tag format embedded in the facts jsonl)

As an example, two rows from the defense-mechanisms file's reference table:

Mechanism Observable Signals DO DON'T
Rationalization long explanations on failure / "because..." chains validate the reason, then redirect to the future argue directly against the justification
Passive Aggression "I'll do it" + no movement / strategic delay name the behavior neutrally call it "you're being passive-aggressive"

The agent cross-references facts against this table to tag signals, decides the dominant mechanism, and generates situation-indexed rules.

Situation categories

DO/DON'T rules are indexed by situation category. nemawashi-reply looks at the category and situation and loads only the framework files it needs:

Category Situation
When Requesting you're asking them for something
During Conflict disagreement / tension
When Reporting delivering good / bad news
Routine Collaboration day-to-day interaction

At reply time it doesn't load every framework — it narrows to the 2-3 relevant to the situation. That also cuts the context-window cost.

Gotchas

  • Drift between the registry and the real files: at first I synced by hand, and it always broke. I moved check-frameworks.sh into pre-commit for automatic detection.
  • Parallel-agent races: if each agent writes the same frameworks/<slug>.md, it obviously breaks. Strictly mapping 1 agent = 1 file avoids it.
  • The temptation for agents to share state: there are moments you want to "look at the other frameworks' results and adjust." Doing that regresses to the monolithic design, so it's banned — adjustment happens synchronously in the synthesis pass.
  • The Tier 2 threshold: attachment-style often has thin signal, so I made it Tier 2. The framework itself needs criteria to surface "I don't know" explicitly as a Data Gap.

Results

  • Adding a new framework is 3 steps (table + file + reply mapping), touching none of the existing frameworks
  • Re-running analyze doesn't break the other frameworks
  • Parallel dispatch shrank wallclock to roughly one framework's worth with all 6 agents running at once
  • Each framework file is independently readable, so you can view just the framework you want (nemawashi-show <person> --framework=defense-mechanisms, etc.)

Wrap-up

  • Drop the monolithic profile.md and decompose into 1 framework = 1 file × 1 agent
  • Make the framework registry the single source of truth, and detect drift with a check script
  • Parallel dispatch shortens wallclock; keep synthesis synchronous
  • Situation-indexed framework loading keeps the context cost down at reply time

References

  • supernemawashi (GitHub)
  • Thomas-Kilmann Conflict Mode Instrument
  • Transactional Analysis (Eric Berne)
  • Self-Determination Theory (Deci & Ryan)
  • Attachment Theory (Bowlby & Ainsworth)

This post was written with AI assistance and reviewed by the author.

title: Prompt Engineering for Beginners (Part 2): The Anatomy of a Good Prompt
description:
Part 1 of our Prompt Engineering from Scratch series, we explored how AI generates answers, what tokens and context windows are, and why the way we communicate with AI matters.

We learned one important lesson:

Getting better results from AI isn't always about using a more powerful model. Sometimes, it's about giving clearer instructions.

But knowing that we should write better prompts is one thing.

How do we actually write them?

What information should we include? How specific should our instructions be? And how do we know whether our prompt is good enough?

That's exactly what we'll explore in Part 2.

We'll break down six useful components of a well-structured prompt, understand what each one does, and learn how to combine them using simple, real-life examples.

No complicated terminology. No programming knowledge required.

Let's get started.

In Part 2, we'll learn the six useful building blocks of a good prompt, how to combine them, and how to test whether our prompts are working.

And don't worry. You don't need any technical background.

Let's begin with something we all understand.

1. Why Isn't a Simple Prompt Always Enough?

Imagine you're asking a friend to help you write an email.

You say:

Write an email for me.

Your friend would probably have a few questions.

Who is the email for?

What is it about?

Should it sound formal or friendly?

How long should it be?

Without that information, your friend has to guess.

AI faces a similar problem.

A basic prompt

Let's say you type:

Write an email asking for leave.

The AI might produce an email, but it doesn't know important details.

For example:

  • Who are you writing to?
  • Why do you need leave?
  • How many days do you need?
  • What tone should the email use?
  • Should the email be short or detailed?

Now let's make the prompt clearer.

A more detailed prompt 

Write a professional email to my manager
requesting two days of leave.

I need leave on Monday and Tuesday
because of a family commitment.

Keep the email polite and under 120 words.

Include a subject line.

This is much clearer.

You've given the AI the information it needs to create a more suitable response.

Does that guarantee the perfect email?

No.

But it reduces unnecessary guessing.

And that's the foundation of a good prompt.

A good prompt doesn't need complicated words. It needs clear instructions and enough relevant information.

2. The Six Building Blocks of a Good Prompt

When writing a prompt, there are six useful components you can think about.

These components help you explain what you need, how you want the task completed, and what the final answer should look like.

Component What it means Simple example
1. Role Who should the AI act as? Act as a helpful writing assistant.
2. Context What background information does it need? I'm writing to my manager about taking leave.
3. Examples Can you show what a good answer looks like? Here is an example of my writing style.
4. Task What exactly should it do? Write an email requesting two days of leave.
5. Constraints What rules should it follow? Keep it polite and under 120 words.
6. Output Format How should the answer be presented? Include a subject line and email body.

These six components provide a useful framework for writing clear prompts.

But here's something important: you don't need all six components every time.

For a simple question like:

What is the capital of Nepal?

A short prompt is perfectly fine.

For more complicated tasks, such as analyzing a document or writing a detailed report, additional information becomes more valuable.

The goal isn't to make every prompt longer.

The goal is to make every prompt clear enough for its purpose.

Now let's understand each component.

3. Component 1: Role - Who Should the AI Act As?

Imagine you're asking someone for advice.

If you need help preparing for an exam, you might ask a teacher.

If you need help improving your writing, you might ask an editor.

If you need help planning a trip, you might ask a travel guide.

Different roles suggest different ways of approaching a task.

You can use a similar idea when prompting AI.

Without a role 

Help me improve this paragraph.

With a role 

Act as a friendly writing tutor.

Help me improve this paragraph using
simple English.

Explain what you changed and why.

The second prompt gives the AI a clearer direction.

It suggests the type of assistance and explanation you want.

What is a system prompt?

You might hear the technical term system prompt.

In many AI applications, a system message contains higher-level instructions about how the assistant should behave.

For example, an application might instruct its AI assistant to use a particular language or follow certain rules.

However, when you type:

Act as a writing tutor.

into a normal chat, you're generally giving a role instruction as a user, not changing the application's actual system message.

You don't need to access system settings to use role-based prompting.

And a role doesn't give the model magical expertise or guarantee accurate answers.

It simply helps guide how the model approaches and presents the task.

When is this useful?

When you want a particular style of help, such as teaching, editing, planning, or reviewing.

4. Component 2: Context - Give the AI the Background Information

Imagine someone asks you:

What should I do?

You'd probably respond:

About what?

Without knowing the situation, it's difficult to give useful advice.

That's exactly why context matters.

Context is the background information that helps AI understand your situation or task.

Without context 

Write an email requesting leave.

With context 

I'm an employee writing to my manager.

I need two days of leave on Monday
and Tuesday because of a family commitment.

My manager prefers short and
professional emails.

Now the AI knows more about your situation.

It can use that information when preparing the email.

Another example

Imagine you're asking AI to recommend a laptop.

Basic prompt:

Recommend a laptop.

Prompt with context:

I'm a university student.

I mainly use my laptop for online classes,
writing assignments, browsing, and watching videos.

My budget is around $600.

Recommend suitable laptops and explain
why they would fit my needs.

The second prompt gives the model a much clearer picture of what you're looking for.

Can you provide too much context?

No.

More information isn't always better.

Imagine asking someone to help you choose a laptop, then telling them your entire life story.

Most of that information wouldn't help them.

The same applies to AI.

Provide the background details that matter for the task, and avoid including unnecessary personal or sensitive information.

Good context means relevant information, not simply more information.

5. Component 3: Examples - Show the AI What You Want

Sometimes it's easier to show someone what you want than to explain it.

Imagine you're asking a friend to design an invitation card.

Instead of describing every detail, you might show an example and say:

I want something similar to this.

AI can also use examples to understand the pattern, style, or structure you expect.

Without an example 

Rewrite this message professionally.

With an example 

Rewrite my message in a professional
but friendly tone.

Example:

Original:
"Hey, send me the report."

Improved:
"Could you please send me the report
when you have a chance?"

Now rewrite this message:

"I need the meeting details."

The example demonstrates the kind of change you want.

It shows the AI how to make a request sound more polite without changing its meaning.

A little technical detail: Zero-shot and Few-shot prompting

These are two terms you might encounter.

Zero-shot prompting means asking the AI to perform a task without providing examples.

For example:

Rewrite this sentence professionally:

"Send me the file."

Few-shot prompting means providing one or more examples before asking the AI to perform the task.

For example:

Example 1:
"Send me the file."
→ "Could you please send me the file?"

Example 2:
"Call me tomorrow."
→ "Could you please call me tomorrow?"

Now rewrite:
"Give me the document."

The examples help demonstrate the pattern.

However, examples aren't always necessary, and they don't automatically work better than clear instructions.

For simple tasks, a direct instruction may be enough.

We'll explore zero-shot and few-shot prompting in more detail in Part 3.

When should you use examples?

When you want a specific writing style, structure, classification, or repeated pattern.

6. Component 4: Task - Explain Exactly What You Need

This is one of the most important parts of a prompt.

The task tells the AI what it should actually do.

It sounds obvious, but vague tasks can lead to vague answers.

Example 1: Too vague 

Help me with my resume.

What kind of help?

Should the AI check grammar?

Improve the wording?

Shorten it?

Suggest missing sections?

Example 2: Clear task 

Review my resume.

Identify unclear sentences and
suggest improvements.

Keep my existing experience and
achievements accurate.

Do not invent qualifications or
work experience.

Now the AI knows what to focus on.

Another example

Basic:

Summarize this article.

Clearer:

Summarize this article in five bullet points.

Focus on the main findings.

Explain any difficult terms in
simple English.

Notice something?

We haven't used complicated technical language.

We've simply explained the task more clearly.

A useful habit: Before sending a prompt, ask yourself:

If someone who had never met me read this instruction, would they understand what I wanted them to do?

If the answer is no, you may need to make the task clearer.

7. Component 5: Constraints - Set Clear Rules and Limits

Now imagine you're asking someone to write a short speech.

You tell them:

Write a speech about teamwork.

They might write a ten-minute speech.

But you only have two minutes to speak.

The problem isn't necessarily the speech itself.

You forgot to explain the time limit.

That's where constraints come in.

Constraints are the rules or limitations you want the AI to follow.

They help make the output more suitable for your needs.

Example 

Write a short speech about teamwork.

Rules:
- Use simple English.
- Keep it under 200 words.
- Include one everyday example.
- Avoid difficult technical terms.
- End with an encouraging message.

Here, you've made your expectations much clearer.

Common types of constraints

Type Example
Length Keep it under 150 words.
Language Use simple English.
Tone Keep it polite and friendly.
Content Include three practical examples.
Restrictions Don't invent facts or statistics.
Structure Use short paragraphs.

Can constraints be too strict?

Yes.

If you add too many conflicting rules, the AI may struggle to follow them.

For example:

Explain this topic in detail using only ten words.

Those instructions work against each other.

So try to keep constraints realistic and relevant.

Remember: Constraints guide the AI, but they don't guarantee that every rule will always be followed.

That's why checking the final answer is still important.

8. Component 6: Output - Format Decide How the Answer Should Look

Imagine asking someone to organize your monthly expenses.

They could give you a long paragraph describing everything.

Or they could present a simple table.

Which would be easier to understand?

Usually, the table.

That's why output format matters.

Output format tells the AI how you want the final answer to be organized.

Without a format 

Compare online learning and
classroom learning.

The AI might produce several paragraphs.

With a format 

Compare online learning and
classroom learning.

Present the comparison in a table.

Include:
- Cost
- Flexibility
- Interaction
- Advantages
- Disadvantages

Finish with a short summary.

Now the structure is clear.

Common output formats

Format When it's useful
Paragraph Explanations and general writing
Bullet points Short summaries and quick ideas
Numbered steps Instructions and tutorials
Table Comparisons and organized information
Checklist Planning and reviewing tasks
Code Programming-related tasks
JSON When software needs a structured data format

A little technical detail: What is JSON?

JSON is a way to organize information using labels and values.

For example:

{
  "name": "Aarav",
  "age": 22,
  "city": "Kathmandu"
}

You don't need to use JSON in everyday prompting.

It's mainly useful when applications or programs need information in a consistent structure.

For most beginners, requesting a paragraph, table, or list is enough.

The takeaway: Choosing the right output format can make an answer easier to read, check, and use.

9. Putting All Six Components Together

Now let's combine everything we've learned.

We'll use the same email example from the beginning.

Basic prompt 

Write an email asking for leave.

This might work, but it leaves several details unclear.

Structured prompt 

ROLE:
Act as a professional writing assistant.

CONTEXT:
I'm an employee writing to my manager.
I need two days of leave on Monday and
Tuesday because of a family commitment.

EXAMPLE:
Use a polite and professional tone similar to:
"I would like to request your approval
for two days of leave."

TASK:
Write an email requesting the leave.

CONSTRAINTS:
- Keep it under 120 words.
- Use simple and professional language.
- Do not invent additional personal details.

OUTPUT FORMAT:
Include:
1. Subject line
2. Greeting
3. Email body
4. Closing

This prompt gives the AI much clearer instructions.

What changed?

Component What we added
Role Professional writing assistant
Context Leave dates, reason, recipient
Examples Preferred writing tone
Task Write a leave-request email
Constraints Word limit, language, accuracy
Output Format Subject, greeting, body, closing

We haven't used any magic words.

We've simply organized our instructions.

Important: Do we always need six sections?

Absolutely not.

The same request could be written naturally in a few sentences:

Write a polite email to my manager requesting leave on Monday and Tuesday because of a family commitment. Keep it under 120 words, use simple professional English, and include a subject line.

That may be enough.

A well-structured prompt doesn't have to be long or complicated. It just needs to provide the information the task requires.

The six components are a guide, not a rule that every prompt must follow.

10. Basic vs. Structured Prompts: What's the Difference?

Let's compare a few everyday examples.

Situation Basic prompt More structured prompt
Learning Explain photosynthesis. Explain photosynthesis to a 12-year-old using simple English and one everyday example.
Writing Write a birthday message. Write a short, funny birthday message for my best friend. Keep it under 60 words.
Planning Make a study plan. Create a seven-day study plan for someone who can study two hours daily. Present it in a table.
Summarizing Summarize this document. Summarize the document in five bullet points, focusing on the main findings and important numbers.
Comparing Compare these phones. Compare these phones by price, battery, camera, and storage in a table.

Notice that the improved prompts aren't necessarily much longer.

They simply explain what matters.

Does a structured prompt always give a better answer?

Not necessarily.

For straightforward tasks, a simple prompt can work perfectly.

For complicated tasks, clear instructions often help.

And sometimes the model may still make mistakes despite having a well-written prompt.

That's why we need a way to test whether our changes actually improve the result.

11. A Real-World Example: Summarizing a Long Document

This example connects closely with my work testing AI models on real documents.

Imagine you upload a 50-page report and type:

Summarize this report.

The AI might give you a useful general summary.

But suppose you actually need:

  • The report's main purpose
  • Important findings
  • Financial information
  • Major risks
  • Recommendations

Your original prompt didn't mention those expectations.

So you might have to ask several follow-up questions.

Now let's try a more structured approach.

ROLE:
Act as a research assistant.

CONTEXT:
I've uploaded a report that I need
to understand without reading every page.

TASK:
Summarize the report.

Include:
1. The main purpose of the report.
2. Five important findings.
3. Key financial figures, if available.
4. Major risks or limitations.
5. Important recommendations.

CONSTRAINTS:
- Use simple English.
- Keep the summary under 500 words.
- Do not invent missing information.
- Clearly mention if something is not found.

OUTPUT FORMAT:
Use headings and bullet points.

Where possible, include page references
so I can check the original information.

This prompt gives the model a clearer structure.

It also makes the output easier to verify.

For example, if the AI reports a financial figure, you can check the page where that figure appears.

Of course, the model could still overlook information or provide an incorrect page reference.

A structured prompt improves clarity and makes verification easier. It doesn't eliminate the need to check important results.

12. For the Curious: How Developers Use Structured Prompts

If you're not from a technical background, you can skip this section.

Everything we've learned so far is enough to start improving your prompts.

But if you're curious about how developers use these ideas, here's a simple example.

Suppose a developer asks:

Write code to calculate the total price.

The AI doesn't know the programming language, the calculation rules, or how to handle unusual inputs.

A clearer request might look like this:

ROLE:
Act as a Python programming assistant.

CONTEXT:
I'm building a small shopping application.

TASK:
Write a function that calculates the total
price of products in a shopping cart.

CONSTRAINTS:
- Each product has a price and quantity.
- Reject negative prices or quantities.
- Explain the calculation clearly.
- Include two example calculations.

OUTPUT FORMAT:
Return the Python code followed by
a short explanation.

This follows the same six-component idea.

The only difference is the task.

A developer may also provide database information, existing code, error messages, or other technical details.

But the main principle remains the same:

Give the AI enough information to understand the task, and clearly explain how you want the answer.

Generated code still needs to be reviewed and tested before being used in a real application.

13. The Prompt Engineering Workflow

Now that we know how to build a prompt, what should we do if the first answer isn't good enough?

Should we rewrite everything?

Should we keep adding random instructions?

Not necessarily.

A better approach is to improve the prompt step by step.

Here's a simple workflow.

Step 1: Specify Decide What You Want

Before writing a prompt, identify:

  • Your goal
  • The information AI needs
  • The kind of answer you expect
  • Any important rules or limitations

For example:

I want a short explanation of climate change for a young student.

Step 2: Save Keep Your Original Prompt

Don't immediately replace your first prompt.

Keep a copy.

For example:

Version 1:

Explain climate change.

This is your starting point.

You can compare future versions against it.

In technical settings, saving and tracking changes is sometimes called versioning.

But you don't need special software to do this.

A notebook or text document works perfectly.

Step 3: Test Change One Thing at a Time

Let's improve the prompt.

Version 2: Change the audience

Explain climate change to a 12-year-old.

Now compare the answer with Version 1.

Did it become easier to understand?

Next, return to Version 1 and test a different change.

Version 3: Change the length

Explain climate change in 100 words.

Now compare again.

This helps you understand whether specifying the audience or limiting the length made the answer more useful.

If you change five things at once, it becomes harder to identify which change helped.

AI responses can vary even when you use the same prompt, so repeat important tests before drawing strong conclusions.

Step 4: Improve Combine What Works

After comparing the results, you can combine useful instructions.

For example:

Explain climate change to a 12-year-old.

Use simple English.

Keep it under 100 words.

Include one everyday example.

You now have a clearer prompt based on what you've learned.

Step 5: Reuse - Save Your Best Prompts

If a prompt works well for a task you repeat often, save it.

For example:

Explain [TOPIC] to [AUDIENCE].

Use simple language.

Keep the explanation under [WORD LIMIT].

Include [NUMBER] everyday examples.

You can replace the words inside the brackets whenever you need to use the template again.

This is one of the practical benefits of prompt engineering.

Instead of starting from scratch every time, you build a collection of instructions that you can reuse and improve.

A simple workflow to remember

Specify → Save → Test → Improve → Reuse

In professional applications, teams may also track prompt versions, run repeated tests, compare results, and monitor performance after releasing an AI feature.

But for beginners, the same idea starts with something much simpler:

Keep your original prompt, change one thing, and check what happens.

14. Your Prompt Checklist

Before sending an important prompt, ask yourself:

  • [ ] Goal: Have I clearly explained what I want?
  • [ ] Context: Have I provided the necessary background information?
  • [ ] Role: Would specifying a role make the task clearer?
  • [ ] Examples: Would an example help show the result I expect?
  • [ ] Constraints: Have I mentioned important limits or rules?
  • [ ] Output Format: Have I explained how the answer should be presented?
  • [ ] Accuracy: Have I told the AI what to do if information is missing?
  • [ ] Verification: Can I check whether the result is correct?

You don't have to check every box for every question.

Use the ones that matter for your task.

15. Your 5-Minute Exercise: Build Your Own Prompt

Let's practice what we've learned.

Open your preferred AI chatbot.

We'll start with a simple request.

Step 1: Write a basic prompt 

Make a study plan for me.

Read the answer.

Is it suitable for your situation?

Does it know what subject you're studying?

Does it know how much time you have?

Step 2: Add context 

I'm a student preparing for an exam
next week.

I can study for two hours every day.

Make a study plan for me.

Compare the result with your first answer.

Step 3: Add useful constraints 

I'm a student preparing for an exam
next week.

I can study for two hours every day.

Create a seven-day study plan.

Include short breaks.

Keep the activities realistic.

Step 4: Specify the output format 

I'm a student preparing for an exam
next week.

I can study for two hours every day.

Create a seven-day study plan.

Include short breaks.

Present the plan in a table with:
- Day
- Study topic
- Duration
- Activity

Notice how the prompt becomes more specific.

The goal hasn't changed.

You've simply made your expectations clearer.

Step 5: Experiment

Now change only one part of the prompt.

For example:

  • Change the study time from two hours to one hour.
  • Or change the output format from a table to a checklist.
  • Or specify a particular subject.

Compare the results.

Ask yourself:

Which instruction changed the answer, and did that change make it more useful?

That's the habit I want you to develop throughout this series.

16. Quick Recap: The Six Components

Here's everything we've learned in one table.

Component Simple question to ask yourself
Role Who should the AI act as?
Context What does the AI need to know?
Examples Can I show what a good answer looks like?
Task What exactly do I want it to do?
Constraints What rules or limits matter?
Output Format How should the answer look?

And remember:

You don't need all six components for every prompt.

A simple question can have a simple prompt.

A complicated task may need more detail.

The purpose of prompt engineering isn't to make communication complicated.

It's to make it clearer.

What's Coming in Part 3?

In Part 3, we'll explore six useful prompting techniques:

  1. Zero-shot prompting: Asking AI to complete a task without examples.
  2. Few-shot prompting: Showing examples of the kind of answer you want.
  3. Chain-of-thought prompting: Approaches involving intermediate reasoning steps for more complicated tasks.
  4. Role-based prompting: Guiding AI through a particular role.
  5. Constraint-based prompting: Using clear rules and limitations.
  6. Meta-prompting: Using AI to help design or improve prompts.

We'll explain each one using practical examples and discuss when it might be useful.

Final Thoughts

In Part 1, we learned that language models don't automatically know what we expect from them.

Today, we learned how to communicate those expectations more clearly.

And here's the most important lesson:

A good prompt isn't measured by how long or complicated it is. It's measured by how clearly it communicates the task and how useful the result is.

You don't need to use special commands.

You don't need to memorize complicated terms.

And you certainly don't need a programming background.

Start with a simple prompt.

See what works.

Change one thing.

Compare the results.

And keep improving.

That's how you begin developing a prompt-engineering mindset.

One Question Before You Go

What's one task you regularly ask AI to help you with?

Writing emails? Studying? Summarizing documents? Planning your day?

Share your basic prompt in the comments, and let's see how we can improve it using the six components.

This is Part 2 of 6 in my "Prompt Engineering from Scratch" series. I work with and test open-source AI models on real documents, and I'm sharing what I learn along the way.

Follow the series if you'd like to understand AI and learn practical prompting techniques, one step at a time.

Further Reading

  • OpenAI: Prompt Engineering Guide
  • OpenAI: Best Practices for Prompt Engineering
  • Microsoft Learn: Introduction to Prompt Engineering

title: Sentinel-IR 0.2.1: When "eval" Hides Behind an Alias
description:
Sentinel-IR 0.2.1

https://www.npmjs.com/package/sentinel-ir/v/0.2.1

Thanks for support..
Release: "Sentinel-IR-MCP v0.2.2 on GitLab" (https://gitlab.com/jakubrojicek11/sentinel-ir-mcp/-/tree/v0.2.2?ref_type=tags)

Package: "sentinel-ir-mcp@0.2.2 on npm" (https://www.npmjs.com/package/sentinel-ir-mcp/v/0.2.2)

A focused improvement in AST-based analysis, six regression tests, and a closer look at two tricky JavaScript control-flow paths.

The first 30 seconds

What happens when dangerous code execution does not look like "eval()"?

Sometimes JavaScript stores "eval" in another variable and calls that variable later. A static analyzer that only looks for direct calls can miss the connection.

In Sentinel-IR 0.2.1, I focused on two situations where this can happen: "switch" fallthrough and "try/catch" control flow.

The update adds six regression tests. The goal is simple: detect the dangerous path when it is real, but avoid raising an alarm when the control flow makes that path impossible.

No magic. Just better reasoning about code.

Part 1: The 3-minute explanation for everyone

First, what does Sentinel-IR actually do?

Sentinel-IR is a small structural analysis layer for code.

Instead of sending an entire JavaScript or TypeScript source file to an AI model, it extracts structured facts using Tree-sitter.

Think of it as giving the AI a map instead of handing it an entire city.

The resulting information can include:

  • Imports and exports.
  • Routes and environment variables.
  • Filesystem, network and process operations.
  • Potentially dangerous code patterns.
  • Risk signals and their source locations.

This makes it easier for another system to reason about code without treating every line of source as equally important.

Project: "Sentinel-IR on GitLab" (https://gitlab.com/jakubrojicek11/sentinel-ir)

The problem: a function can have another name

Consider this:

const execute = eval;

execute("1 + 1");

A beginner might look for the word "eval" and assume the problem is easy.

But the function is being called through another variable.

That variable is an alias. The analyzer must understand what it refers to, not just what its name looks like.

And JavaScript has a few places where this gets complicated.

Problem one: switch fallthrough

Look at this example:

let execute = (value) => value;

switch (mode) {
case 0:
execute = eval;

case 1:
    execute("1 + 1");
    break;

}

Notice something?

There is no "break" after "case 0".

JavaScript continues into the next case. The alias assigned in the first case can therefore be used in the second one.

A simple analyzer may treat these cases as completely separate blocks and miss the connection.

Think of "break" as a stop sign. Without it, the baton keeps moving.

Problem two: try/catch

Another example:

let execute = (value) => value;

try {
execute = eval;
throw new Error("Something happened");
} catch (error) {
execute("1 + 1");
}

The alias is assigned before the exception.

When the exception moves execution into "catch", the analyzer needs to understand that the assignment can reach the code there.

But the opposite matters too.

An assignment that happens after an unconditional throw cannot influence the catch block. An assignment in a try block without a later explicit throw should not automatically make the catch block look dangerous either.

This is where false positives and false negatives start competing for attention.

What changed in 0.2.1?

The update improves those two control-flow situations.

It adds checks for:

  • Aliases carried through "switch" fallthrough.
  • "break" statements that stop that flow.
  • Later assignments that overwrite an alias.
  • Assignments before a throw that can reach "catch".
  • Throws occurring before an alias assignment.
  • Try blocks without a later explicit throw.

The result should be more accurate detection, not simply more things marked as dangerous.

Part 2: The developer section

What changed inside the AST analysis?

The important change is not a new search for the word "eval".

It is more accurate tracking of alias assignments and their visibility across control-flow paths.

The implementation contains dedicated helpers for:

  • Identifying equivalent AST nodes.
  • Tracking function and execution contexts.
  • Determining whether switch fallthrough is possible.
  • Checking whether a try-to-catch path is reachable.
  • Evaluating whether an alias assignment remains visible at a call site.

A parser detail worth mentioning

During the investigation, I encountered a subtle issue with Tree-sitter node wrappers.

Two JavaScript objects can represent the same logical AST node without being the same object reference.

Comparing them using:

nodeA === nodeB

is therefore not reliable for this kind of comparison.

The updated implementation compares the node type and source boundaries instead:

function evalAliasSameNode(a, b) {
return Boolean(
a &&
b &&
a.type === b.type &&
a.startIndex === b.startIndex &&
a.endIndex === b.endIndex
);
}

This gives the analysis a stable way to recognize the same logical node.

Source: "AST implementation in v0.2.1" (https://gitlab.com/jakubrojicek11/sentinel-ir/-/blob/v0.2.1/src/ast-facts.js)

The six regression tests

The six new cases are documented in the release test suite.

Test scenario| Expected result
Alias passes through switch fallthrough| Critical
"break" blocks the alias flow| Low
Later case overwrites the alias| Low
Alias assigned before throw reaches catch| Critical
Throw happens before assignment| Low
No later explicit throw in try| Low

The tests verify more than a boolean detection result.

They also check that:

  • The source parses successfully.
  • "operations.dynamicEval" matches the expected result.
  • The risk classification is correct.
  • The "dynamic_code" risk signal agrees with the result.

Here is the core shape of the regression assertions:

const facts = AstFacts.extract(source);

assert.equal(facts.ast, true);

assert.equal(
Boolean(facts.operations.dynamicEval),
expected
);

assert.equal(
AstFacts.riskOf(facts),
expected ? "critical" : "low"
);

assert.equal(
facts.riskSignals.some(
signal => signal.signal === "dynamic_code"
),
expected
);

Full tests: "test/ast-facts.test.js, v0.2.1" (https://gitlab.com/jakubrojicek11/sentinel-ir/-/blob/v0.2.1/test/ast-facts.test.js)

Validation results

The release work was tested locally before tagging.

Validation| Result
Existing tests| 100 passed
New regression tests| 6 passed
Complete test suite| 106/106 passed
Packaged tarball smoke checks| 7/7 passed

The package was also installed into a clean consumer project for a separate smoke test.

That matters because a successful source test does not automatically prove that the packaged artifact works after installation.

What this does not mean

Sentinel-IR is not a complete JavaScript interpreter.

Its control-flow analysis is a conservative approximation, not a full simulation of every possible runtime path. It works with structural facts extracted from source code and has documented limitations.

It should be treated as an analysis component, not as a guarantee that dangerous code will always be detected.

That distinction matters, especially when an AI agent uses the output to make decisions.

Final thoughts

Version 0.2.1 is a focused release.

It does not introduce a new language or a completely new architecture. It improves one important part of the existing analyzer: understanding when an alias to dynamic code execution can actually reach a call site.

Sometimes progress in static analysis is not about detecting more patterns.

Sometimes it is about understanding why two pieces of code are connected, and when they are not.

And occasionally, the biggest bug is hiding behind a missing "break".

Sentinel-IR 0.2.1 is released.

Project links

  • "GitLab repository" (https://gitlab.com/jakubrojicek11/sentinel-ir)
  • "Sentinel-IR 0.2.1 Release" (https://gitlab.com/jakubrojicek11/sentinel-ir/-/releases/v0.2.1)
  • "Version 0.2.0 source" (https://gitlab.com/jakubrojicek11/sentinel-ir/-/tree/v0.2.0)
  • "Version 0.2.1 source" (https://gitlab.com/jakubrojicek11/sentinel-ir/-/tree/v0.2.1)
  • "New regression tests" (https://gitlab.com/jakubrojicek11/sentinel-ir/-/blob/v0.2.1/test/ast-facts.test.js)

https://www.npmjs.com/package/sentinel-ir/v/0.2.1

Built and tested as an independent project. Feedback, edge cases and reproducible examples are welcome.

title: Most pack-opening simulators invent their pull rates — here is what ours actually look like
description:
Almost every pack-opening simulator does the same thing: the percentages are hard-coded constants. No sample size, no source date, and no way to tell whether a rate came from a published study or from someone's best guess. If the number is wrong, you cannot even tell that it is wrong.

PullSim is my attempt to build one the other way round. This post is about the awkward part: what the published samples actually support, and where they contradict themselves.

TL;DR — the three sets we model have rarest-tier rates of 0.19%, 0.56% and 0.08%. The widest is roughly 7× the narrowest. Each of those numbers rests on a single-digit count of observed packs, which is why every rate ships with the interval next to it instead of a bare percentage.

A rate without a sample size is not a measurement

Here are the three sets we model, with the sample each rate rests on:

Set Packs in the source sample Rarest modelled tier Rate Reported 95% interval
Ascended Heroes 2,000 Mega Hyper Rare 0.19% ±0.18%
Prismatic Evolutions 1,200 rarest modelled tier 0.56% ±0.41%
Phantasmal Flames 5,000 rarest modelled tier 0.08% ±0.08%

A single hard-coded table reused across every set cannot be right for all of them — 0.56% and 0.08% are the same species of claim and a factor of seven apart. That is exactly what most simulators ship.

The interval is the interesting part

Look at the Mega Hyper Rare row: 0.19% with an interval of ±0.18%. The interval is almost as large as the estimate itself. That is arithmetic, not noise. 0.0019 multiplied by 2,000 gives about 3.8 expected hits, so the entire estimate for that tier rests on roughly four packs out of two thousand.

Phantasmal Flames tells the same story from the other direction: 0.08% of 5,000 packs is also about four packs, on a sample two and a half times larger.

That is the actual state of knowledge, and printing it is the whole difference between a measurement and a number someone typed.

The per-tier schema is deliberately boring: ratePct, ciPct and samplePacks sit next to poolSize, sourceUrl and sourceDate for every tier, plus alternateRatePct wherever the source article contradicts itself. Null means not established — never zero.

Where the source articles contradict themselves

I found three cases and kept all of them visible instead of quietly picking one:

  1. Ascended Heroes, Ultra Rare — 4.81% in the main table, 20.77% in a detailed section. The main-table figure drives the simulation (it is the set-level summary); the other value is preserved as a note.
  2. Prismatic Evolutions, Double Rare — 16.51% ±2.05% in the main table, 16.94% ±0.79% in the detailed section. The main-table value drives the simulation; the alternate is preserved.
  3. Prismatic Evolutions, Specific Double Rare — the article reports 0.94%, but dividing the adopted 16.51% by its 25 cards gives about 0.66%. I could not reconcile the two, so I derive the single-card estimate myself instead of quoting the reported figure.

A dataset that hides these becomes easier to read and less true at the same time.

Normalising percentages is a bug, not a simplification

Each published tier rate is already an absolute per-pack probability inside a specific slot. The tempting fix is to divide every tier by the sum of the tiers so the numbers add up to 100%. That answers the wrong question.

Prismatic Evolutions' Special Illustration Rare rate is 2.22%. Flatten the slot so the listed hits must sum to a full outcome and that figure climbs to roughly 29%. No sample supports that. What disappeared was the ordinary reverse-holo remainder — the most common outcome in the slot. The correct model draws one random number, walks the tiers by their unmodified cumulative rates, and returns the base card when no threshold is crossed.

What the data cannot support yet

Null means not established, never zero:

  • God Packs and Demigod Packs. The Prismatic source discusses both and notes what may have been two Demigod Packs, but could not confirm them. The description is stored, the rate stays null.
  • Poké Ball Foil / Master Ball Foil. These are patterns across cards, not standalone rarity categories, so dividing by the available pool gives a deliberately conservative single-card estimate rather than an invented one.
  • Delta Reign. Listed, no confirmed rate yet.

The data is open

The whole table — per-tier sample counts, card-pool sizes, source links, and every source conflict above — is published under CC BY 4.0:

  • Dataset card: https://huggingface.co/datasets/zin294/pullsim-pull-rates
  • Source repository: https://github.com/zin294/pullsim-pull-rates

The arithmetic behind every figure, written up with the three conflicts spelled out: https://pullsim.com/how-we-calculate/

If you model pack economics, or you just want to know what you are actually buying, recompute the numbers above and tell me where they break.

title: Introducing Strongcopy, a macOS App That Confirms Your Copies
description:
What is this article about?

I recently released Strongcopy.

Strongcopy is a macOS app that lets you confirm that something was actually copied to the clipboard. Copy-and-paste mistakes are hard to notice in time. Sometimes you only realize that you failed to copy something when you go to paste it.

Strongcopy is a tool to prevent such mistakes. When data lands on the clipboard, a small badge appears for a moment so you can confirm the copy.

User experience

The Strongcopy landing page shows the small badge that appears when you copy something. You can see the Copied badge next to the mouse pointer.

The badge flashes beside the mouse pointer the moment the clipboard contents change, then disappears in under a second. The menu bar icon tells you that the app is running, and the badge tells you that your copy has just gone through.

Privacy and safety

Strongcopy doesn't read, log, or retain your clipboard contents. It needs neither Accessibility nor notification permission, and it makes no network connections. In fact, Strongcopy's codebase is small enough that you can read and understand it yourself. The source code is available on GitHub.

Strongcopy runs as a background accessory app.

It has no Dock icon; all you see is a single icon in the menu bar. Its menu offers little more than About, Open at Login, and Quit. It's a simple little app.

Feedback and requests

If you'd like, please take a look at the Strongcopy page and let me know if anything catches your attention or if there's something you'd like improved.

title: Virtual Ofrenda & Story Alchemist: remembering someone with an AI that never leaves your device
description:
What I Built

When someone dies, the memories that matter most are rarely the grand ones. They are the yellow cardigan, the Sunday porch, the way someone laughed in a thunderstorm. I wanted to build a small, quiet place to put those down.

Virtual Ofrenda & Story Alchemist is a private web app. You type or speak a few memories of someone you miss. A small open-weight model, running on your own device, turns them into a short tribute story and a poem, and builds a candlelit digital ofrenda (altar) from the things you mentioned: candles, marigolds, a favourite book, a hot mug of cider.

The theme asked for something that honors the past in the spirit of Día de los Muertos. The ofrenda tradition is much bigger than any app, so I borrowed only its simplest idea: that people stay with us while we tell their stories, and that we make small, physical places to hold them.

It has three parts:

  • Voice-to-Memory. Record a memory in the browser and it is transcribed locally with whisper.cpp. You can edit the text, or just type.
  • Story Alchemist. One tribute story and one poem, written from only what you said.
  • Altar Decorator. The model picks the objects in your memory, and each one lands on a three-tier altar and fades in, one by one.

The page says "Runs on your device" because it does. There are no accounts, no cloud APIs and no tracking. I tested it in airplane mode.

Demo

The video shows the typing path from start to finish: a memory about a fictional woman named Eleanor, then the altar, the story and the poem. I recorded it on the same phone the app runs on, and the waiting in the video is shortened, because generating a tribute takes a few minutes on this hardware.

I left voice input out of the recording. It works, but on my phone Whisper needed about two minutes for an 11-second clip, so typing is the dependable path there.

Code

nikhil-kumar-swe / virtual-ofrenda

Virtual Ofrenda & Story Alchemist

A private web app for remembering someone you have lost. You speak or type a few memories of them, and a small open-weight AI running on your own device turns those memories into a tribute story and a short poem, then decorates a candlelit digital ofrenda (altar) with the things you mentioned: candles, marigolds, a favourite book, a bright yellow raincoat.

Nothing leaves the device. There are no cloud APIs, no accounts and no tracking. The whole project was built on a low-end device with 2 GB of RAM.

Built for the DEV Hacktoberfest 2026, Week 4 challenge ("Ghost in the Machine").

  • Demo video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wHRRkFlyoqc

What it does

  1. Voice-to-Memory. Record a memory in the browser. It is transcribed locally with whisper.cpp (tiny.en) and lands in a text box where you can edit it. Typing works just as well and is the main…
View on GitHub

The repository is MIT licensed and has setup steps, the model list and the commands to start each server. The model files are not included, so the README tells you how to download them.

How I Built It

The constraint. I built this on an Android phone with 2 GB of RAM and a 32-bit ARM processor, using Termux. My first plan was a 7 to 8 billion parameter model, and then a tiny Gemma through Ollama. Ollama does not run on 32-bit ARM, and a 7B model would not have fit in that memory anyway.

The open pieces. So I went smaller and more direct:

  • Gemma 3 270M (instruction-tuned, Q8_0, about 300 MB) writes the story, the poem and the list of altar items. It runs through llama.cpp's llama-server, built from source on the phone with -DGGML_NATIVE=OFF -DGGML_LLAMAFILE=OFF. It generates about 6.7 tokens per second.
  • Whisper tiny.en through whisper.cpp's whisper-server turns speech into text.
  • Laravel with Blade, Tailwind and SQLite runs the app. A queued job calls the model, and the browser polls for the result, so the story, the poem and the altar items appear as they arrive.

Take the model away and the app has no story, no poem and no altar choices to show. Everything else is plumbing around it.

Making a tiny model behave. A 270M model will happily make things up, and in a tribute that matters. So the app does not trust it blindly:

  • Every altar item the model suggests is checked against your own text. Candles and marigolds are always added.
  • The poem is built line by line from your own sentences. A model rewrite is used only if it passes the same check.
  • Near-duplicate items are merged, so "green shards" and "frosted green shards" become one.
  • If a server is offline, you get a clear message and a retry button, not a crash.

What still goes wrong. I tested it on three memories of different lengths (about 38, 85 and 130 words). These are the honest results:

  • The stories added no invented facts, but mostly because they repeat your own words. The small model stays very close to its input. On the Eleanor memory, the story was almost word for word what I had typed.
  • It can get who did what wrong. On a short memory about a man named Marcus, the story began "I always carried a pocketful of sea glass" instead of "Marcus always carried…". In an earlier test it wrote that someone was "always ready with a smile and a gentle touch", which no one had said.
  • The poem can add imagery. It invents no people or events, but it can add phrases like "secrets held tight" that were never in the memory.
  • Altar items are sometimes ideas, not objects. The model picked "quiet invitation" as an item for Eleanor's altar, and it shows up with the default dove icon. It is in the screenshot above.

Here is Eleanor's poem, as the model wrote it:

Yellow cardigan scent
Lavender whispers on porch
Bird wings, watercolor splashes
Ending's a quiet invitation
Remembered with love.

It is not Rilke. But every image in it came from the person who typed the memory, and I would rather ship that than something more beautiful that was made up.

I built it between Oct 29 and the morning of Nov 1 (IST), before the contest deadline, and every commit was made in that window.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

A memory of someone you have lost is some of the most private writing a person will ever do. If this app had to call a hosted model, every one of those memories would leave the device and sit on someone else's server. I did not want to build that, and I would not want to use it.

Open weights made a different design possible. Gemma is small enough to run locally, and it is open enough that I could serve it myself, with no key, no account and no network. When the internet is off, it still works.

Open tools did the rest of the work. llama.cpp and whisper.cpp run on hardware that the friendlier tools do not support. My phone's 32-bit chip could not run Ollama, but it could run llama.cpp built from source. That is the difference between "this idea needs a data center" and "this idea fits in a pocket".

Openness also makes the project easy to improve. If you have a laptop, you can serve a larger open model with llama.cpp and point the same app at it by changing the model name and URL in .env. The app itself does not need to change. Nobody has to ask permission.

The Spirit of It

The constraint I started with turned out to be the idea. A small model cannot be trusted to be clever, so I made the app's promise modest: using only what you tell us. It does not try to write a beautiful eulogy for someone it never met. It gives your own words back, arranged with care, and puts a few candles around them.

There is plenty I would still like to do: a page that lists past tributes (today you return to one by its link), prompt starters for people who do not know where to begin, and a faster speech model. But the core is there, and it fits on a phone with 2 GB of RAM.

If you try it and it gets something wrong, I would like to hear about it.

Prize Categories

Gemma. The project is built around Google's open-weight Gemma 3 270M model, which does the writing and choosing in every tribute: the story, the poem and the altar items. It runs locally through llama.cpp, with no hosted API anywhere in the app.

title: How long a liquor license takes in Texas, New York City and Los Angeles (data from 1,000+ applications)
description:
Disclosure: I run PourWire, which turns state liquor license and building permit filings into a daily list of restaurants and bars that are about to open. The numbers below come from that pipeline plus the states' own open data. The CSV is public under CC BY 4.0.

The question "how long does a liquor license take" has a different answer in every state, and most answers online are guesses. Here is what the filings say as of October 2026.

The short answer

Where Agency Typical time Measured on
Texas (5 metros) TABC median 24 days from submission to issue (middle half 18 to 34) 144 MB and BG applications filed since June 2026
New York City NY State Liquor Authority applications pending a median of 118 days (middle half 62 to 212); 32% over 6 months 920 restaurant and bar applications pending in the five boroughs
Los Angeles County California ABC median 67 days from application to issue (middle half 54 to 72) 23 issued type 41, 47 and 48 licenses filed since July 2026

How it was measured

Texas. TABC publishes pending applications and issued licenses as two datasets on data.texas.gov. We matched our MB (mixed beverage) and BG (wine and beer) applications in Houston, Dallas-Fort Worth, Austin, San Antonio and Waco-Temple to the original issue date in TABC License Information by owner and permit.

New York City. The SLA queue is the story. data.ny.gov "Current SLA Pending Licenses" lists every application still in review with its received date, so the age of what is waiting today is the honest number. Of the NYC applications we have tracked since June, 25 have been issued so far, a median of 105 days after the SLA received them. That figure is capped by our start date, so the real average is higher.

Los Angeles. California ABC keeps one license number from application to issue, so filing to issue is a direct join. Every new application goes through a 30-day public notice period before ABC investigates, which is why almost nothing issues in under a month (the fastest we saw was 36 days).

Get the data

  • CSV of the wait times with sample sizes and source links: us-liquor-license-applications on GitHub (data/liquor-license-wait-times.csv), plus the last 30 days of new applications across every metro we track, refreshed weekly. Also on Hugging Face.
  • Step by step lookup guides with the license class codes explained:
    • Texas: pending TABC applications, MB, BG and FB
    • New York City: SLA wait times, classes 340, 240 and 370
    • Los Angeles: ABC wait times, types 41, 47 and 48

If you are opening a restaurant, the practical takeaway is to file early in New York, budget about two months in Los Angeles, and expect about a month in Texas. If you sell to new restaurants, the pending lists are a 1 to 4 month head start on who is about to open.

Corrections and better joins are welcome in the GitHub repo issues.

title: The Hollow Horror: Every knock has a story.
description:
Github - https://github.com/VedanshVashist/hollow-horror-archive.git
Live - https://hollow-horror-archive.vercel.app/

The Hollow

An interactive midnight archive of original ghost stories and hand-drawn haunted scenes.

Open a random door to reveal a new story and illustration. Watch the night move around the page, then scroll deeper into the archive. The project is built for the web's oldest ghosts: plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.

Features

  • Eight original, bite-sized horror stories. Each visit to Summon another story picks a different one.
  • Locally generated SVG scenes—no image service, API key, external asset host, or tracking script.
  • Scroll-linked hero parallax and random Count Orlok sightings as you move down the page.
  • Locally bundled vampire artwork, with source and license details in ASSETS.md.
  • A flying vampire, slow-moving bats and pumpkins, a foreground spider, drifting fog, and scroll-triggered reveals.
  • A motion pause button and support for the device's reduced-motion setting.
  • Responsive layout, keyboard focus styles, skip navigation, and screen-reader announcements.
  • No build step and no runtime dependencies.

Run locally

You can open index.html directly, or serve the files locally for the most reliable browser behavior:

python -m http.server 4173

Then visit http://localhost:4173. Stop the server with Ctrl+C.

Hacktoberfest

The Hollow welcomes open-source contributions all year, including during Hacktoberfest. The event format changes over time; for 2026, pull requests no longer count toward rewards. Check the official Hacktoberfest rules for the current activities and eligibility. Contributions here are welcome whether or not they qualify for an event activity.

Deploy to Vercel

  1. Push this repository to GitHub.
  2. In Vercel, choose Add New → Project and import the repository.
  3. Keep the project at the repository root. Vercel will detect a static site; leave the build command empty.
  4. Choose Deploy. The site has no environment variables to configure.

Contribute

Story ideas, new SVG scenes, accessibility improvements, responsive fixes, and documentation are welcome. Read CONTRIBUTING.md before opening a pull request. You can also start with the bug and feature-request templates under .github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/.

Good first contributions include:

  • Add a story in script.js and give it one of the existing scene types.
  • Add a new scene to hauntedLandmark() in script.js and pair it with an original story.
  • Improve a small-screen layout or a keyboard/screen-reader interaction in styles.css and index.html.
  • Improve the contribution guide or add a new issue template.

Keep stories original, keep the page usable without motion, and keep the project dependency-free unless a change has a clear reason.

Project files

File Purpose
index.html Page structure and accessible controls
styles.css Theme, responsive layout, and animation
script.js Story selection and SVG scene generation
assets/vampires/ Locally bundled vampire artwork used in scroll sightings
ASSETS.md Artwork sources and license information
LICENSE MIT license for the project's original code and materials
HACKTOBERFEST_DEV_POST.md Copy-ready DEV post draft; replace the repository and demo links before publishing
favicon.svg Project icon
vercel.json Static Vercel deployment settings

License

The project's source code and original project materials are released under the MIT License. The bundled third-party artwork has separate terms listed in ASSETS.md; it is not relicensed under the project MIT license.

Prize Categories

Best Use Of Copilot CLI

title: I don't have a single photo of my great-grandparents. So I built an altar for the people nobody remembers.
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine

There is an idea from Día de los Muertos that I keep coming back to.

A person dies three times. Once when their body stops. Once when they are buried. And a final time, when the last person who remembers them is gone.

I went looking for a photograph of my great-grandparents to put on an ofrenda. There isn't one. Nobody in my family has a single picture of them. I don't know their faces at all.

So I went to the public archives instead, and found page after page of people in the same situation as my great-grandparents. Portraits from India, a hundred years old and more, labelled with a single line:

Unidentified woman.

Milk-woman, studio photograph.

Indian Christian, India, ca. 1910.

Someone loved each of these people. Someone paid for that photograph, dressed them in their best clothes, told them to hold still. And now nobody knows their names.

So I built them an altar.

A woman photographed for a lantern slide around 1910. Her name was not recorded. Above, the photo as it survives. Below, the same photo after Living Portraits.

What I Built

Living Portraits is a digital ofrenda for old photographs. You place a photo on the altar, and it comes back to you in one short sequence I call the Return:

  1. The photo appears as it is today: faded, creased, black and white.
  2. A thin line of candlelight passes down the photo and mends it.
  3. Colour spreads outward from the person's face, the way a memory comes back.
  4. The portrait settles into depth. Move your cursor, or tilt your phone, and it shifts gently, as if you were standing in front of a real print, while candlelight flickers brighter on whatever is nearest to you.

Under every portrait is everything we know about them, which is often almost nothing. A name if there is one. Her name was not recorded if there isn't. A link to the archive the photo came from and its licence, so you can check it is real. And a number showing how closely the restored face still matches the original.

Light a candle

If the final death comes when no one remembers you, the smallest thing we can do is remember.

Under each portrait there is one button: Light a candle. A fourth candle catches on the altar's shelf, and the server keeps count, one candle per visitor. It isn't much. But a woman whose name nobody wrote down, a hundred years ago, now has a number next to her that only goes up.

You can also place your own family's photos on the altar, and save their Return as a short video to send to the family group.

The Version I Threw Away

My first version animated the faces. One open-source model, a few lines of code, and Srinivasa Ramanujan's portrait from 1913 turned its head and broke into a wide, toothy grin.

It looked impressive for about two seconds. Then it felt scary and awkward. A man who never smiled like that for any camera was smiling at me because a model decided he should. These are real people. They can't agree to be made to smile for us, and they can't be asked.

So I deleted it. In Living Portraits the face is never moved, never re-posed and never given words. The photo comes back to life through light, colour and depth, the way a real photograph does when you carry it to a window. Every download is labelled AI-restored.

That decision changed the whole project, and I think it made it better.

Demo

Try it live: http://139.59.7.49 (light a candle for someone while you're there)

Watch the 68-second demo: demo video. A photo is placed on the altar, processed live on DigitalOcean, returns, and gets its first candle. The narration was generated with ElevenLabs.

Here is a photo being placed on the altar and processed live on the DigitalOcean server:

How It Works

Four open-source models run one after another on a single small server. The browser does the rest.

Mend. GFPGAN v1.4 repairs blur, scratches and damage on the face. I blend its output with the original at 60% instead of 100%, so the person keeps their own face rather than a polished stranger's.

Colour. DDColor predicts colour for black-and-white and sepia prints. It only predicts the colour; every bit of light and detail comes from the original photograph.

Depth. Depth Anything V2 estimates how near or far each part of the photo is. That depth map is what lets the portrait shift when you move, and what makes the candlelight fall on the face before the wall behind it.

Check. A face-recognition model (ArcFace, through facexlib) compares the face before and after restoration, and that score is printed under every portrait.

The server, a small FastAPI app, sends back three images: the photo as it was, the photo restored, and the depth map. The Return itself is a short WebGL shader running in your browser. The candlelight sweep, the colour spreading out from the face (located by the face detector), the depth and the flicker are all drawn live, so the original photo is never baked into a video.

Three Problems I Didn't Expect

1. Restoration makes everyone look like a stranger

Face-restoration models are trained to make faces look good, and "good" drifts toward young, smooth and symmetrical. For a stranger's photo, that's fine. For someone who can't tell you what they really looked like, it's a quiet kind of erasure.

So I measure it. The ArcFace check compares the face before and after for every photo. Across the eleven archive portraits I tested, ten scored 0.88 or higher, and the median was 0.94. On this scale, around 0.5 already means "probably the same person". The one low score, 0.74, was a side profile, which face models struggle with in general.

2. Sepia is not colour

Most 19th-century portraits are albumen prints: brown ink on cream paper, not black on white. My first black-and-white detector looked at saturation, decided these prints were already in colour, and skipped them. Half of my archive photos came back untouched.

The fix was to stop asking "is there colour?" and ask "does the colour depend on anything except brightness?" In a toned print, dark means brown and light means cream, and that's all. So I fit colour as a function of brightness and look at what's left over:

def is_black_and_white(img_bgr):
    small = cv2.resize(img_bgr, (256, 256))
    lab = cv2.cvtColor(small, cv2.COLOR_BGR2LAB).reshape(-1, 3).astype(np.float32)
    L, a, b = lab[:, 0] / 255, lab[:, 1], lab[:, 2]
    X = np.stack([np.ones_like(L), L, L * L, L ** 3], 1)   # colour as a curve of brightness
    leftover = sum(np.std(c - X @ np.linalg.lstsq(X, c, rcond=None)[0]) for c in (a, b))
    return leftover < 4.0   # sepia and grey prints leave almost nothing behind

Real colour photos leave a lot behind. Sepia and grey prints leave almost nothing. It now sorts every archive photo I have correctly.

3. The colours were too loud

DDColor's first results were vivid in a way old photographs never are: magenta suits, orange hands. I scale the predicted colour back by a quarter. The portraits look less like an advert and more like a hand-tinted print, which is closer to the truth of the era.

Built on DigitalOcean

The whole altar lives on one DigitalOcean CPU-Optimized Droplet, and DigitalOcean is a big part of why one person could build and ship this in a weekend.

It sits close to the people it's for. The portraits are from India, and so are many of the families I hope will use it, so the Droplet runs in DigitalOcean's Bangalore region.

Dedicated cores, steady timing. Restoring a photo is heavy, continuous number-crunching. On a CPU-Optimized Droplet with 4 dedicated vCPUs, a photo takes about 12 seconds, every time, with no noisy neighbours slowing it down.

One machine runs everything. The four models, the FastAPI server, the candle counts and the web page itself all live on the same Droplet as a single systemd service. There is no separate GPU service, no third-party AI API, and nothing else to keep in sync.

From a blank Droplet to live with one script. setup.sh in the repo installs the models on a fresh Ubuntu Droplet, and the service file keeps the app running across restarts. Every update during the build was a copy and a service restart.

It doesn't need a GPU. I planned to rent a GPU Droplet. Then I removed the face animation, the heaviest model, and found everything else fits comfortably on CPU: about 12 seconds per photo on the Droplet, against about 5 seconds on my laptop's 4 GB RTX 3050.

The cost is small and predictable. The Droplet costs $0.125 an hour, which works out to roughly $0.0004 of compute per photo, and the whole build ran on DigitalOcean's Hacktoberfest credit.

That matters for who can use this. A family, a small local archive or a school history project can run their own altar for a few dollars a day, or switch it off when no one is visiting.

Where It Falls Short

  • Colour is a guess. DDColor doesn't know what colour her sari really was. The page says so under every portrait.
  • Side profiles are harder. Face models are trained mostly on faces looking at the camera.
  • Faded sepia prints get only a hint of colour, because the paper tone dominates.
  • Hand-tinted prints are left alone. One 1860s portrait was read as already coloured. It may well be hand-tinted, so leaving it untouched is the honest result.

Why Open Source Matters Here

Commercial apps already "bring old photos to life". To use them, you upload your family's photographs to a company's servers, usually on a subscription, and accept whatever the model decides to do to the faces of people who can't object.

Every decision that shaped this project was only possible because the models were open:

  • When face animation felt wrong, I could remove it.
  • When restoration drifted away from the real face, I could measure it and turn it down.
  • When the colours were too loud, I could change them.
  • When sepia prints were skipped, I could fix the detector that a closed API would have hidden from me.

And the photographs never leave a server the family controls. Nothing is sent to an AI company, and nothing can be taken away by a subscription ending or an app shutting down. A memory deserves at least that.

The Moment It Landed

Her first candle was lit while I was recording the demo.

The script uploaded a portrait from the 1880s, a young woman in her best sari with every ornament she owned, captioned Her name was not recorded. The Return played, the colour came back into her face, and then the button was pressed and the count changed from nothing to 1 candle lit.

It's a small number. But it's one more than she had yesterday. Her portrait is in the gallery on the live site. If you visit, light one for her.

Prize Categories

Best Use of DigitalOcean. The entire app, from the four models to the API, the candle counts and the page, runs on one DigitalOcean CPU-Optimized Droplet, deployed with the setup script and systemd service in the repo. It shows that open-source image models don't need a GPU to be useful to a family.

Best Use of ElevenLabs. The demo's narration was generated with ElevenLabs, and the repo includes the script and the tools that cut the screen recording to each narrated paragraph.

Code

Tanhaker / living-portraits

Restore, colour and give depth to old family photos for the ofrenda. Open-source AI, the face is never changed.

Living Portraits

Bring an old family photo to the ofrenda. Living Portraits mends its creases, returns its colour and gives it depth, using only open-source models on a server you control.

The face is never moved, re-posed or given words. The photo comes back to life through light, colour and depth instead.

Built for the DEV Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge, Week 4: Ghost in the Machine.

The Return

When a photo is placed on the altar, the page plays one short sequence on a WebGL canvas:

  1. The photo appears as it is today: faded, creased, black and white.
  2. A line of candlelight sweeps down and mends it.
  3. Colour blooms outward from the person's face.
  4. The portrait settles into depth. It shifts gently with your cursor or as you tilt your phone and candlelight flickers brighter on what is nearer.

The page can record the Return as a video to…

View on GitHub

Built with help from an AI coding assistant. Every portrait shown is public domain or CC0, from Wikimedia Commons, with sources listed in the repository README.

title: I Built IntentChord to Bring Human Control to AI Coding Agents — Contributors Welcome
description:
AI coding agents can write code, modify files, and report that a task is complete.

But a successful-looking response doesn't necessarily answer some important questions:

  • Was the agent working on the correct source?
  • Was the change within the approved scope?
  • Is the reported result supported by actual evidence?
  • Who decides whether the work is accepted?

These questions led me to build IntentChord.

What is IntentChord?

IntentChord is a local-first, human-governed development workflow that connects an owner's intent to workspace context, confirmed scope, agent-specific execution contracts, evidence-based review, and a final human decision.

Its central principle is simple:

An AI agent's report is not the same as verified execution evidence, and an agent's claim of success is not the owner's approval.

What's in the project?

The repository includes:

  • Task and scope authority management
  • Workspace discovery, indexing, and source-context foundations
  • Governed execution contracts for Codex, Claude Code, and Gemini CLI
  • Execution evidence and report-verification logic
  • Human review and decision workflows
  • A Next.js, React, TypeScript, and PostgreSQL-based application

The project is still evolving and is not presented as a production-certified system.

I'm opening the project to contributors

I've made the source public because I'd like to develop IntentChord with other developers.

I'm particularly interested in contributions involving code quality, testing, developer onboarding, architecture discussions, and improvements to the human-in-the-loop workflow.

There are already beginner-friendly and documentation tasks available in GitHub Issues.

Repository: https://github.com/hesham-m/IntentChord

Contribution opportunities: https://github.com/hesham-m/IntentChord/issues

The project is source-available under PolyForm Noncommercial 1.0.0, rather than an OSI-approved open-source license. Please review the repository's license and contribution guidelines before contributing.

I'd be interested to hear how other developers handle agent authority, scope changes, and evidence verification in their AI-assisted development workflows.

What would you improve or challenge in this approach?
