title: 👻 RepoGhost: Bringing Forgotten Codebases Back to Life with Local AI
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine.

What I Built

I built RepoGhost, a local AI-powered repository analyzer designed to bring forgotten and abandoned codebases back to life.

Every repository has a story, but understanding an unfamiliar project can sometimes feel like exploring a haunted house. There may be unfinished tasks, confusing file structures, undocumented functions, and code that nobody remembers writing.

That's where RepoGhost comes in! 👻

Users can upload a repository as a ZIP file, and RepoGhost scans it to discover:

  • Repository Overview: Detects source files, programming languages, and project structure.
  • Forgotten Tasks: Finds TODO, FIXME, and HACK comments that may have been left behind.
  • Python Syntax Findings: Identifies basic Python syntax issues.
  • Chat with the Ghost: Ask questions about the repository and get AI-powered explanations.
  • Haunted Project Report: Generates an AI-assisted report to help developers understand their codebase.

I interpreted the theme Ghost in the Machine as giving a voice to forgotten codebases. RepoGhost acts like a friendly ghost that helps developers understand what is happening inside a project, even when its original developers are no longer around.

Demo

🎥 Video Demo:

Note: RepoGhost is designed primarily for local execution, so the demo can showcase the application running on your machine.

Code

💻 GitHub Repository: https://github.com/Sourodip1804/RepoGhost

Contributions, feedback, and suggestions are welcome!

How I Built It

I built RepoGhost using a combination of open-source technologies and local AI inference.

AI Model:

  • Qwen2.5:3B – An open-weight language model used to understand repository context, answer questions, explain code, and generate reports.
  • Ollama – Runs the model locally, allowing RepoGhost to communicate with the AI without depending on a hosted AI API.

Backend:

  • Python
  • FastAPI
  • Repository scanning and file analysis
  • ZIP extraction and processing
  • REST API endpoints for uploading repositories, chatting, and generating reports

Frontend:

  • React.js
  • Vite
  • CSS
  • Lucide React icons

How it works:

  1. The developer uploads a repository ZIP file.
  2. The FastAPI backend safely extracts and scans the repository.
  3. RepoGhost identifies programming languages, source files, and unfinished task markers.
  4. Relevant repository context is prepared for the AI model.
  5. Qwen2.5:3B processes the context through Ollama and generates explanations or answers.
  6. The frontend displays scan results, AI conversations, and the generated project report.

One of my main goals was to keep the AI workflow local. The project does not need a paid cloud AI API to perform its core AI tasks.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

Open innovation made this project possible in a way that would have been difficult to achieve with a closed AI API alone.

Using an open-weight model like Qwen2.5:3B with Ollama gave me the opportunity to experiment with local AI inference, understand how models interact with application backends, and build an AI-powered tool without depending on paid API access.

It also offers some important advantages:

  • Privacy: Repository source code can remain on the developer's machine when using the local setup.
  • Accessibility: Developers can experiment without needing a paid AI API subscription.
  • Customization: The model and AI workflow can be modified according to project requirements.
  • Transparency: Developers have more control over the tools and infrastructure powering their AI applications.
  • Community: Open-source models and frameworks make it easier for developers to learn, contribute, and build on existing work.

For me, open innovation is not just about using free tools. It is about having the freedom to understand, experiment, modify, and build something useful.

The Spirit of It

The most interesting part of building RepoGhost was thinking about how much knowledge gets trapped inside old repositories.

A developer might leave a project unfinished, forget how a particular function works, or return to an old codebase after months or years.

Instead of manually exploring every file, imagine asking:

"Hey Ghost, what is this project actually doing?"

And getting an explanation from the code itself.

That is the idea behind RepoGhost: every codebase deserves a second life.

Prize Categories

  • Open-Source AI Challenge – Ghost in the Machine (Week 4)

Building RepoGhost has been a great learning experience. I explored local LLM integration, Ollama, FastAPI, React, repository analysis, and the practical challenges of connecting an AI model with a real application.

There is still plenty of room to improve, and I would love to hear your feedback and suggestions!

Let's bring forgotten codebases back to life. 👻

Hacktoberfest #OpenSourceAI #Ollama #Qwen #React #Python #FastAPI #OpenSource #AI

title: Is Sellzivo Legit or a Scam? An Honest Look Before You Buy
description:
Is Sellzivo Legit or a Scam? An Honest Look Before You Buy

Short answer

Sellzivo is a real, live online store that sells discounted AI tools and software subscriptions. It is not a fake storefront with no product behind it: the shop at sellzivo.com/shop is live, orders go through a real checkout, and support runs through its Telegram shop. That said, it is an independent reseller, it is a relatively new store, and its products are digital — so it is worth understanding exactly what you are buying before you pay. This article sticks to verifiable facts, not hype.

What Sellzivo actually is

Sellzivo is a digital store for AI tools and software subscriptions — things like ChatGPT, Canva, Notion, Adobe, ElevenLabs and similar tools — sold as team seats and premium plans, with instant delivery and guest checkout. You can pay by card or crypto, and there is a reseller program for people who want to sell the same products themselves.

The business is based in South Jordan, Utah, United States. Its contact email is support@sellzivo.com, its shop is at https://sellzivo.com/shop, and its Telegram shop is https://t.me/sellzivobot.

Sellzivo is an independent reseller and is not affiliated with ChatGPT, Canva, Notion, Adobe, ElevenLabs, or any other brand it sells. That matters: you are buying a seat, plan, or access arrangement through a reseller, not buying directly from the brand itself.

How buying from Sellzivo works

  1. Browse the shop and open the product page for the plan you want. Read the full description on that page — it tells you what kind of access you are getting.
  2. Check out as a guest on the website, or order through the Telegram shop.
  3. Delivery is instant in the normal case, and the delivery details are shown on the product page.
  4. If anything is unclear, ask support on Telegram before you pay, not after.

That last point is the most useful habit with any reseller: a genuine seller can explain, before payment, exactly what you will receive.

Checks anyone can do in two minutes

  • Open the shop yourself: https://sellzivo.com/shop. A scam storefront usually cannot sustain a full, browsable catalog with working product pages.
  • Check the support route: https://t.me/sellzivobot. Be careful with lookalikes — only the official shop link and the official bot are Sellzivo. Anyone messaging you from a different handle claiming to be Sellzivo is not verified.
  • Read the refund policy before you buy. Sellzivo's policy is no returns and no refunds on digital products. That is a strict policy, and it is stated openly — but it also means you should be sure about the product before paying, because there is no change-of-mind refund.
  • Start small. If you are trying Sellzivo for the first time, buy one product first, confirm delivery and access work as described, and only then buy more.

The honest limitations

No honest "is it legit" article should skip the downsides, so here they are:

  • Sellzivo is a newer store, not a decade-old retailer. Newer does not mean fake, but it does mean there is less long-term track record to lean on.
  • Products are digital, so the usual "return it in the box" safety net does not exist. The no-returns, no-refunds policy is the trade-off for the lower price.
  • Some products are coupon codes or seats for your own account, and those need to be redeemed promptly after purchase. Read the product page for any activation window.
  • Because Sellzivo resells rather than owns these brands, availability and plan details can change. The product page at the time you buy is the description that counts.

None of that is, on its own, a sign of a scam. It is the normal shape of a discount reseller — and it is exactly why the "read the page, ask first, start small" advice matters.

Red flags that would change the answer

If any of these showed up, it would be a reason to stop and stay away: a seller asking you to pay to a personal wallet or account outside the official shop, a "Sellzivo" account on Telegram or social media that is not linked from sellzivo.com, pressure to pay quickly for a "today only" deal that is not on the shop itself, or a refusal to explain what access you will receive before payment. As of this writing, the official shop and bot do not work that way.

Verdict

Is Sellzivo legit? On the publicly verifiable facts — a live store, a working checkout, a named support channel, and an openly stated digital-products policy — yes, it is a legitimate reseller storefront, not a scam site. Is it risk-free? No reseller purchase is. Go in with the checklist above: use only the official shop and bot, read the product page, understand the no-refund policy, and start with a single order.

title: What if the history of a codebase could help explain the code nobody wants to touch?
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine

NecroGit: A Little Séance for Legacy Code

Every codebase has a past.

Sometimes that past is a beautifully maintained changelog. Sometimes it is a function named do_not_delete_final2(), three deprecated imports, and a Git history that only the person who wrote it really understood.

Then that person leaves.

The code stays.

For Week 4's Ghost in the Machine challenge, I built NecroGit: a command-line tool that treats legacy-code maintenance like a bit of software archaeology. It looks for signs of bitrot, examines Git history for clues about how a project evolved, and uses an open-weight language model to help explain unfamiliar code and propose repairs.

The goal isn't to pretend a model can bring a developer back from the dead. It's to make the traces they left behind more useful to the next person who has to maintain the project.

What I Built

NecroGit is a Python CLI for developers inheriting repositories they didn't write.

It brings a few kinds of investigation into one workflow:

  • Inspect: scan Python files for known deprecated APIs and suspicious legacy patterns.
  • Summon: examine Git commits and author activity for historical context.
  • Explain: ask a language model to explain an unfamiliar function using the source and available repository context.
  • Patch: generate a proposed diff that a developer can review before applying.
  • Memory: keep a small repository dossier so useful context can carry between sessions.

The part I care about most is the connection between these steps. Finding a deprecated import is useful. Understanding why the surrounding code exists is better. Getting a proposed change that you can inspect, test, and reject if necessary is better still.

NecroGit is meant to assist the maintainer, not replace their judgment. Git history can offer clues about a previous developer's habits; it cannot tell us with certainty what that person intended. Likewise, an AI-generated patch is a proposal, not proof that the fix is correct.

Demo

Repository: github.com/avrojitduttaj/necrogit

The quickest way to see the workflow is to install the project in a Python environment, open a repository in your terminal, and try the inspection command:

necrogit inspect .

Then explore the other commands with:

necrogit --help
necrogit summon .
necrogit memory

The exact arguments for explain and patch depend on the installed CLI version; check each command's --help before running it.

Live demo / walkthrough: [Add a verified demo URL or video here]

I don't want to pass off a mockup as a working demo, so this post links to the source repository. If I add a hosted walkthrough, I'll put the verified URL here.

Code

The source is available here:

Explore NecroGit on GitHub

Live Deployment: NecroGit — The Repository Medium

A few of the implementation choices:

  • Python's ast module provides a structured way to inspect source code without executing it.
  • GitPython reads repository history and commit metadata.
  • Click provides the command-line interface, with Rich for readable terminal output.
  • HTTPX connects the engine to an OpenAI-compatible local model endpoint.
  • Repository dossiers can be stored locally, with optional Backboard integration in the project.

The intent is to keep the first step—static inspection—useful even when an AI model isn't available. The AI-assisted commands should fail clearly when inference isn't configured, rather than pretending they succeeded.

How I Built It

I built NecroGit around a simple question: what if Git history were more than a list of commits?

The scanner handles the deterministic part. It parses Python syntax and checks for patterns the tool knows about. The Git-history component gathers evidence such as authorship, commit dates, and commit messages. The AI engine can then use the available code and context to generate an explanation or a proposed diff.

For the open-model path, NecroGit is designed to work with Gemma 2 through Ollama, using a local OpenAI-compatible endpoint. That makes it possible to experiment with the model on your own machine rather than making a hosted, closed API the only way to run the project.

This separation matters:

  1. Rules find known patterns. They are predictable, testable, and don't need a model.
  2. Git history supplies evidence. It gives context, but it isn't a source of certainty about intent.
  3. The model helps interpret and draft. It can explain code and suggest changes, but its output still needs review and tests.

During development, I also added tests for deprecated-import detection, Git and non-Git directories, prompt construction, connection failures, local memory persistence, and CLI behavior. Those tests have been useful for catching mismatches between the intended user experience and what the command actually does.

One lesson from building a CLI is that a feature isn't finished just because the Python function works. Packaging, command registration, Windows paths, model endpoints, and readable error messages are all part of the product. I'm still tightening those edges, and I want to be honest about that rather than call the tool production-ready before it earns the label.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

For a tool that reads source code, where inference happens is part of the design.

A developer may be working with a private repository, a client's code, or an abandoned internal service. Sending that code to an external API should never be an invisible default. A local model gives the developer a path to keep inference on their own machine, subject to how they've configured the rest of their environment.

Open-weight models also make the system more replaceable. Developers can experiment with different models and local runtimes instead of tying the whole experience to one provider's API, pricing, or product decisions.

And the non-AI parts remain ordinary, inspectable software. The scanner's rules can be read and tested. The Git-history analysis can be audited. A proposed patch is visible as a diff.

That doesn't mean every setup is automatically offline or private: optional integrations and telemetry need to be configured and disclosed carefully. But open tooling gives developers more control over those trade-offs—and for a maintenance tool that may touch sensitive code, that control is important.

My Agent Session

[https://dev.to/agent_sessions/finding-the-necrogit-devrelay-session-link-xmpym5]

This section is optional. I will only link a real saved session; I won't invent an embed or session URL.

The Spirit of It

There's something eerie about opening a repository and finding a whole history of decisions with nobody left to explain them.

A commit message says “temporary workaround.” The workaround is still there six years later. A function has a strange name because it once fixed a production incident. A dependency is obsolete, but nobody remembers which behavior relied on it.

The ghost isn't really the old developer. It's the missing context.

NecroGit is my attempt to make that context a little easier to recover—from the code, from the commit history, and from the tools we can run ourselves. Not to resurrect the past exactly as it was, but to help the next maintainer move forward without blindly deleting it.

🏆 Prize Categories I'm Targeting

  • [ ] Overall Challenge Winner — $250

    NecroGit aims to make legacy-code maintenance easier by combining Git-history archaeology, AI-assisted code explanations, and safer patch proposals.

  • [ ] Best Use of Gemma — $200

    Gemma 2 powers NecroGit's local AI inference workflow, helping explain historical design decisions and draft modernization patches while keeping source code on the developer's machine.

  • [ ] Best Use of Backboard — $100

    NecroGit implements persistent repository dossiers, with local JSON storage and an optional Backboard synchronization path for retaining maintainer context across sessions.

  • [ ] Best Use of Sentry Agent Tracing — $100

    NecroGit includes instrumentation for tracing AI inference and memory operations, with breadcrumbs and structured context to help diagnose the resurrection workflow.

Deployment

NecroGit's web workbench is deployed on Render to make the project website accessible online. Render is used as a hosting and deployment platform, not as an AI integration.

The core NecroGit CLI remains a local developer tool, while the hosted website serves as the public-facing project experience.

Built by @avrojitduttaj.

If you've inherited a codebase that feels haunted, I'd love to know: what's the strangest piece of legacy code you've had to explain?

title: Afterlight: The Memory Keeper --- A Local-First AI Sanctuary for Stories & Remembrance
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge
Week 4: Ghost in the
Machine.

What I Built

Afterlight: The Memory Keeper is a privacy-first, local-first AI
memory preservation platform created individually for Hacktoberfest Week
4: Ghost in the Machine.

Afterlight helps people preserve and rediscover meaningful stories,
photographs, voice recordings, family traditions, and personal memories.
It brings together two interpretations of the challenge theme:

  1. Ghost in the Machine: Forgotten stories and recordings can feel like voices trapped in old photographs, tapes, and folders. Afterlight uses local AI to transcribe, organize, search, and creatively reinterpret saved memories.
  2. Día de los Muertos: The Virtual Ofrenda offers a customizable digital space to honor loved ones through photographs, remembrance messages, favorite foods, songs, flowers, traditions, and associated stories.

Afterlight is designed around a simple principle:

Your memories belong to you. Your stories should not depend on a
server you do not control.

The Problem

Family stories and personal histories are often scattered across paper
notes, old photographs, audio recordings, phones, and disconnected
folders. Finding a particular detail can be difficult, and valuable oral
histories may remain inaccessible because they have never been
transcribed or organized.

At the same time, sending intimate memories, photographs, and voice
recordings to third-party AI services can create privacy and
data-ownership concerns. Hosted AI services can also introduce recurring
usage costs and dependence on a provider's availability, pricing, and
terms.

The Solution

Afterlight brings memory preservation and AI-assisted discovery into a
local-first application:

  • Memory Vault: Preserve stories, photographs, dates, people, locations, tags, and personal experiences in an organized archive.
  • Voice of the Past: Transcribe uploaded oral-history recordings with locally running speech recognition, review the transcript, and save it with related memories.
  • AI Memory Companion: Ask natural-language questions about saved memories. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) finds relevant records and presents the supporting sources.
  • Virtual Ofrenda: Create a customizable Día de los Muertos-inspired remembrance altar with portraits, candles, marigold-inspired decorations, offerings, and tribute messages.
  • Ghost Echoes: Create atmospheric fictional stories inspired by selected memories, with a clear notice that generated stories are creative fiction---not real communications from deceased people.
  • Memory Timeline: Explore saved stories and events chronologically.
  • Privacy & Model Control Center: Inspect the local AI runtime, available models, local data controls, export options, and setup status.

The application is designed to keep personal records and AI inference on
the user's machine. Any offline claims in this submission should reflect
the exact features verified with the network disconnected.

📖 Executive Summary

AFTERLIGHT is a privacy-first, locally powered AI memory preservation platform developed for the Hacktoberfest Week 4 Challenge — "Ghost in the Machine".

It unifies two poignant themes:

  1. The Ghost in the Machine: Awakening forgotten family memories, cassette recordings, and heirloom photographs through local open-source AI retrieval and atmospheric creative storytelling.
  2. Día de los Muertos (Day of the Dead): Honoring departed ancestors through an interactive, culturally reverent virtual altar (ofrenda) adorned with flickering candlelight physics, golden cempasúchil petals, traditional offerings, and printable tribute keepsakes.

Every AI capability in Afterlight—from speech-to-text audio transcription and dense semantic vector retrieval to conversational memory companion RAG—runs 100% locally on your own machine using open-weight models (Qwen2.5 3B, faster-whisper, ChromaDB).

How I Built It

Afterlight uses a modular, local-first architecture. The frontend
communicates with a local FastAPI backend. The backend manages
persistent records, local files, retrieval, transcription, and requests
to the local model runtime.

1. Frontend & Experience

  • Framework: React with TypeScript and Vite.
  • Styling: Tailwind CSS with a dark, cinematic visual identity.
  • Visual direction: Midnight backgrounds, warm amber and candlelight accents, marigold-inspired details, framed photographs, and restrained atmospheric animation.
  • Interface: Responsive pages for the dashboard, Memory Vault, Voice of the Past, AI Memory Companion, Virtual Ofrenda, Ghost Echoes, Memory Timeline, and privacy controls.

2. Backend & Local Persistence

  • Backend: Python and FastAPI for local REST APIs.
  • Database: SQLite for structured memory records, people, photographs, recordings, transcripts, ofrendas, stories, and related metadata.
  • File storage: Photographs and audio are stored as local files; the database stores their metadata and local references rather than Base64 copies.
  • Validation: Pydantic schemas and file validation are used at API boundaries.
  • Data ownership: Local records can be backed up and exported by the user.

3. Open-Weight AI & Local Inference

  • Runtime: Ollama provides a local interface for running compatible open-weight language models.
  • Default model target: qwen2.5:3b (or another compatible model selected in the application).
  • Model flexibility: The AI service is separated behind a model adapter so compatible local models can be changed without rewriting feature logic.
  • AI tasks: Memory summaries, contextual question answering, categorization, remembrance-writing assistance, and fictional story generation.
  • No mandatory hosted LLM: The core AI design does not require OpenAI, Gemini, Claude, or another hosted LLM API.

Model availability, model licenses, and actual tested model names should
be confirmed against the implementation before publishing.

4. Local Speech Recognition

  • Engine: faster-whisper, using a locally available Whisper model.
  • Workflow: Upload audio → transcribe locally → review/edit transcript → save transcript and associate it with a memory.
  • Formats: Support depends on the installed FFmpeg configuration and the formats enabled by the application.
  • Privacy: Audio is processed locally when the local transcription pipeline and model are installed.

5. Semantic Search & Grounded Memory Companion

  • Embeddings: A locally installed sentence-transformers model, such as all-MiniLM-L6-v2.
  • Vector store: ChromaDB for semantic retrieval.
  • Retrieval flow: Embed the question → retrieve relevant memory chunks → load their source records → provide context to the local LLM → return an answer with source references.
  • Grounding: The assistant should state when saved memories do not contain enough information. It should not present unsupported model-generated details as facts.
  • Source visibility: Responses should link to the memory records used as context, allowing users to inspect the original material.

6. Creative Storytelling & Remembrance

  • Ghost Echoes: Generates original atmospheric fiction inspired by user-selected memories.
  • Virtual Ofrenda: Provides a customizable digital remembrance space for portraits, stories, offerings, and messages.
  • Ethical boundary: Generated stories are clearly labeled as fiction. The application does not claim to contact, recreate, or speak for deceased people.
  • Cultural respect: Ofrenda elements are customizable; the experience does not assume that every user follows the same traditions.

7. Testing & Verification

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

For Afterlight, open innovation is directly connected to privacy,
ownership, accessibility, and long-term control.

Memories can include intimate family stories, personal photographs, and
recordings of people who trusted us with their words. A
memory-preservation tool should not require those materials to be sent
to a third-party AI provider.

1. Privacy & Data Sovereignty

Local inference allows supported AI operations to run on the user's own
machine. Afterlight is designed to keep its memory archive, photographs,
recordings, and local database under the user's control rather than
making a hosted AI service the default destination for personal
material.

2. Model Choice & Freedom to Experiment

A local model adapter makes it possible to test and switch between
compatible models. Developers can compare model quality, hardware
requirements, languages, and response behavior without redesigning the
entire application around one provider.

3. Offline Access & Independence

Once the application dependencies, model weights, and required assets
have been downloaded, supported local workflows can operate without an
internet connection. This reduces dependence on a hosted service being
available whenever someone wants to revisit a memory.

4. Accessibility Without Per-Request AI Fees

Local inference avoids mandatory per-request hosted LLM charges. It does
not mean the application has no costs: users still need suitable
hardware, storage, electricity, and initial downloads. However, it gives
people another way to use AI without a recurring API bill.

5. Community Adaptation & Longevity

An open implementation can be inspected, modified, extended, and adapted
by contributors. Communities can experiment with language support,
oral-history workflows, accessibility improvements, and culturally
appropriate remembrance experiences.

Honest Technical Trade-offs

  • Hardware: Local inference performance depends on RAM, CPU/GPU, quantization, and model size.
  • Storage: Model weights, audio recordings, photographs, and vector indexes require disk space.
  • Initial setup: Ollama, Python packages, frontend dependencies, and model assets generally need to be installed or downloaded before offline use.
  • Performance: CPU-only transcription and LLM inference may take longer than hosted GPU services.
  • Model licensing: Each model has its own license and usage conditions. Check and document the exact license of every model distributed or recommended.
  • Offline scope: Do not describe the entire application as offline unless every claimed workflow has been tested without network access.

What Worked Better With an Open-Based Approach?

The local-first architecture makes privacy and model choice design
properties rather than optional settings in a hosted service. It also
allows the project to keep working with locally installed models without
requiring a particular commercial AI provider's API.

title: From a Simple "Mark as Seen" to Feedgrab & Ghostify: Story of My Life!
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine

TL;DR: I keep seeing the same posts on most of the DEV home feed tabs: Discover, Following and Curated.

Wanted to fix it by implementing a simple Mark as Seen browser extension. Then one thing led to another, and I ended up building three projects: one already abandoned, and two ongoing (Feedgrab & Ghostify).

Note for users: This is still under development, so if you see errors, please look for updates: https://github.com/SweaDev/ghostify/releases

Note for judges: v1.0.0 was completed within the submission period; later releases are updates.

Backstory

These days, I spend too much time on DEV.

  • Deleted my old X/Twitter account because it gives me a headache! Created a new one only as a placeholder.
  • Deactivated my Facebook account, because it's… well, that's a story for another day!

So most of the time I spend online is here on DEV and YouTube.

But the problem with DEV (and YouTube too) is that I keep seeing the same posts in the feed!

Open DEV in the morning: there's that post. Open it at lunch: there it is again. Open it at night: guess who's back! I've read it. I've reacted to it. I may have even commented on it. Still there, staring at me like it hasn't been introduced yet.

So on October 26, I did what any sane developer would do: I opened my editor instead of closing the tab.

Attempt #1: myDEV (RIP 🪦)

The plan was simple:

  • Put a ✓ button on every post card, right next to Bookmark.
  • Click it, and the post disappears from the feed and goes into a new myDEV tab.
  • Done. Go back to reading.

And it worked! For about an hour. Then I opened YouTube and saw the same video for the 14th time this week, and realized myDEV only knew how to read one site, with selectors I hard-coded by hand. The moment DEV changes a class name, it's dead. And for YouTube, I'd have to start over.

It took me a few days to admit it, but today I finally archived it. Rest in peace, myDEV. You were too specific for this world.

Attempt #2: Feedgrab

What I actually needed wasn't a DEV plugin. I needed something that could look at any page and say: "this is a feed, these are the items, and this one is the same item you saw before, even after infinite scroll re-rendered it."

That became Feedgrab, a TypeScript library that:

  • detects feeds on a page (structural heuristics, optionally refined by an LLM), or takes CSS/XPath selectors you type;
  • lets you confirm or fix its guesses in a Shadow DOM overlay;
  • turns the feed into one de-duplicated stream of items that keeps up with infinite scroll;
  • never removes anything unless you ask it to.

It runs in browser extensions, headless browsers and on the server, with the same API.

Attempt #3: Ghostify

And then, finally, the thing I wanted in the first place. On top of Feedgrab. With a ghost. 👻

What I Built

Ghostify is a browser extension (Chrome + Firefox) for feeds that keep showing you the same posts.

Hover a post, click the ghost, and it's gone from the feed. For good. Reload, scroll, come back tomorrow: it stays gone.

But it's not deleted. It becomes a ghost. Ghostify keeps a copy, so you can find it again, read it later, or snooze it until the weekend.

That's my take on Ghost in the Machine: the posts you've already seen don't die, they just stop haunting your feed and move into the machine. Quietly. Politely. Until you call them back.

What it does:

  • The ghost button shows up on the post under your pointer. Click it, the post vanishes, and an Undo toast gives you 5 seconds of regret.
  • The Ghostify page keeps everything in three tabs: Ghosted, Later and Snoozed.
  • Snooze a post until later today, tomorrow, the weekend, next week, or any date. When time's up, it shows up in Back from snooze.
  • Search your ghosts by keyword, or switch on Semantic and just describe what you remember ("that post about JavaScript adding objects and arrays").
  • Auto-ghostify rules in plain English, per site: "recurring weekly discussion threads I have already read". A local decision model checks new feed items against them and ghosts the matches. If it gets one wrong, Not this brings the post back, and that rule never touches it again.
  • Add any site. On any page with a feed, click Add this site. Feedgrab proposes the feeds, you confirm them in its overlay, and choose whether they're for the logged-in or logged-out view.
  • New tab flavor, if you want your ghosts on every new tab.

Demo

No store listing (yet!), so the demo is: install it, open DEV, start ghosting. It takes about a minute:

  1. Download a zip from Releases: ghostify-<version>-chrome.zip or ghostify-<version>-firefox.zip.
  2. Chrome: unzip, open chrome://extensions, turn on Developer mode, click Load unpacked. Firefox: open about:debugging#/runtime/this-firefox, click Load Temporary Add-on… and pick the zip.
  3. Open https://dev.to/ logged out, hover a post, click the ghost.

Here's a quick tour. (The screenshots represent what a user would see.)

The toolbar popup lists your recent ghosts. Click the 👁 to unghost one, and it shows up in the feed again:

Click a ghost to see its details, the AI summary and tags:

Write auto-ghostify rules in plain English, per site:

And pick a model for each job:

Code

SweaDev / ghostify

Ghostify Feed Browser Plugin (beta)

Ghostify

Ghostify is a browser extension (Chrome and Firefox) for feeds that keep showing you the same posts. Hover a post, click the ghost, and it disappears from the site's feed for good. Ghostify keeps a copy so you can find it again later.

v1.0.0. Ghostify works on the dev.to home feeds out of the box, and you can add any site. It has a full Ghostify page with snooze and search, and optional AI that runs locally with Ollama or with your own OpenRouter, Gemini or OpenAI key.

Features

  • The dev.to logged-out home feeds (Relevant /, Latest /latest, Top /top/*) are recognized automatically, through feedgrab.

  • The ghost button shows on the post under your pointer. Clicking it hides the post and saves it, and an Undo toast lets you take it back.

  • Ghosted posts stay hidden when you reload, and also when they come back…

View on GitHub

SweaDev / feedgrab

Feed Detector

Feedgrab

A TypeScript library that finds and describes content feeds in web pages (post timelines search results, product grids, article lists) and turns them into one de-duplicated stream of items with exclusion reports (ads, promoted posts, injected widgets).

  • Detect feeds automatically (structural heuristics, optionally refined by an LLM), by inspecting an element, or from CSS/XPath selectors you type.
  • Confirm/edit the proposals in a Shadow-DOM overlay, or programmatically with headless helpers.
  • Iterate a unified feed that keeps up with infinite scroll (MutationObserver) or pagination (ingest), with a report per item: kept, excluded (and why), or pending.
  • Exclude items by specificity-ranked selector rules, built-in ad rules, or plain-language LLM criteria. Nothing is removed unless you call a removal helper.

It runs in browser extensions (Chromium + Firefox, MV3), headless browsers (Playwright/Puppeteer injected bundle), and server-side (Bun/Node with a parsed DOM), using the same API everywhere.

Install

…
View on GitHub

How I Built It

The open-source AI part

AI is optional and off by default. Ghostify is perfectly happy as a dumb "hide this post" button. Turn AI on, and it gets three jobs, each with its own model:

Job Default (local, via Ollama) Used for
Embeddings embeddinggemma-2 Semantic search over your ghosts
General gemma4:e2b Summaries and tags for each ghosted post
Decision d3:2b Checking new feed items against your auto-ghostify rules

All three are open-weight and small enough to run on a laptop. Start Ollama so it accepts requests from extensions, and that's it:

ollama pull embeddinggemma-2
ollama pull gemma4:e2b
ollama pull d3:2b
OLLAMA_ORIGINS="chrome-extension://*,moz-extension://*" ollama serve

If you'd rather use a hosted model, every job can switch to OpenRouter, Gemini or OpenAI with your own key. The plumbing is the AI SDK, so swapping providers is a dropdown, not a rewrite.

A few things I'm happy about:

  • Fallbacks everywhere. If the decision model is down, the general model handles the rule check. If embeddings fail, search falls back to keywords. Nothing breaks because Ollama isn't running.
  • Embeddings are tagged with the model that made them. Change the embedding model and Ghostify ignores the old vectors instead of mixing them up. Reindex fills the gaps.
  • One honest gap: d3's response format isn't documented (yet). Ghostify reads the shapes it knows, treats anything else as "no match", and logs it. Better to miss a ghost than to hide something you wanted to see!

The extension part

  • WXT for one codebase that builds Chrome MV3 and Firefox, plus the new-tab flavor.
  • React 19 + Tailwind v4 for the popup, the Ghostify page and settings.
  • Dexie (IndexedDB) for ghosts, embeddings and keys. Everything stays in your browser. No account, no sync, no server.
  • Feedgrab for finding feeds and items, and for hiding them. Ghostify never touches a feed node itself; it asks Feedgrab's removeItem to hide it, and its own UI lives in a separate Shadow DOM.

Security was a bit of a rabbit hole:

  • Content scripts never see API keys. They don't even open IndexedDB. Everything goes through typed messages to the background script, and the background talks to the model.
  • Keys aren't in storage.local either, because content scripts can read that. They live in a Dexie table on the extension's own origin.
  • In content scripts, Feedgrab gets a proxy instead of a model, which also shrank the bundle from 380 KB to 71 KB. Nice side effect!

The "how did you build all this in a week" part

I didn't write most of the code by hand. I used a coding agent.

But I didn't just say "build me an extension" either. I've been using a small spec-driven flow I call specx:

  1. Spec: I wrote the spec by hand. It's 17 lines. Literally a paragraph and a list of features.
  2. Plan: the agent turned it into a plan with the stack, architecture and a Decisions log.
  3. Tasks: then into 23 tasks across 4 phases, each with the spec/plan line ranges it needs, the files it touches, and a Done check.
  4. Build loop: take the first unblocked task, read only what it references, implement it, run its Done check plus lint + typecheck + tests, tick the box, commit. Repeat.
  5. Phase check: at the end of each phase, follow the README from a clean state, build, load it in the browser, fix what's broken, tag a release.

The rules live in AGENTS.md, so any agent can pick it up. Every judgment call goes into the plan's Decisions log, so I can see why something was done the way it was. And there's one commit per task, so git log reads like a changelog.

Phase 1 was "ghost a post on DEV". Phase 4 was "auto-ghostify with local AI". Each phase ended with something I could actually load and use, not a pile of half-wired modules.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

Because the thing Ghostify reads is my browsing.

Think about what an AI feature in a feed extension actually sees: every post on every feed you scroll, what you hide, what you save for later, what you search for. That's a pretty detailed picture of a person. I don't want that going to anyone's API by default. Not even mine.

With open-weight models, it doesn't have to:

  • Gemma 4 E2B, EmbeddingGemma 2 and d3:2b run on my laptop. Summaries, tags, semantic search and the rule checks all happen locally. With Ollama, nothing leaves the machine.
  • It costs nothing per post. Auto-ghostify checks every new item in the feed. With a paid API, that's a meter running every time I scroll. Locally, it's just my fan spinning a bit.
  • It keeps working. No rate limits, no deprecation emails, no "this model will be retired on…".
  • A small, specialized model is enough. I don't need a giant model to answer "is this a weekly discussion thread?" A 2B decision model is the right size for the job, and I could only pick it because it's open.

And it's not just the models. Ghostify is built on open source all the way down: WXT, React, Dexie, the AI SDK, Biome, Vitest… and Feedgrab, which I split out because I wanted it to be reusable. If someone wants to build a "hide the reruns" extension for YouTube, or a feed reader for a site that doesn't have RSS, the hard part is already there. MIT licensed. Go for it.

A closed API would have given me a smarter summary, maybe. Open models gave me a tool I'm actually comfortable running on everything I read.

My Agent Session

The whole project was built in agent sessions, following the specx flow above. The best way to see them is the commit history: one commit per task, from Scaffold WXT React project to Add auto-ghostify rules with rescue.

The Spirit of It

I keep thinking about the name.

Most "hide this" features are really "delete this". You click, it's gone, and you'll never find it again. That always felt a bit wrong to me. I did read that post. Some of them were good! I just don't need to see them every time I open the home page.

So in Ghostify, nothing dies. It becomes a ghost. It stays in the machine, with its title, its author, a little summary, and a few tags, waiting until you call it back. A bit like Día de los Muertos for posts: not here anymore, but not forgotten either.

And somewhere in an archived repo, myDEV is resting peacefully, knowing it started all of this. 🕯️

Prize Categories

  • Best Use of Gemma: Ghostify uses Gemma 4 E2B (gemma4:e2b) for summaries and tags, and EmbeddingGemma 2 (embeddinggemma-2) for semantic search, both running locally through Ollama by default.

Thanks for reading! And if a post of yours disappears from my feed, don't take it personally. It just means I've probably already read it, seen it, or will read it later. 👻

title: Wisp: A Terminal Ghost That Never Runs Your Commands
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine

What I Built

Wisp is a tiny haunted-terminal companion. Give it command text and, optionally, an exit code; a local open-weight model responds with one spooky-but-friendly line.

I took the challenge's haunted-terminal idea and made the ghost deliberately harmless: Wisp never executes the command, watches the shell, reads shell history, or installs hooks. It only reacts to the text I explicitly pass in. That makes it a little less like possession and a little more like a ghostly rubber duck.

Demo

Wisp is a CLI, so there is no hosted web demo. Here are two real runs:

$ node dist/src/cli.js "git status"
The files whisper of changes you've forgotten...

$ node dist/src/cli.js --exit-code 1 "npm test"
The shadows whisper of unfinished cycles...

Code

Wisp on GitHub

How I Built It

Wisp is written in TypeScript for Node.js 22 or newer. It has no runtime npm dependencies. It sends the supplied text and optional exit code to Ollama's local /api/generate endpoint and asks Gemma 3 4B to answer in character. The model response is constrained to a short, single line; the CLI also handles missing models, invalid responses, and server timeouts.

The tests use Node's built-in test runner and a mocked HTTP response, so they don't need a running model. GitHub Actions builds and tests the project across Node 22, 24, and 26.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

With the default Ollama URL, inference happens on my machine. After the one-time model download, Wisp can generate its replies without sending command text to a hosted model API or needing an API key. I can also switch the model instead of being locked to one provider.

That local boundary depends on the configuration: if I point OLLAMA_URL at a remote server, the command text goes there instead. And the model's line is creative output, not a report of what the command actually did; Wisp never sees the command's output.

Prize Categories

  • Best Use of Gemma: Wisp uses Gemma 3 4B locally through Ollama.

The Spirit of It

A failed test usually gives you a stack trace. Wisp gives you a tiny ghost story instead. Under the spooky voice, it is still just a local model responding to text I chose to share with it.

title: Ghost Tales: Learn English Through Ghost Stories, Running Locally with Gemma
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine.

What I Built

Ghost Tales (ভূতের কথা in Bengali) is a small web app that teaches English through ghost stories, with Bengali beside every sentence. A local model, Gemma through Ollama, writes each story and translates it on my own Mac.

You pick a place, such as an old zamindar mansion or a river ghat at dusk. You pick a mood: spooky, or a gentle "memory ghost". You can name the hero. The story is typed out one sentence at a time, and each sentence is then translated into Bengali. The two languages sit side by side.

I live in Bangladesh. I wanted a language tool that needs no account, no subscription and no constant connection. A story you enjoy is easier to remember than a list of words, and a tool that runs on your own machine is easier to trust.

The ghost in my machine is the model itself. It lives in my own computer and tells stories by lamplight.

Demo

In the video I switch Wi-Fi off on screen, and it stays off for the rest of the recording. Story writing, translation and the Listen button all worked on my Mac that way. The narration was generated with ElevenLabs. The quiet ambient sound in the middle of the video is the app's own, synthesized in the browser and captured with system audio; the Listen voice is not included. The recording is edited: some waiting time was cut or sped up.

The app has three learning helpers:

  • Side by side: English on one side, Bengali on the other.
  • Learn mode: the English is blurred. Read the Bengali, guess the English, then click to reveal it.
  • Listen: the browser reads each sentence aloud with a speech voice from my system. On my Mac both an English and a Bengali voice were available, and both sound robotic. I did not check whether every voice runs locally or online.

Here is the last pair from the run in the screenshot above, unedited:

Some memories never leave us, they just become part of the home.
কিছু স্মৃতি কখনো আমাদের ছেড়ে যায় না, সেগুলো শুধু ঘরের অংশ হয়ে যায়।

Code

https://github.com/AnamulAI/ghost-tales

One index.html file, a README and an MIT licence. No framework, no build step, no external fonts or scripts. To run it: ollama pull gemma4:12b, then python3 -m http.server 8000 in the folder, and open http://localhost:8000.

Submission snapshot: tag submission-v1 (view).

How I Built It

Gemma, locally, through Ollama. The page calls Ollama on http://localhost:11434 and uses gemma4:12b (a 7.7 GB download). I tested on an Apple M4 Mac with 16 GB of RAM. In my own testing the model writes natural Bengali, which is the main reason I chose it.

Two steps, not one. Step one streams an English story of about 12 short sentences, at level A2 to B1. Step two sends each sentence to the model on its own and asks for the Bengali only. Small models tend to be more accurate on short inputs; a whole-story translation has more room to drift, skip lines or add notes.

The think: false finding. Gemma 4 can "think" before it answers. In a manual test in the Ollama app, one short translation spent about 25 seconds thinking. That is far too slow for a dozen sentences, so the app sends think: false (and retries without it if an Ollama version rejects the field). With thinking off, three test stories took 23 to 31 seconds in total, and a single sentence took about 1.1 to 1.3 seconds on average (raw outputs are in sample-stories.md). The 25-second figure came from a different manual test, so it is not a controlled comparison, but the gap made the choice easy.

Telling the story slowly. By default each English sentence is typed out over a few seconds, then the Bengali fades in. There is a faster pace and a tap mode. In one test run at the default pace, the last sentence appeared about 50 seconds after Begin, and all twelve translations were done a few seconds later.

Local only, on purpose. The model picker reads your installed models from Ollama and hides any with "cloud" in the name, because some Ollama models run on remote servers. That keeps story writing and translation on the machine.

The look and the sound. The page is a haunted storybook by lamplight: a layered night scene with a moon, fog and fireflies that shift as you move the mouse, and a palette for each mood. Sound is synthesized in the browser with the Web Audio API, with no audio files: a quiet ambient bed for each place, and short effects triggered by words in the sentence on screen. Sound is off until you press the Sound button. I tried the visuals and sound only on my own Mac, in one browser.

Honest limits.

  • Translation mistakes happen. My AI assistant checked three test stories and found a few clear defects: a stray Russian word at the start of one line, a garbled phrase, and a stray Latin letter inside a word. Most lines looked fine, but a small model's Bengali still needs review by a person. The page says so.
  • The Listen voices are robotic, and Bengali speech needs a Bengali voice on your system.
  • I have not run a user study, so I do not know yet how much it helps people learn.
  • My code is MIT licensed. The Gemma model has its own terms, which I have not reviewed in detail.

What comes next. Test it with real learners, add a "check my translation" mode, review the Bengali with native speakers, and try an open text-to-speech model for more natural voices.

AI tools helped build this project. I used Claude and Claude Code for code, tests and drafts, and I ran the app myself on my Mac, including with Wi-Fi switched off.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

A model that runs on your own machine can't be switched off, repriced or turned into a data pipeline. That matters most for learners with little money or a patchy connection. Open weights also let me inspect, swap and test the model: when I wanted a faster setting, I changed one flag and measured the result.

The Spirit of It

Ghost stories are how many of us first learned how language can pull you in. It felt right that a ghost story be the thing a machine tells, in two languages, on a computer that stays in the room with you.

Prize Categories

  • Best Use of Gemma: the whole app is built around Gemma (gemma4:12b) running locally through Ollama, for both story writing and Bengali translation.
  • Best Use of ElevenLabs: I used ElevenLabs (Eleven v4, voice "Wyman - The Storyteller", with audio tags for tone) to generate the narration for the demo video. It is not used inside the app, on purpose: story writing and translation stay on the computer.

title: My Pool Has 4 Threads, DNS Gets 2
description:
In Node, the word "asynchronous" does not describe a single thing. Some calls
really are handed to the kernel and come back when the operating system is
ready; others are placed on one of four background threads and wait their turn.
The second kind is libuv's work pool, its size is four, and that number appears
in Node's documentation in a single aside: "its current default value".

What led me to that number was my cover generator. In batch mode
generate-hero.ts drains its queue with four workers — a hard-coded 4 inside
the script — and each worker is one sharp call. In a separate run, in a
separate process, my social posting script names nine external hosts in its
source. Both are "asynchronous", both sit on their own four threads, and I had
no idea how much of those four either one was holding. I wanted to measure this
properly, once. The result was sharper than I expected: dns.lookup can never
take more than two of those four threads, and neither libuv's documentation
nor Node's mentions that limit.

Who lands in the pool

Node's command-line documentation spells out the list: all fs calls except the
file watchers and the explicitly synchronous ones, asynchronous crypto calls
such as crypto.pbkdf2, scrypt, randomBytes and generateKeyPair, all
zlib calls except the explicitly synchronous ones, and dns.lookup. The
warning that follows is fair: because the pool has a fixed size, if one of these
takes a long time, other "seemingly unrelated" ones get slower.

The sneakiest member of that list is dns.lookup, because you are usually not
the one deciding to call it. In Node's lib/net.js, the connect path says it in
one line: const lookup = options.lookup || dns.lookup;. So net.connect,
http, https and fetch — undici, which sits underneath fetch, uses
net.connect for plain HTTP and tls.connect for TLS, and both pass through
that same line — resolve names through dns.lookup unless you supply your own
resolver. The first step of every outbound HTTP request queues on the same four
threads as your file reads.

The dns.resolve* family is not on that list. Node's documentation draws the
line clearly: those functions do not use getaddrinfo(3), they always query
over the network, and they do not use libuv's threadpool. Keep that distinction
in mind; we will come back to it with a measurement at the end.

The lab: my own resolver, a fixed 300 ms

Measuring against a real DNS server is pointless; if the latency moves, you
cannot read the table. So I wrote a 49-line UDP server: it holds every incoming
query for exactly 300 ms, then answers 127.0.0.2, sets TTL zero (no caching),
and most importantly it counts how many distinct names are in flight at the
same time. Instead of guessing concurrency from the client side, I let the
resolver count it.

The lab ran in a node:26-alpine container: Alpine 3.24, Node v26.13.0, libuv
1.52.1, aarch64, 14 cores. /etc/resolv.conf has one line: nameserver
127.0.0.1. The client calls dns.lookup for 24 distinct names at once, with
family: 4, so each name sends a single A query and the resolver's A/AAAA
behaviour stays out of the table. The numbers below are medians of three runs.
Alpine uses musl; since the limit measured here lives in libuv, the resolver
library does not change the result, but the nsswitch.conf argument later in
this article applies to glibc setups.

UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE Concurrent queries counted by the resolver 24 names, total
unset (4) 2 3,695 ms
1 1 7,414 ms
2 1 7,427 ms
3 2 3,703 ms
4 2 3,712 ms
6 3 2,480 ms
8 4 1,859 ms
16 8 934 ms

The second column is exactly half the pool size, rounded up.

What amuses me most in this table is the relationship between the second and
third rows. Going from one thread to two moves the total for 24 names from 7,414
ms to 7,427 ms — that is, nowhere. I doubled the threads and what I gained on
the DNS side is smaller than the measurement noise. But going from two to three
cuts the time in half. Adding one thread buys nothing once and a factor of two
the next time.

The reason sits in libuv's source, on line 46 of src/threadpool.c:

static unsigned int slow_work_thread_threshold(void) {
  return (nthreads + 1) / 2;
}

libuv sorts work into three kinds: UV__WORK_CPU, UV__WORK_FAST_IO and
UV__WORK_SLOW_IO. src/unix/getaddrinfo.c submits its request as
UV__WORK_SLOW_IO; src/unix/fs.c submits every file operation as
UV__WORK_FAST_IO, and user code calling uv_queue_work submits as
UV__WORK_CPU. Slow-I/O work piles up in a separate queue and only a single
"there is slow work" marker goes into the main queue. When a thread picks up
that marker and starts running slow work, a counter goes up; if the counter has
reached the threshold, the thread pushes the marker back to the tail of the
queue and looks for other work.

So this is not an accident but a deliberate guard: it exists so a slow name
lookup cannot swallow the whole pool and block file reads. I have no objection
to the logic. My objection is that the limit is written down nowhere. libuv's
own documentation covers the default, the absolute maximum, and that the pool is
global and shared across all loops; for its scope it says "all file system
operations, as well as getaddrinfo and getnameinfo requests". Not one sentence
about the half-pool threshold. Node's UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE section does not have
it either: there the advice is simply to set a value greater than 4.

Follow that advice and DNS can use at most half of whatever you set. Write 8 and
the ceiling on your name-resolution concurrency is 4. It is a ceiling, not an
allocation: when there is no DNS work those slots do not sit idle, they take
other work.

Who starves whom

The direction of the threshold matters, because it is asymmetric. Two scenarios,
both with the pool at its default four threads:

A) With 32 pending dns.lookup calls (each answered by my 300 ms resolver)
I squeezed in one fs.readFile and one pbkdf2. The fs.readFile waited 0 ms,
the pbkdf2 2 ms. Thirty-two names are queued and the file read goes straight
through. The guard works.

B) With 32 pending pbkdf2 calls — a computation that takes 208 ms on its
own — I squeezed in one dns.lookup and one fs.readFile. The fs.readFile
waited 1,719 ms, the dns.lookup 2,018 ms.

The arithmetic of that second line lands exactly: 32 × 208 ms on four threads is
a 1,664 ms queue, and the measurement is 1,719 ms. DNS's 2,018 ms comes from the
same place — 1,719 ms of queue plus my resolver's fixed 300 ms, totalling 2,019
ms. The resolver answers in 300 ms while dns.lookup takes two seconds, and 85
percent of that has nothing to do with resolving a name.

The lesson here runs the other way: some investigations that start with "our DNS
is slow" are looking in the wrong place. What fills the pool is not name
resolution but the crypto, compression or image work in the same process. The
slow-I/O threshold stops DNS from choking everyone else; nothing stops everyone
else from choking DNS.

Where the threshold sits on my own pipeline

The same question goes to my cover generator, since that is where it started.
came from. generate-hero.ts makes a single sharp call: it rasterises the SVG
at 200 dpi, fits it to 1200×630 and writes a PNG with compressionLevel: 9. On
my Mac (Node v22.16.0, libuv 1.49.2, sharp 0.35.5, libvips 8.18.7, 14 cores)
that call takes 75 ms on its own. On an idle pool an fs.readFile takes 0.2 ms.

I started the same call N times concurrently and squeezed in a read of a real
article file:

Concurrent covers How long fs.readFile waited
1 0 ms
2 0 ms
3 0 ms
4 9 ms (three runs: 1 – 31 ms)
8 62 ms (three runs: 56 – 69 ms)

The threshold is exactly at four. Up to three there is still a free thread in
the pool, so the read never waits; the moment a fourth cover enters, it starts
waiting. I will not lean on the 9 ms in the fourth row — across three runs it
wandered between 1 and 31 ms, because the instant a thread frees up is a matter
of chance. At eight the number is steady: about 60 ms.

Something caught my eye here. My script does not only write two PNGs per article
and exit; in --all mode it drains the queue with four workers, and that four
is a constant I put there myself: Array.from({ length: 4 }, ...). The comment
next to it says it "gains parallel I/O". So when I rebuild the covers for all
2,772 posts I fill the entire pool, and the fourth row of the table is exactly
that point. When I wrote that 4 I did not know the pool was also four; the two
numbers matching is a coincidence, what follows from it is not — during an
--all run every fs read and every dns.lookup in the same process queues
behind it.

The absolute values are small, I know. What interests me is not the absolute
value but that the threshold is visible at all. And one more thing: there is not
a single line in my repository that mentions UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE. Not in the
scripts, not in the systemd units, not in the workflows. I have been running
on four threads and until today I had not chosen that deliberately.

When exactly is the pool born

Node's documentation says that setting process.env.UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE "is not
guaranteed to work" and gives a reason: the pool would have been created "as
part of the runtime initialisation much before user code is run". The warning
itself is right; the reason does not hold on the Node in this lab.

libuv's pool is lazy. The first line of uv__work_submit is uv_once(&once,
init_once) — the pool is born when the first piece of work is submitted. We can
count it from outside, because since libuv 1.50.0 the threads are named
libuv-worker:

# process is up but nothing has hit the pool yet
$ ls /proc/<pid>/task/*/comm | xargs cat | grep -c libuv-worker
0

After a single dns.lookup, that same count returns whatever
UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE says — 4 if you wrote 4, 128 if you wrote 128, for one
request. That is precisely libuv's sentence about preallocating the maximum
number of threads allowed. Five rows, same lab, on where the value is set:

Where it was set Concurrency counted by the resolver 24 names
nowhere (default 4) 2 3,695 ms
first line of the JS: process.env... = '16' 8 930 ms
the same line after one fs.readFile 2 3,720 ms
UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE=16 in the shell 8 923 ms
node --env-file=uv.env 8 934 ms

The third row vindicates the documentation's warning, but for a different
reason: the setting is not missed because the runtime built the pool early; it
is missed because someone submitted work to the pool before you did. A library
that reads a file with top-level await, or a dependency that calls
randomBytes, quietly makes your setting irrelevant. So the advice stands: do
not set this value from inside your code. The two honest paths in the table
above are the shell environment and --env-file; both land before the first
job.

The bill for growing it

The ceiling is 1024 (libuv 1.30.0 raised it from 128) and each thread wants an 8
MiB stack (since 1.45.0; before that it was the platform default). Readings from
the container's /proc/<pid>/status after a single dns.lookup:

UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE libuv-worker VmSize VmRSS Total threads
unset (4) 4 848 MiB 61 MiB 11
8 8 880 MiB 61 MiB 15
128 128 1,841 MiB 61 MiB 135
1024 1024 9,021 MiB 75 MiB 1,031

Going from four to eight adds 32 MiB to VmSize: four threads × 8 MiB, exact.
At 1024 the virtual size reaches 9 GiB while resident memory stays at 75 MiB —
the stacks are paged lazily, just as libuv's documentation says. So the thing to
worry about is not RSS; it is virtual address space in an environment capped by
ulimit -v, and a scheduler that now has 1,031 threads to deal with.

My decision: for a process like my blog pipeline, which writes a couple of
images per article and talks to five platforms, 16 is more than enough. Values
in the hundreds only make sense in a process that genuinely makes hundreds of
concurrent slow calls, and even there the real question is not the pool size but
why those calls are concurrent.

How to leave the limit behind entirely

The cleanest exit is not to grow the pool but not to use it. dns.resolve4 runs
on c-ares; the query happens on the event loop, not in the pool. I asked the
same 24 names of the same 300 ms resolver, with the default four-thread
pool:

Method Concurrent 24 names
dns.lookup 2 3,695 ms
dns.resolve4 24 312 ms

All twenty-four in flight, and the total is the duration of one query. More than
an eleven-fold difference, and I never touched the pool.

It is not free, of course. Node's documentation states the difference honestly:
dns.resolve* does not read /etc/hosts, and it does not use nsswitch.conf
and resolv.conf the way dns.lookup does. So there is no guarantee it gives
the same answer as ping. In a container, service names written into
/etc/hosts, mDNS, search domains — all of that disappears on this path. The
middle ground the documentation points to is more sensible: resolve the name
with dns.resolve() and use the address, or replace the lookup option that
APIs such as socket.connect() and dgram.createSocket() accept with your own
implementation — which is also exactly where a cache belongs.

Questions to ask about your own setup

  • How many distinct hosts does your process talk to? Each one means a default dns.lookup, and they all share at most two threads.
  • Does the same process do image processing, zlib, pbkdf2 or heavy file reads? If so, what fills the pool is probably not DNS but those.
  • Is UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE set from inside the code? If you cannot prove no work hit the pool before that line, the setting may be ignored.
  • Do you know how many threads your pool opened with? On Linux, counting libuv-worker in /proc/<pid>/task/*/comm takes two seconds (libuv 1.50.0 and above); on macOS you need sample or vmmap.
  • If you have a slow-resolver problem, should the answer be dns.resolve? Yes if you have no dependency on /etc/hosts and nsswitch; otherwise your own lookup.
  • If your traffic goes through global fetch, how do you hand it a lookup? fetch takes no such option; the path runs through undici's dispatcher — setGlobalDispatcher(new Agent({ connect: { lookup } })).
  • You opened eight worker_threads and assume you have eight pools? The thread count and the queues in threadpool.c are static: there is one pool per process. Eight workers share the same four threads and the same two DNS slots.
  • What happens when your nameserver dies? A getaddrinfo that has already started cannot be cancelled — uv__work_cancel can only pull work that has not begun off the queue — so two threads stay pinned for as long as timeout × attempts in resolv.conf says.

Limits without counters

Not one measurement in this article produces an alert. There is no counter that
goes up when the pool fills. The tooling is not entirely absent: perf_hooks
has a 'dns' entry type that tells you how long dns.lookup took, and the gap
between the node.threadpoolwork.async and .sync traces gives you the time
spent queueing. But the first one does not tell you why it took that long, and
the second is never emitted by the pool's two busiest customers — dns.lookup
and fs — because neither goes through the code that emits it. The limit is
there; in practice the only evidence is in your p99.

I ran into the same shape in the CPU quota
article: a process using
seventeen percent of its quota, throttled half a million times in ten days,
invisible to every dashboard that looks at averages. In the keepalive
article the
setting was right but almost no application read it. Here is a third variant:
the setting is documented, it is recommended, and half of the recommendation is
lost on the way — and the place it is lost is written on line 46 of the source.

Two threads out of four. If you did not choose that deliberately, libuv chose it
for you.

Official Sources

  • Node.js — UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE (CLI documentation)
  • Node.js — DNS: Implementation considerations
  • libuv — src/threadpool.c (v1.x branch)
  • libuv — Thread pool work scheduling documentation
  • libuv — src/unix/getaddrinfo.c (v1.x branch)
  • Node.js — lib/net.js (main branch)
