title: Braintree's Vault Knows the New Card. Your Retry Still Used the Old One.
description:
The strangest Braintree failures start with good news. A customer's card was replaced, the network account updater did its work, and the Vault quietly held a fresh number with a later expiry. Support could see the update. Billing could see the update. Then the scheduled retry ran, charged the old payment method token, and failed again for exactly the same reason.

That is not an account updater failure. It is a plumbing failure between storage and execution: the system that stores credentials is not necessarily the system that decides which credential a retry will present. This teardown follows one renewal through that gap, step by step, because the fix is rarely to retry harder. It is to prove, before each attempt, which token will actually be used.

The annotated sequence

T-minus 30 days: the subscription is created. The customer checks out, Braintree tokenizes the card, and your subscription record stores a reference to that payment method. Annotation: note what you stored. Many teams store a token on the subscription or invoice at creation time, not a live pointer that says, in effect, always use this customer's current default method. That distinction looks harmless on day one and decides everything on day ninety.

T-minus 12 days: the issuer replaces the card. Fraud, loss, or a routine reissue triggers a new number. Account updater services pass the new credentials to the Vault, and the vaulted record is refreshed. Annotation: refreshed where? An update can land on the customer record while a second, older token still exists alongside it — a duplicate from a repeat checkout, a saved backup card, or a method attached to a different customer profile created by a support tool. The Vault knowing is not the same as your retry knowing which Vault entry to choose.

Day 0: the first renewal declines. The charge runs against a token that now points to cancelled credentials, or against the stale duplicate. The decline looks like a money problem when it is really an identity problem: which card did we mean? Annotation: record the token fingerprint, last four, and expiry actually attempted, not just the decline code. Without that, every later step is guesswork.

Day 1 to 3: dunning starts, correctly and uselessly. Your emails ask the customer to update a card they believe they already updated, because their bank told them the merchant would get the new details automatically. Trust leaks here. Annotation: before sending a card-update request, check whether a newer vaulted method already exists. If it does, the honest message is not update your card; it is we are retrying with the details your bank sent us.

Day 4: the retry re-reads stale state. A job loads the subscription, pulls the payment method captured when the invoice was created, and submits it again. The Vault's newer credentials never enter the picture because nothing re-resolved the customer's current default at retry time. For more on how Braintree dunning handles replaced cards, that re-resolution step is the hinge the whole sequence turns on.

Checks to run before any retry

First, re-fetch, do not remember. At retry time, load the customer fresh and resolve the current default payment method, then compare its fingerprint with the one that failed. If they differ, retry the new one and log the swap. If they match, you have a genuine decline to treat.

Second, deduplicate the Vault. List every method on the customer, flag duplicates and orphaned tokens, and make one method unambiguously primary. Retries should never have to guess.

Third, separate hard from soft signals. An expired or replaced card calls for credential repair. Insufficient funds calls for timing, ideally around when the customer is paid. Authentication or do-not-honor responses call for stopping and contacting the customer, not for burning attempts.

Fourth, check the descriptor. The name the customer sees on their statement should match the name on your emails and your product. A retry that finally succeeds can still turn into a chargeback or a panicked support ticket if the descriptor looks unfamiliar, especially after a confusing week of failure notices.

What to log so this is debuggable

Log, for every attempt: subscription ID, token attempted, fingerprint and last four, whether account updater had supplied a successor, the decline category, and the source of the token — subscription record, invoice snapshot, or fresh customer lookup. With those six fields, a stale-token failure announces itself in one query. Without them, teams blame the issuer, add more retries, and make the noise worse.

None of this requires heroic engineering. It requires treating a retry as a new decision, not a replay. Swipe Again's failed payment recovery exists for subscription businesses that want that decision made carefully — decline-aware retries and clear customer messaging for a flat $179/mo — but the checks above are worth doing in any stack, today, before the next cohort renews against a card that was replaced weeks ago.

title: Before You Ship a Task App, Test Its Data Export
description:
A task app can look great during a demo. You create a task, assign it to someone, add a deadline, and move it across a board.

Then you click Export.

The download contains task titles and dates. The comments are missing. Attachments are only links. Completed work has disappeared because a filter was active.

The file opens, but it does not contain everything the team expected.

For developers, this is a useful reminder: an export button is a feature with its own requirements. Downloading a file is only the first step.

I run WhatsOnTech, where we publish guides about software and everyday business technology. This article looks at a question that matters to both software buyers and developers: can people take their work with them in a form they can actually use?

The example below uses a fictional task app. It is a suggested testing approach, not a claim that I tested every product mentioned.

Disclosure: I run the website linked in this article. This article was prepared with AI assistance.

Decide What the Export Is Supposed to Do

Before choosing a file format, decide why someone needs the export.

A manager preparing a weekly report may only need task names, owners, deadlines, and status.

A team moving to another app may need much more: descriptions, comments, checklists, attachments, and the relationships between records.

Someone recovering from data loss needs a tested restoration process.

These are different jobs.

An export designed for reporting can be useful without recreating an entire workspace. The problem starts when the interface calls that file a complete backup.

Write a clear description of the feature before building it:

Export the selected tasks and their main fields for spreadsheet reporting. Comments and attachment files are not included.

That explanation may sound less impressive than “Export everything,” but it sets an expectation the product can meet.

Understand the Work Before Choosing the Fields

A personal reminder and a shared project do not carry the same amount of information.

“Send the invoice” might need a title, deadline, and completion status.

“Prepare the new website homepage” could involve several people, review comments, image files, subtasks, and approval history.

This difference also matters when choosing software. Our Microsoft To Do vs Trello comparison explores the distinction between simple lists and work organised into stages.

For developers, the lesson is to export the information that gives a task its meaning.

A card titled “Update the page” is not very useful after migration if the page address, feedback, and assigned person have been lost.

Start by listing the fields people rely on during normal work. Then decide which export includes each field.

Use a Small Dataset With Deliberate Edge Cases

Testing with three tasks called “Task 1,” “Task 2,” and “Task 3” will miss many problems.

Instead, create a small test workspace with records that challenge the export.

Include:

  • Two tasks with the same title but different IDs.
  • One completed task and one archived task.
  • A task without a deadline.
  • A description containing commas, quotation marks, and line breaks.
  • Text in more than one language.
  • A task with several checklist items.
  • Two attachments that share the same filename.
  • A task with more than one comment.
  • A deadline with a specific time.
  • A date-only deadline with no time attached.

Record what you expect before downloading anything.

For example, your fictional workspace might contain 12 tasks, 7 comments, 4 checklist items, and 3 attachments.

Those counts give you something concrete to compare against. They are not proof of completeness by themselves, but they make missing data easier to notice.

Use invented information for this test. Real customer records are unnecessary.

Make Export Scope Visible

A common source of confusion is the difference between “what I can see” and “everything in the workspace.”

If a user filters the screen to show open tasks, should Export include only those tasks?

Either behaviour can be reasonable. It needs to be explicit.

The export screen could offer:

  • Current filtered view.
  • All tasks I am allowed to access.
  • Include completed tasks.
  • Include archived tasks.

Show a summary before the download:

This export includes 12 tasks, including completed tasks. Archived tasks are excluded.

For larger systems, the export should also explain its timing. If a team changes records while a long export is running, the resulting file may contain information collected at different moments.

Use a consistent snapshot where practical, or document how the export handles changes during generation.

The user should not have to guess what “all” means.

Choose CSV or JSON for a Clear Reason

CSV is useful for rows and columns. People can open it in a spreadsheet, sort tasks, and create simple reports.

JSON can represent nested information such as a task with several comments and checklist items.

Neither format guarantees completeness.

Format Useful for What needs attention
CSV Spreadsheet reports and simple transfers Nested records, text formatting, dates, and spreadsheet interpretation
JSON Structured records and custom migration tools Schema documentation, relationships, and importer compatibility
ZIP package Records plus attachment files File organisation, missing files, and a contents summary
PDF A readable snapshot Limited usefulness for importing structured data

A well-documented CSV may be more useful than an unexplained JSON file.

For a structured export, include a format version, export time, field descriptions, and a clear explanation of how records connect.

Keep stable identifiers. Two tasks with identical titles should remain distinguishable after export.

Learn From a Real Export Limitation

Trello provides a practical example of why these details matter.

According to Atlassian’s export documentation, board members can export raw JSON, while boards in Premium Workspaces can also be exported as CSV. Comments are not included in the CSV export.

For Workspace exports, including raw attachments is a separate option. Without it, the export links to attachments hosted on Trello.

Atlassian also states that importing the exported JSON or CSV to recreate a Trello board is not currently supported.

That does not make the exports useless. It means exporting, reporting, migration, and restoration are separate capabilities.

When evaluating any app, check the documentation for the exact export option you plan to use. Different formats and export levels can include different information.

Check Attachment Files, Not Just Their Names

An attachment entry may contain a filename and a web address without containing the file itself.

That can work while the original account remains available. It may fail later if permissions change, the file is removed, or the link expires.

If an export promises attachment files, check that they are actually present.

Download a sample package, disconnect from the original service, and try opening the included documents and images.

Also test duplicate filenames. Two different files named “brief.pdf” should not overwrite each other.

A package can keep files in separate folders based on task or attachment IDs. A contents list can connect each file to its original record.

If a file could not be included, report it clearly. A successful download message should not hide skipped attachments.

Keep Dates and Text Meaningful

Dates deserve more attention than they usually receive.

“05/06/2026” can mean different dates depending on the reader’s locale.

A date-only deadline should remain a date. Converting it unnecessarily into a timestamp can make it appear on a different day in another time zone.

For timed events, use a documented representation with a time-zone offset or UTC convention. Where local scheduling matters, preserve the relevant time-zone information too.

Text needs similar care.

Check that:

  • Commas stay inside the correct field.
  • Quotation marks survive the export.
  • Multiline notes remain attached to one record.
  • Urdu and other non-English text remains readable.
  • Identifiers with leading zeros stay intact.

A file that opens without an error can still contain changed values.

Compare actual field values, not just the appearance of the first few rows.

Separate Export, Sync, and Backup

These three features are related, but they serve different purposes.

An export provides a copy of selected information.

Sync carries changes between connected locations.

Backup is intended to support recovery under defined conditions.

A team may use all three.

For example, syncing a folder can make an exported file available on another computer. It does not automatically protect that file from a deletion that also syncs.

Our guide to cloud backup versus sync explains this distinction from the user’s perspective.

For your own app, describe recovery in practical terms:

  • Which records can be recovered?
  • How old can the recovery point be?
  • How long are copies retained?
  • Are attachment files included?
  • What access is required to restore them?
  • Has the recovery process been tested?

An occasional manual export can contribute to a backup plan. Its value depends on its coverage, storage, age, and whether someone can use it to recover the information they need.

Test the Return Journey

If your app promises restoration, test the complete journey.

Create a test workspace, export it, and restore it into a separate empty test environment.

Then compare the result with the original.

Check record counts, field values, attachment contents, and relationships. Make sure comments belong to the correct tasks and checklist items retain their completion status.

If the destination creates new IDs, verify that the relationships are mapped correctly rather than expecting every ID to remain unchanged.

Repeat the import.

Does it create duplicates? Update existing records? Refuse to continue? The behaviour should be deliberate and documented.

If your app supports export but not import, say so. Do not describe a readable archive as a tested restore package.

Never delete the original workspace just to find out whether restoration works.

Treat Spreadsheet Export as a Security Feature

User-entered text may behave differently after it leaves your application.

Some spreadsheet programs interpret values beginning with certain characters as formulas. This creates a risk known as CSV or formula injection.

Correctly escaping commas and quotation marks does not, by itself, solve that problem.

OWASP notes that protections depend on the spreadsheet application and how the file is opened, saved, and reopened.

For a related DEV discussion, see spreadsheet exports and formula-injection controls.

Keep the original data unchanged in your application. Apply suitable handling when creating a spreadsheet-facing export, and test it with the applications you support.

A separate machine-readable export may be appropriate when users need exact original values.

Export permissions also matter. The download must not reveal private fields or other users’ records simply because the export query has fewer restrictions than the normal screen.

Make Large Exports Honest About Failure

A small workspace may export quickly. A large one may require background processing.

Give the job clear states such as preparing, ready, failed, or completed with omissions.

If only part of the data was exported, say so. Provide a useful summary of what was included and what failed.

Avoid giving every download the same filename. A descriptive name with an export date makes older copies easier to distinguish.

Protect the generated file appropriately. A private workspace should not become a publicly accessible download.

If download links expire, tell users when they need to create another export.

Use a Release Checklist

Before releasing an export feature, check more than the download button.

Check What a useful result looks like
Export scope Included and excluded records are clear
Record counts Counts match the selected scope
Text Quotes, line breaks, and different languages survive
Dates Date-only values and timed events retain their meaning
Attachments Promised files are present and open correctly
Relationships Comments and subtasks remain linked correctly
Permissions Restricted records and fields stay restricted
Spreadsheet behaviour Untrusted text is handled for supported applications
Repeated import Duplicate handling follows the documented rule
Partial failure Missing items are reported
Restoration Tested if recovery is promised

Keep the test dataset so you can run these checks again when the data model changes.

A newly added field is easy to display in the app and easy to forget in an export.

Build the Exit Alongside the Entrance

Onboarding helps people bring their work into an app. Export helps them keep control of that work later.

Both deserve careful design.

Start with a clear purpose, test with realistic sample records, and explain the limits of each format. If you promise recovery, test recovery.

The goal is not to produce the largest possible download. It is to give people a copy they can understand and use for the purpose you promised.

Before shipping another task feature, try taking the existing work out of your app. What survives that journey tells you a great deal about the quality of the export.

title: Step-by-Step Email Event Notification APIs Explained — Auditable Compliance Records
description:
Short answer: a B2B SaaS compliance notice needs a small Node.js intake service that authenticates event notifications, writes an immutable evidence record, and keeps message content on a separate retention schedule. A delivery event is evidence of a downstream observation, not proof that a person read the notice.

The bill is usually shaped by retention, not by the outbound request. Duplicated raw payloads, rendered bodies, indexes, attachments, and logs outlive their purpose unless their life is designed. An example policy might retain normalized evidence for 30 days, raw event envelopes for 7 days, and no body after its hash and required metadata are recorded. Those are policy examples; legal requirements set the real window.

What is the bill actually storing?

Data Purpose Retention question
Notice metadata Links a notice to tenant and policy Is an ID enough?
Event envelope Preserves what the source reported When is the original shape no longer needed?
Normalized status Supports reports and reconciliation Can it outlive the raw payload?
Message content Supports review or discovery Is a hash sufficient?
Operational logs Explains retries and failures Can identifiers be logged without addresses?

Store the notice ID, tenant ID, recipient fingerprint, event type, source event ID, observed time, and content hash in durable evidence. Keep the raw payload in short-lived object storage only when investigation requires it. Keep message bodies in a separately governed store with a tested deletion job.

This is a trade-off. Expiring raw data can remove fields that were never promoted into the evidence schema. Expiring the body can leave an auditor able to prove what happened without reconstructing the prose. Define the evidence contract first. Retention is a data-model decision.

A delivered event can mean that a downstream system accepted a message; it does not establish that the recipient read it. A bounced event needs its reason and the time observed. Keep the system's notice ID beside the external event ID so a repeated notification does not become a second compliance notice.

Consider a 30-day audit window. On day one, the normalized record can answer which tenant issued the notice, which recipient fingerprint was targeted, which event source reported the outcome, and when the service observed it. On day eight, the raw envelope may be gone. That is acceptable only if the normalized schema already captured the event type, source identity, timestamps, content hash, and verification result. If the investigation needs a field that was left in the expired envelope, the retention policy has saved storage by spending auditability. This is the kind of failure that appears months after an apparently successful integration, when the team has forgotten which adapter supplied which field. Write the contract while the payload is still in view.

{
  "notice_id": "notice_01J9EXAMPLE",
  "tenant_id": "tenant_42",
  "recipient_fingerprint": "sha256:...",
  "event_type": "delivered",
  "provider_event_id": "evt_7f2",
  "observed_at": "2026-10-31T08:15:00Z",
  "content_sha256": "sha256:...",
  "raw_payload_expires_at": "2026-11-07T08:15:00Z"
}

Use a uniqueness rule on the source identity you trust. Record late events, but do not silently let them rewrite a newer terminal state. Do not put a full recipient address into ordinary logs. A fingerprint supports correlation, but it remains sensitive when the input and hashing process are available to an attacker.

How should the Node.js intake be wired?

This step-by-step integration has four boundaries: authenticate, parse and validate, normalize, and persist idempotently. Email APIs belong at the edge; the rest of the application should receive a narrow internal event shape.

import crypto from "node:crypto";

function fingerprintRecipient(address, secret) {
  return "sha256:" + crypto.createHmac("sha256", secret)
    .update(address.trim().toLowerCase()).digest("hex");
}

function normalizeEvent(payload, secret) {
  if (!payload.notice_id || !payload.type || !payload.event_id) {
    throw new Error("missing event identity");
  }
  return {
    notice_id: String(payload.notice_id),
    tenant_id: String(payload.tenant_id),
    recipient_fingerprint: fingerprintRecipient(String(payload.recipient), secret),
    event_type: String(payload.type),
    provider_event_id: String(payload.event_id),
    observed_at: new Date().toISOString(),
    content_sha256: payload.content_sha256 ?? null
  };
}

export async function acceptEvent(request, deps) {
  const payload = await request.json();
  await deps.auth.verify(request, payload);
  const event = normalizeEvent(payload, deps.secrets.recipientFingerprint);
  await deps.evidence.insertIfAbsent(event, { rawPayload: payload, expiresInDays: 7 });
  return { status: 202 };
}

202 means accepted for processing, not delivered. Parsing and signature checks need a bounded body size, replay protection where supported, and a defined malformed-event response. Write the original only after verification. If a write fails after success is returned, the service has lied; if an error follows a successful write, the sender may retry. Idempotency is correctness.

Which failure mode does each boundary contain?

Failure mode Containment Evidence
Duplicate delivery Unique source event ID and replay-safe insert First-seen time and duplicate count
Late event State ordering rule or event timeline Event time and observed time
Signature mismatch Reject before normalization Redacted request ID and reason
Database outage Bounded backoff or durable queue Attempts and final disposition
Unknown event type Quarantine for review Type and schema version
Accepted without delivery Separate accepted and delivered states Transition history

The subtle case is a retry storm. Separate permanent validation failures from transient infrastructure failures, cap attempts, and expose queue age. A dead-letter record should identify human work without becoming another uncontrolled payload copy.

SPF concerns a sending domain's authorization model. It does not define a webhook schema or prove that a recipient read a message. The intake still needs an authenticated event channel, replay protection, and a record of the verification decision.

Measure acceptance rate, verification failures, duplicate rate, time from receipt to durable evidence, queue age, and notices with no terminal observation after a chosen window. Measure by tenant too; a healthy aggregate can hide one tenant with a consistently wrong domain policy.

Test duplicate delivery, reordered events, unknown types, expired signatures, oversized bodies, and a database timeout after insert. Assert both the response and the evidence left behind. Add a schema version and preserve the old reader until the retention window closes. The cleanup job should count candidates, deletions, and failures.

How can I integrate email event notification APIs step-by-step?

Start with the evidence contract, then connect the email APIs, then exercise the failure paths. The order matters: integrating first and defining evidence later usually leaves a provider-shaped record that cannot answer a compliance question cleanly.

The first design often keeps every payload forever because storage feels cheap and evidence feels valuable. Access review later shows that the system retained more personal data than the audit question required. Promote the fields that answer that question, shorten the rest, and document what cannot be reconstructed after expiry.

One short rule is enough: preserve proof, expire copies.

The least complex implementation is a thin adapter, an idempotent evidence store, and an explicit retention policy. Add queues, reconciliation, or extra channels only when they remove a demonstrated operational burden, because each state transition must also be audited.

Further reading

  • RFC 7208, Sender Policy Framework (SPF): https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7208
  • RFC 5322, Internet Message Format: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc5322
  • RFC 3339, Date and Time on the Internet: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3339

title: 2026 Node.js Error Tracking Library Integration: Best Practices for Silent Import Failures
description:
2026 Scheduled Import Observability: Proving Results Before Assigning Operational Cost

The constraint changes the design: a scheduled e-commerce import that produces no result may never throw, so a Node.js error-tracking library cannot prove that the job ran. Use the library for exceptions, add an explicit completion record with a stable run identifier, and have a separate heartbeat check detect a missing result before assigning the operational cost to a source or cost center.

Short answer: initialize Sentry, Rollbar, or a similar library before application work, capture uncaught and HTTP errors, and wrap the import boundary for explicit reporting. Then record successful and empty outcomes separately. A missed schedule needs a Healthchecks-style monitor or an equivalent polling check; it is not an error event.

The distinction is easy to miss.

What should the import system prove?

For every scheduled import, I want one answerable question: did the expected result arrive before the business deadline? The completion record should carry job_name, run_id, source, started_at, finished_at, rows, and cost_center. The last field is deliberate. If marketplace, catalog, and inventory feeds share workers, an error count cannot explain whose operational cost is rising.

There are three useful outcomes:

  • failed: the worker reported an exception or an HTTP failure.
  • completed_empty: the run finished, but produced zero rows where zero is suspicious.
  • missing: no completion signal arrived before the deadline.

Only the first outcome is naturally visible to an error-tracking SDK. The other two require an application event and a deadline check. OpenTelemetry describes logs as a signal whose records can carry attributes, which is a useful model for correlating error events, completion events, and deadline checks without pretending they are one signal.

Keep the business cost calculation outside the error tracker. A zero-row result may be a legitimate supplier response, a broken credential, or a scheduler that never fired. The tracker preserves evidence; a small attribution job applies the business rule after the run state is known.

Why does a missing import need another signal?

Absence is not an exception. Consider a nightly catalog import expected by 02:00 UTC. The worker may never start, wait behind a stuck process, or exit before it initializes the library. In all three cases, a design built only around try/catch has no event to send.

The minimum design is a pair of writes: emit an error when a failure is observed, and emit a completion event after the durable result is committed. A scheduler or Healthchecks-style service checks for the latter. Give that check a tolerance window. A deadline that is too strict converts ordinary queue delay into an incident storm, while one that is too generous delays cost attribution.

Use the same run_id in error context, completion log, queue message, and cost ledger. Trace and span fields can help correlate records when available, but this design does not depend on a distributed-trace query or a span tree.

No exception is required.

That is the awkward part. A catalog feed can return a valid response, write zero rows, and leave the error tracker quiet; the system must retain the schedule, source, row count, deadline, and cost center long enough for an attribution job to distinguish a legitimate empty feed from a missed run. I would make that distinction in the workflow, because a library cannot infer whether zero is normal for one supplier on one day. The import worker should also rethrow after reporting an exception. Swallowing it makes the scheduler believe the run succeeded, which corrupts both operational status and cost attribution.

The application contract can stay provider-neutral. This Python example shows the capture boundary for a REST capability; the Node.js worker can implement the same contract through its chosen SDK or HTTP client. The operational limits matter too: use a 10-second request timeout, make four bounded attempts, and treat HTTP 429 as a retryable response rather than a reason to loop forever. Those are explicit client choices, not promises about provider latency.

import os
import time
import uuid

import requests


def capture_error(error_payload):
    api_key = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]
    base_url = os.environ["INFRAI_BASE_URL"].rstrip("/")
    response_url = f"{base_url}/v1/errors/capture"
    headers = {
        "Authorization": f"Bearer {api_key}",
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
        "Idempotency-Key": str(uuid.uuid4()),
    }

    for attempt in range(4):
        response = requests.post(
            response_url,
            headers=headers,
            json=error_payload,
            timeout=10,
        )
        if response.status_code != 429:
            if not response.ok:
                raise RuntimeError(
                    f"error capture failed: {response.status_code} {response.text}"
                )
            return response.json()

        retry_after = response.headers.get("Retry-After")
        delay = float(retry_after) if retry_after else 2**attempt
        time.sleep(delay)

    raise RuntimeError("error capture rate limit did not clear after retries")

The key comes from an environment variable, the method is explicit, a 429 honors Retry-After, and non-success responses remain visible. The idempotency key prevents a retry after a network timeout from recording the same failure twice. Do not send this authorization header to a separate URL returned for another operation.

Which tools fit the evidence?

The comparison should follow the missing proof, not the popularity of a dashboard. Sentry is a natural fit when the main requirement is SDK-based exception capture and context. Rollbar belongs in the same shortlist for application error monitoring. Datadog is a broader observability choice when error records need to sit beside other operational telemetry. None of those labels, by themselves, answers “did this scheduled import produce a result?”

Option Strong fit Boundary for silent imports Cost attribution implication
Sentry Capturing application exceptions with project context A missing completion still needs a positive event and a deadline check Add cost_center and run_id to captured context, then calculate attribution outside the error stream
Rollbar Error monitoring for application failures A worker that never emits an error remains invisible Keep the run ledger separate so a low error count cannot be mistaken for low import cost
Datadog Joining error records with wider observability practice The monitoring design still needs an explicit import-success signal Use a common identifier and meter the workflow independently from incident volume
Healthchecks-style monitoring Detecting a missed scheduled check-in It does not replace stack traces or application context Attribute the missed run to the job and source, then link supporting error records
A plain REST error capability Sending error evidence without installing a provider SDK It is still not a heartbeat or alerting rule engine Preserve the internal event contract and assemble the missing checks separately

That last row is where Infrai can fit. Infrai's one REST API is pure HTTP: no SDK to install, and any language or runtime can send the request. Its API is also self-describing, so the discovery surface can show the request and response contract before a worker is wired to it; that reduces the friction of replacing an SDK-backed capture edge during a provider change. The internal event contract can remain stable while the service behind the capability changes, so swapping the provider does not require changing application code. Infrai also uses one key and one bill across the platform, which reduces credential and invoice sprawl without changing the observability limits. The platform has 295 routes across 20 modules under one key, but that breadth does not turn error capture into a heartbeat monitor or a notification system.

The 2026-10-29 capability snapshot also makes the limitations material. Infrai has no built-in threshold notifications, distributed span-tree query, source-map deobfuscation, session replay, or heartbeat monitoring in the stated capability boundary. Its client-side checking model is polling-based, and the observability facts do not establish a declared filter contract for log search or metric query. Choose Sentry when SDK-centered exception context is the priority, Datadog when a wider observability estate matters more, and a Healthchecks-style tool when missed schedules are the primary failure. Choose the REST capability only when a provider-neutral HTTP contract is more valuable than an integrated debugging suite; it isn't a replacement for one.

How should I integrate the Node.js library?

Install the selected library with npm and initialize it before application work begins. Configure middleware for uncaught exceptions and HTTP errors, then wrap the import worker as well; middleware catches request failures, while a scheduled worker may run outside an HTTP request entirely. Attach user information only where it is appropriate and lawful, and prefer a stable internal identifier over an email address.

The test should be repeatable. Trigger one controlled exception and verify that the report includes the import name and run_id. Run a successful import and verify the completion event. Then suppress the completion event in a test environment and confirm that the heartbeat check marks the run as missing. A green error dashboard with no missing-run test does not establish that the integration works.

The provider-specific SDK is an implementation detail. The durable contract is the useful part: error reports include the run context, successful work emits a completion record, and retries use the same idempotent run identifier. Do not use a trace tree as a substitute for this contract; the available logs may carry trace_id and span_id without providing distributed trace exploration.

A rollout rule that survives provider changes

Start with one import whose business owner can define “late.” Record the expected schedule, allowed delay, source, and cost center before enabling notifications. Compare observed exceptions, completed runs, and expected runs over a fixed test window. The gaps are the product decision.

Keep error capture, completion recording, and missed-run detection as replaceable edges around one internal event contract. This permits a move from Sentry to Rollbar, Datadog, or a plain REST capability without rewriting the import worker's business logic, while keeping the uncomfortable truth visible: an error tracker can explain a failed run, but only a positive completion signal can establish that a run occurred.

Sources

  • OpenTelemetry Logs signal concepts
  • Sentry Node.js documentation
  • Rollbar Node.js documentation
  • Datadog Node.js error tracking
  • Healthchecks.io documentation

title: AI Agent Cancellation: Stop Work That Continues After the User Clicks Stop
description:
A Stop button can be honest in the browser and still be a lie in production. The chat stream disappears, but a model request may be generating, a browser tool may be clicking, and a background worker may be one step away from sending an email.

That is not a cosmetic bug. It is a broken contract. Users interpret “Stop” as “do not do more work for me.” Your system needs to translate that request across every layer, record what actually stopped, and make the remaining uncertainty visible. This guide gives you that contract.

The key idea is simple: cancellation is a state transition, not a boolean and not a client disconnect.

The five meanings hidden behind “Stop”

Teams often store one cancelled flag and call it a day. That collapses several different facts:

Event What it proves What it does not prove
Browser aborts a stream The browser stopped listening The server or model stopped working
API accepts a cancel request The request was recorded Every child task observed it
Worker sees the request New work should not begin An in-flight tool did not finish
Provider accepts cancellation The cancellation reached that provider No already-buffered output or usage exists
Run becomes terminal Your ledger has a final outcome An external write was reversed

Keep those facts separate. A robust lifecycle might be:

running → cancel_requested → cancelling → cancelled

with other terminal paths such as completed, failed, and needs_reconciliation. The last state is important. If a payment, ticket, or record write was in flight when cancellation arrived, pretending it is cancelled can make a later retry unsafe.

Define the cancellation contract before wiring a button

Write down the semantics your product promises. A useful default is:

  1. A user can request cancellation for a run they are authorized to control.
  2. No new model turn, tool call, or queued step starts after the durable request is observed.
  3. In-flight work gets a best-effort cancel signal and has a deadline for acknowledging it.
  4. The API never reports cancelled until the orchestrator records a terminal decision.
  5. Side effects already dispatched are reconciled, not guessed away.
  6. A cancelled run does not silently resume; resumption creates a new attempt or requires an explicit resume action.

This contract gives product, API, and operations teams the same vocabulary. It also prevents a dangerous UX pattern: changing the button label to “Stopped” the moment the browser disconnects.

Use one durable run record

Put the authoritative state in a database or workflow engine, not in a process-local abort controller. A minimal record can look like this:

type RunStatus =
  | "queued" | "running" | "cancel_requested" | "cancelling"
  | "cancelled" | "completed" | "failed" | "needs_reconciliation";

type AgentRun = {
  id: string;
  tenantId: string;
  status: RunStatus;
  cancelRequestedAt?: string;
  cancelReason?: "user" | "deadline" | "policy" | "operator";
  activeStepId?: string;
  version: number;
  terminalAt?: string;
};

The version field enables compare-and-set updates. It stops a late worker from replacing cancel_requested with running after another worker has already processed the stop request.

Your POST /runs/:id/cancel endpoint should be idempotent. It records the request once, returns the current state, and publishes a cancellation event. Repeated taps, reconnects, and retries should all produce the same outcome.

async function requestCancel(runId: string, actorId: string) {
  return db.transaction(async (tx) => {
    const run = await tx.runs.lockForUpdate(runId);
    assertCanCancel(actorId, run);

    if (["completed", "failed", "cancelled"].includes(run.status)) return run;

    const next = await tx.runs.update(runId, {
      status: "cancel_requested",
      cancelRequestedAt: new Date().toISOString(),
      cancelReason: "user",
      version: run.version + 1,
    });
    await tx.outbox.insert({ type: "run.cancel_requested", runId });
    return next;
  });
}

The transactional outbox is not required by every stack, but the principle is: persist the decision before notifying workers. A process crash between an in-memory publish and a database write should not make a stop request disappear.

Propagate cancellation across every boundary

An agent run usually crosses more boundaries than a normal web request. Treat cancellation as a signal that travels with the run.

Browser and streaming edge

AbortController can stop fetch and response-body consumption in the browser, as MDN documents. Use it to stop rendering and then call your durable cancellation endpoint. Do not rely on disconnect detection alone: mobile networks reconnect, tabs sleep, and a user may close a page without meaning “cancel.”

const controller = new AbortController();

stopButton.onclick = async () => {
  controller.abort("user_pressed_stop"); // end local streaming now
  await fetch(`/api/runs/${runId}/cancel`, { method: "POST" });
  showStatus("Stopping…");
};

The status is “Stopping,” not “Stopped,” until the run event feed reports a terminal state. If an SSE connection reconnects, replay events from a monotonic sequence number rather than starting another run.

Orchestrator and model calls

At step boundaries, read the durable record. In long model streams, also pass a cancellation primitive that can close the network request or invoke a provider-specific cancellation API where available. A close tells your HTTP client to stop waiting; it does not automatically prove upstream inference stopped or that no tokens were billed.

Use an absolute run deadline as well. Pass the remaining time, not a fresh full timeout, to each downstream call. A run that spends 50 seconds retrieving should not receive another 60 seconds of model time merely because each layer starts its own clock.

Parallel tools

Parallelism makes cancellation interesting. If a run launches a search, an internal lookup, and a write tool together, cancellation must reach each child. But not all children have the same policy:

  • Read-only tools can normally be abandoned or cancelled.
  • A write before its commit point can be cancelled.
  • A write after dispatch needs a receipt or authoritative read-back.
  • Cleanup work may need a short shielded window so it can record the correct final state.

In Python, cancellation is cooperative: asyncio injects CancelledError at an await point, and the official guidance is to use try/finally for cleanup and generally propagate the exception afterward. Do not catch it broadly and continue doing more agent work.

async def execute_step(run_id: str):
    try:
        await assert_not_cancelled(run_id)
        result = await call_tool_with_deadline(run_id)
        await persist_result(run_id, result)
    except asyncio.CancelledError:
        await record_step_interrupted(run_id)
        raise

Queued and durable work

A cancellation request must invalidate queued messages too. Workers should acquire a lease, re-check the run state immediately before each externally visible action, and release the lease on exit. A message already in a queue is not permission to execute it.

For longer-running orchestration, model cancellation and external-step cancellation as explicit workflow commands. Systems such as Temporal distinguish cancellation commands from ordinary completion; the general lesson applies even if you use Postgres and workers instead of a workflow engine.

If you need the underlying persistence pattern, see AI Agent Durable Queue: Stop Long-Running Work From Dying Mid-Task.

Never confuse cancellation with rollback

Cancellation prevents future work. Rollback tries to compensate for past work. They are related but not interchangeable.

Imagine an agent creates an invoice and then receives a stop request before it records the tool response. The correct terminal state is often needs_reconciliation, not cancelled. Query the payment system by a stable operation key. If the invoice exists, show it as created and offer a distinct authorized reversal. If it does not, mark the step cancelled.

This is why every write tool needs an idempotency key and an operation ledger. The full pattern is covered in AI Agent Idempotency: Prevent Duplicate Charges, Emails, and Records. Cancellation reduces how often you enter an unknown state; it never removes the need to resolve one.

Design an honest user experience

The UI should expose progress without flooding people with internals:

State User-facing message Allowed action
running Working Stop
cancel_requested Stopping work Hide or wait
cancelling Finishing safe shutdown View details
needs_reconciliation Checking an action before closing Retry check or contact support
cancelled Stopped; no new work will run Start a new run

Do not show partial generated text as a completed answer. Mark it as interrupted, keep it separate from the final result, and never automatically feed it into the next agent turn. It may have been cut off mid-instruction or before a tool result arrived.

Structured errors help clients make this distinction. An error envelope should include a stable code, whether a retry is safe, the run state, and a correlation ID. Agent Tool Error Envelopes shows a compatible pattern.

Test the race conditions, not just the button

The happy path is easy: click Stop and see the stream close. Production correctness lives in the races. Add deterministic test hooks before model calls, before a tool dispatch, after dispatch but before receipt storage, and while a worker holds a lease.

Your cancellation test matrix should cover at least:

  1. Cancel while queued: no worker starts the first step.
  2. Cancel during token streaming: client stops, provider result is recorded as interrupted or reconciled.
  3. Cancel between model output and tool dispatch: no tool begins.
  4. Cancel during two parallel tools: every child reaches a known terminal state.
  5. Cancel after a write dispatch: reconciliation runs; the write is never blindly retried.
  6. Cancel during a process crash: a replacement worker respects the durable request.
  7. Duplicate cancel calls: one lifecycle transition and no duplicate cleanup.
  8. Resume attempt after cancellation: it creates a new attempt with explicit provenance.

Capture traces for each test and replay them when the runtime changes. AI Agent Trace Replay is useful for turning an escaped cancellation race into a permanent regression test.

A practical implementation checklist

  • Store run lifecycle state durably, including cancellation reason and timestamps.
  • Make cancellation requests authorized and idempotent.
  • Send a durable signal to workers; do not trust page disconnects as intent.
  • Check for cancellation before every new turn and side effect.
  • Propagate an abort signal and remaining deadline to streams and tools.
  • Record a confirmed terminal state only after worker cleanup finishes.
  • Reconcile writes that crossed a commit boundary.
  • Preserve interrupted output as partial, never as final.
  • Emit lifecycle events that reconnecting clients can replay.
  • Test cancellation at every boundary and after simulated crashes.

A Stop button is a promise about control. Keep that promise by treating cancellation as a first-class workflow outcome, not a disappearing HTTP connection.

FAQ

Does aborting an LLM stream stop the model?

Not necessarily. It reliably stops your client from consuming the response, but the provider may stop asynchronously, may have already buffered output, and may still report usage. Record provider request IDs and reconcile their final status when the distinction matters.

Should a cancelled AI agent run be retried automatically?

Usually no. Cancellation expresses changed user intent. Create an explicit new attempt instead. Only retry internal cleanup or a clearly idempotent read when that work is necessary to reach a known terminal state.

What is the difference between a timeout and cancellation?

A timeout is a system deadline; cancellation can come from a user, policy, operator, or parent workflow. Both can use the same propagation mechanism, but record the cause separately because the correct product response differs.

How do I cancel an agent tool that has already started a write?

Request cancellation, then query the target using the operation key or receipt. If the write committed, treat it as completed and use a separate compensating action if appropriate. Never assume a network timeout means the write failed.

Can I resume a cancelled agent run?

You can, but make it explicit. Persist a checkpoint with its inputs, completed steps, and evidence. Start a new attempt that references the old one, re-checks policy, and never repeats uncertain writes without reconciliation.

What metrics show whether cancellation works?

Track time from request to terminal state, cancelled runs with work still starting afterward, orphaned tool calls, reconciliation rate after cancellation, duplicate cancellation requests, and the fraction of partial outputs mistakenly shown as final.

title: How I Measure a Server: The Knee, Percentiles That Lie, and Little's Law
description:
I did not trust latency numbers until I could make a server slow down on purpose. This post is what came out of three small experiments in my system-design-challenges repo. Each one changed how I read a metric I reach for every day. The code is real, and the numbers below are what the scripts actually measured on this machine, not what I hoped they would be.

Side note: this is the first challenge in a repo I keep for hands-on system design. It starts with the tools for measuring a service before it moves on to architecture, storage, and distributed systems. I work through it by running things, not just reading about them.

The setup: one worker, about 10 ms of work per request

The server is deliberately boring. Every request does roughly 10 ms of CPU-bound work in a spin loop that blocks the event loop, so the whole thing behaves like a single worker: a request that arrives while another is being served waits its turn.

// server.js: a tiny server with a simulated service time
const SERVICE_MS = Number(process.env.SERVICE_MS ?? 10);
const SLOW_CHANCE = Number(process.env.SLOW_CHANCE ?? 0);
const SLOW_MS = Number(process.env.SLOW_MS ?? 0);

function busyWork(ms) {
  const end = performance.now() + ms;
  while (performance.now() < end) { /* spin: this loop is the work */ }
}

const server = http.createServer(async (req, res) => {
  if (random() < SLOW_CHANCE) await sleep(SLOW_MS);
  busyWork(...);
  res.end("ok\n");
});

One worker doing 10 ms of work has a rough capacity of 1000 / 10 = 100 requests per second. Call that an estimate. Scheduling, random service times, and bursts change the measured result, and that uncertainty is the whole point of the first experiment.

Big word: utilisation. The fraction of a worker's capacity that is currently demanded, usually written as a percentage. At 70 requests per second, this server is about 70% busy.

Experiment 1: the knee, or where a queue stops being polite

The obvious way to load-test a server is to send more traffic and watch the average. The problem is that the average is the last number to admit something is wrong.

As incoming work approaches the server's maximum rate, a queue starts forming before every request becomes slow. The high percentiles move first, because the most recent arrivals wait the longest. The experiment ramps the request rate and looks for the point where tail latency bends sharply upward. The knee.

request/s p99
60 69.4 ms
70 157.6 ms

At 70 requests per second the server is about 70% busy. Not full. Yet the slowest 1% of requests have already more than doubled to 157.6 ms. The M/M/1 estimate W = 1 / (mu - lambda) gives 33.3 ms average at that rate, and the measured mean tracked it early on, then drifted as the run got noisier near the knee.

Where the easy answer is not the full truth: people say "a server is fine until it's 100% busy, then you scale it." Not really. A queue forms well before that, and the tail feels it first. The knee is usually a fair bit below full utilisation. Your headroom is yours to choose; the knee just tells you where the comfortable margin ends.

Experiment 2: percentiles that lie, or how fan-out magnifies a small problem

A mean is one number: add every latency, divide by the count. It is easy to compute and easy to quote. It is also very good at hiding the rare, slow call that decides what a real user experiences. Percentiles show the boundary the slower traffic actually crosses: p95 is the latency that 95% of requests meet or beat.

Fan-out makes the problem worse, because a page is only as fast as its slowest parallel dependency. Every extra call is another chance to pick up a slow one. This experiment gave each dependency a 2% chance of taking 200 ms, then drove pages at 40 requests per second with increasing fan-out.

calls per page mean p95 slow pages observed
1 4.0 ms 1.5 ms ~2%
20 63.1 ms 202.1 ms 31%

Read the mean column and the load test "sounds manageable": 4 ms to 63 ms. Read the p95 and the story inverts: 1.5 ms to 202.1 ms. And observe that about 31% of 20-call pages hit the 200 ms wall. The prediction 1 - (1 - 0.02)^20 ≈ 33% matches what the run observed. A 2% dependency, fanned out 20 ways, becomes a roughly one-in-three page failure.

Pros and cons of averaging. A mean gives you one stable number you can graph and compare. Its cost is that it averages away the rare slow calls that shape actual experience. Useful for spotting drift over time; dangerous as your only performance number.

Experiment 3: Little's law as a reality check on your own measurements

Little's law says the average number of requests in the system is L = lambda times W: the arrival rate multiplied by the average time each request spends in the system. The interesting bit is that it holds for almost any stable queue, so it works as a consistency check on your measurements.

rate/s L measured lambda x W M/M/1 L
50 0.95 0.95 0.89
70 2.06 2.06 2.00
80 3.50 3.50 3.41
90 9.11 9.11 6.94

Measured L matched lambda x W across all four rows. The M/M/1 prediction stayed close at low load and drifted farthest at 90 requests per second, which is exactly where you would expect the classroom model to wobble.

Big word: Little's law. The relationship L = lambda x W between requests in flight, arrival rate, and time in the system. Because it holds for almost any stable system, when your measured L and your lambda x W stop agreeing, something is off with your measurement or your model. Investigate.

What I take away

  1. Watch percentiles, not just the average. The mean hid the real damage in both the knee and the fan-out experiments.
  2. Account for fan-out in your tail budget. A 2% dependency turns into a 31% page failure when it is 20 calls wide.
  3. Queues grow before the server looks bad. Latency is the earliest signal of saturation; the knee marks the end of comfortable headroom.
  4. Use Little's law as a sanity check. When L and lambda x W stop agreeing, trust the mismatch and dig in.

Things that may matter, with no over-claiming on my part: these are finite runs on one machine. Event-loop scheduling, a seeded random source, and the load generator all add noise, and the M/M/1 formulas are a teaching model, not a promise. Treat the charts as tendencies and the relationships as intuition, not as a spec you can copy into a capacity plan.

Try it yourself

Clone system-design-challenges and run node challenges/challenge-1-measure-a-server/part-1-the-knee/knee.js, part-2-percentiles-lie/tail.js, and part-3-littles-law/little.js from the repo root. npm test from the root runs the checks. The repo grows module by module, and the numbers on your machine will be a little different, which is part of the lesson.

title: rustgrade: a Rust scanner for the habits coding agents leave behind
description:
For a few months I've been letting coding agents write a lot of my Rust. The code compiles, the tests pass, and then I read it and find the same things over and over: .unwrap() in library code, a std Mutex held across an .await, .clone() sprinkled around until the borrow checker stops complaining.

None of that is a compile error, so the agent has no reason to stop. I wanted something that would make it stop. That turned into rustgrade.

(Full disclosure: in this demo I told the agent to use unwrap so the hook would have something to catch. When I ran it without that instruction, it just wrote the Result itself.)

What it looks for

At its core it's a scanner built on syn. No LLM, no network calls, and it doesn't need to build your crate. Right now it has 8 rules: unwrap/expect outside tests, locks held across .await, unsafe without a // SAFETY: comment, unbounded channels, anyhow in public library APIs, clones and allocations inside loops, and &String / &Vec<T> style parameters.

Here are the three I see agents get wrong most.

Holding a lock across an await:

// Flagged
async fn bump(state: &std::sync::Mutex<Counter>, db: &Db) {
    let mut c = state.lock().unwrap();
    c.n += 1;
    db.save(c.n).await; // guard is still alive here
}

// Better
async fn bump(state: &std::sync::Mutex<Counter>, db: &Db) {
    let n = {
        let mut c = state.lock().unwrap();
        c.n += 1;
        c.n
    }; // guard dropped before the await
    db.save(n).await;
}

The first version makes the future !Send, and it can deadlock if another task on the same thread goes for the lock. It also compiles fine in a lot of setups, which is exactly why it slips through.

Unwrap in a library:

// Flagged
pub fn parse_port(s: &str) -> u16 {
    s.parse().unwrap()
}

// Better
pub fn parse_port(s: &str) -> Result<u16, std::num::ParseIntError> {
    s.parse()
}

Asking for &String when you mean &str:

// Flagged
pub fn greet(name: &String) -> String {
    format!("hello, {name}")
}

// Better
pub fn greet(name: &str) -> String {
    format!("hello, {name}")
}

If you want the reasoning behind any rule, rustgrade rules --explain <rule-id> prints a before/after and what the rule can't see.

The catch with reading only syntax

Skipping type information is what makes it fast, but it also means it guesses. clone-in-loop has no idea whether you're cloning an Arc (cheap) or a big Vec (not cheap), and it doesn't look inside macros. When it's wrong, you silence it inline, and you have to say why:

// rustgrade: allow(unbounded-channel) shutdown signal, at most one message per worker
let (stop_tx, stop_rx) = std::sync::mpsc::channel::<()>();

Those reasons stay in the JSON output, so they can be reviewed in CI instead of disappearing.

Yes, clippy already has lints for some of this (unwrap_used, await_holding_lock, undocumented_unsafe_blocks, ptr_arg, borrowed_box), and rustgrade audit runs clippy as well. The reason the scanner exists is timing. Clippy needs a build. The scanner took about 20 ms on a 445-line file on my machine, which is fast enough to run on every single edit an agent makes.

I also wanted to know how noisy it is on code written by people, so I ran it on 15 well-known crates (tokio, serde, regex, syn and others). They land between A and C, and every finding is in the repo if you want to argue with them.

Using it

You can use it on its own: rustgrade scan and rustgrade audit work in a terminal or in CI, with --fail-on thresholds and SARIF output for GitHub code scanning.

For agents, it installs as a skill plus a few commands in Claude Code, Cursor, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, Copilot and Windsurf. /audit gives a crate a grade from A to F using the scanner, clippy and your tests. /harden throws hostile input at your code and only fixes what a failing test proves is broken.

In Claude Code there's also a hook that scans every edit and hands the findings straight back to the agent.

Did it actually help?

I didn't want to just assume it did, so I measured it. 27 Claude Code runs with Sonnet, three tasks, 9 runs per setup. I counted unwrap/expect in library code with cargo clippy --lib, so test code doesn't count.

  • No rustgrade: 5 left over
  • A short rustgrade section in CLAUDE.md: 0
  • Just the hook, no section: 0

Cost per run barely moved: $0.23, $0.21 and $0.22.

To be honest about it, a plain instruction in CLAUDE.md did just as well as the hook here. The difference is that the instruction only works if the agent follows it, while the hook runs no matter what. In the hook runs the agent never loaded the skill or ran the scanner on its own, so those zeros came from the hook. Whether that matters more in long sessions, or for the other seven rules, is the next thing I want to measure.

It's a small sample, so I'm treating it as a first signal, not a conclusion. One thing that did surprise me: /harden found real bugs, including deadlocks, in thread pools the agent wrote during these evals. Those pools had passed their hidden tests. I reproduced the bugs separately to make sure they were real. Everything is in the repo, including the runs where it found nothing.

I built it with help from Claude Code.

Try it 

cargo binstall rustgrade
rustgrade scan

It's MIT-licensed and I'd love contributions: new rules, fixes for false positives, support for other agents. And since the rules are heuristics, the most useful thing you can send me is a false positive from a real crate, or a rule you think is just wrong.

Repo, numbers and demo: https://github.com/angeldevmobile/rustgrade

title: Introducing Vedha: New Testing framework for Agentic World. Test your web app with an AI agent in 5 minutes (and catch the bugs it would miss)
description:
AI agents are good at clicking through a web app. They're bad at knowing whether it actually worked. An agent sees "Order placed" on the screen and reports success, even when the API behind it returned 500 and saved nothing.

This tutorial sets up an AI agent that tests your app in a real browser and checks what the server did. You'll go from zero to a test you can keep in CI in about five minutes.

We'll use Vedha, an open-source MCP server built on Playwright. It works with Claude Code, Cursor, VS Code and any other MCP client.

Step 1: Add Vedha to your agent (1 minute)

In Claude Code:

claude mcp add vedha -- npx -y @vedhajs/mcp --allow-domain localhost --out ./vedha-out

For Cursor, VS Code or Claude Desktop, add this to your MCP config:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "vedha": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "@vedhajs/mcp", "--allow-domain", "localhost", "--out", "./vedha-out"]
    }
  }
}

Two things to note:

  • --allow-domain localhost is required: the agent can only browse the domains you list. Point it at your dev server, not the open web.
  • If you've never used Playwright on this machine, run npx playwright install chromium once.

Optional: install the agent skill, which teaches the agent how to test with Vedha (declare checks, mark writes, never retry an unknown outcome):

npx skills add HMAKT99/VEDHA

Step 2: Ask the agent to test something (1 minute)

Start your app, then ask:

Test the checkout on localhost:3000: place an order for Ada and confirm it worked.

The agent opens the page and works through the flow with vedha_act. Each call is one browser action, and it can say what success looks like. Here is the call an agent sends to fill the form and submit it:

{
  "op": "fill", "intent": "enter name", "target": { "label": "Name" }, "value": "Ada",
  "then": [{
    "op": "click", "intent": "place the order",
    "target": { "role": "button", "name": "Place order" },
    "mutating": true,
    "expect": { "text_contains": "Order placed" }
  }]
}

mutating: true tells Vedha the click changes data, so it should check what the server did, not just the page.

On a healthy app, this is what the agent gets back (real output, trimmed):

step 1 (step-2): verified
result: verified
effect: server confirmed (POST /api/orders 201; read-back /api/orders confirms POST /api/orders)
changed on the page (3 added, 3 removed):
  + status: Order placed

Vedha saw the 201, then read the order list back to confirm the order is really there.

Step 3: Watch it catch a bug the page hides (1 minute)

Now the same test against a broken backend: the API returns 500, but the frontend still shows "Order placed". This is what the agent gets back (real output, trimmed):

step 1 (step-2): verified
result: failed (health_check_failed): declared checks passed, but the page reported: POST /api/orders returned 500
hint: treat this action as failed: the server or page reported an error even if the page looks fine
requests: POST /api/orders 500
  + status: Order placed
open failure: "place the order" - declared checks passed, but the page reported:
POST /api/orders returned 500. Do not report success unless a later step fixed it.

"Order placed" is on the page, and the agent's own check passed. Vedha still reports the step as failed, says why, and reminds the agent not to claim success. A browser tool that only checks the screen would have reported a pass.

Two more things Vedha does here without being asked:

  • If a submit times out and Vedha can't tell whether the order went through, it reports outcome_unknown and refuses to click "Place order" again until a read-only check settles it. No duplicate orders from a retrying agent.
  • The agent can check server state without leaving the page with vedha_probe (for example GET /api/orders).

Step 4: Turn the run into a Playwright test (1 minute)

Once a flow is verified, ask the agent:

Save that as a Playwright test.

It calls vedha_promote, which writes a plain @playwright/test spec from the verified steps. This is the real output for the order flow above:

// Generated by Vedha from an explored session. Review before committing.
import { test, expect } from "@playwright/test";

test("places an order", async ({ page }) => {
  await test.step("open the shop", async () => {
    await page.goto("/");
  });
  await test.step("enter name", async () => {
    await page.getByLabel("Name", { exact: true }).fill("Ada");
  });
  await test.step("place the order", async () => {
    await page.getByRole("button", { name: "Place order", exact: true }).click();
    await expect(page.locator("body")).toContainText("Order placed");
    await expect.poll(async () => {
      const res = await page.request.get("/api/orders");
      const body = await res.json();
      const items = Array.isArray(body) ? body : [body];
      return items.some((it) =>
        Object.entries({ name: "Ada", qty: 1, product: "Widget" }).every(([k, val]) => it[k] === val),
      );
    }).toBe(true);
  });
});

Notice the last assertion: because Vedha confirmed the order on the server during the run, the generated test checks the server too, not just the text. It also lists its assumptions at the top, so review it before committing.

Step 5: Keep it honest in CI (1 minute)

Commit the spec and run it with your normal Playwright setup. One more line makes the rest of your suite safer too:

npm install -D @vedhajs/playwright-test

import { test, expect } from "@vedhajs/playwright-test"; // instead of "@playwright/test"

With that import, any test whose own checks pass while the app answers with a 5xx, or a write request fails, fails instead of going green. That covers tests written by your agent and by people. (More on guard mode here.)

What you get

  • An agent that tests in a real browser and reports verified, failed or unknown, never "looked fine".
  • Bugs caught that the screen hides: 5xx behind a success message, rejected writes, writes that weren't stored (where the API allows a read-back).
  • Plain Playwright tests to keep, with server checks included.

How much difference does it make? In a small pilot (one model, held-out tasks, 3 trials each), the agent missed 9 seeded bugs with Vedha against 26 with Playwright MCP, using about 30% fewer tokens. Details and limits here.

Try the demo without your own app 

git clone https://github.com/HMAKT99/VEDHA && cd VEDHA
pnpm install && pnpm build
npx tsx examples/demo/run.ts

Repo, docs and benchmark data: https://github.com/HMAKT99/VEDHA (Apache-2.0)

If you try it on your app, I'd like to hear what it caught, and anything it got wrong.

title: How to Learn React Hooks (and Stop Fighting useEffect)
description:
The first React app I wrote with hooks had a useEffect that fetched a user profile. It worked on the first load. Then I added the user ID to the dependency array because the linter told me to, and the network tab filled up with the same request, over and over, until the tab froze.

I fixed it by deleting the dependency array. That was the wrong fix, and it took me an embarrassingly long time to understand why.

Most people learn hooks the way I did: copy a pattern, hit a bug, paste a Stack Overflow answer. You end up knowing a dozen workarounds and none of the ideas underneath. Here's the order I'd learn them in now.

Start with what a render actually is

Before any hook makes sense, you need one mental model. Every time state changes, React calls your component function again, top to bottom. Every variable inside it is created fresh. Every function you define inside it is a new function.

That's why this logs a stale value:

function Counter() {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);

  function handleClick() {
    setCount(count + 1);
    console.log(count); // still the old number
  }

  return <button onClick={handleClick}>{count}</button>;
}

count belongs to the render that created handleClick. It isn't a live variable that updates in place. The new value only exists in the next render. Once that clicked for me, half my "hooks are weird" complaints went away. They weren't weird. I just thought my component was an object that stuck around, and it's really a function that runs again.

useState: learn the updater form early

You'll use useState constantly, so learn the one detail that bites people. If the new state depends on the old state, pass a function:

setCount(c => c + 1);

Call setCount(count + 1) three times in one handler and you get +1, because all three read the same count. Call setCount(c => c + 1) three times and you get +3. I'd also learn that objects in state get replaced, not merged, so setUser({ ...user, name }) is the habit to build.

useEffect is for syncing with things outside React

This is where most of the pain is, and the React docs rewrite at react.dev is the best thing I've read on it. The short version: an effect is for keeping your component in sync with something React doesn't control. A network request, a subscription, a timer, a DOM API, a third-party widget.

The dependency array isn't a list of "when to run". It's a list of every value from the render that the effect reads. If you lie to it, you get stale data. If you include an object or function that's recreated every render, you get my infinite loop.

The fixes I reach for, in order:

  1. Move the function inside the effect, so it isn't a dependency at all.
  2. Depend on primitive values (user.id) instead of whole objects (user).
  3. Ask whether this needs to be an effect in the first place.

That third one matters most. The docs page You Might Not Need an Effect is worth reading twice. Filtering a list, computing a total, resetting a form when a prop changes: none of these need useEffect. You can calculate them during render. A lot of my old bugs came from effects that set state that could have just been a variable.

And write the cleanup. If an effect subscribes, starts a timer or opens a socket, return a function that undoes it. In development, Strict Mode runs your effects twice on mount to flush out missing cleanups, which is why your fetch shows up twice in the console. That's on purpose.

useRef, useMemo and useCallback can wait

useRef is simple once you see it as a box that survives renders without causing one. Use it for DOM nodes and for values you need to remember but never display, like an interval ID.

useMemo and useCallback are performance tools. I'd skip them until you have a real reason, like a slow calculation or a memoized child component that keeps re-rendering. Wrapping everything in them makes code harder to read and usually doesn't make it faster.

Custom hooks come last, and they're just functions that start with use and call other hooks. The first time you pull a useDebounce or useLocalStorage out of two components that both had the same effect, you'll get why they exist.

Build small things that break

Reading about hooks only gets you so far. These four tiny projects cover almost every common mistake:

  1. A counter with a "+3" button, to learn the updater form.
  2. A search box that fetches results as you type, to learn dependencies, cleanup and race conditions.
  3. A stopwatch with start and stop, to learn useRef for the interval ID.
  4. A dark mode toggle saved to localStorage, pulled into a custom hook.

Do them without a tutorial open. When something loops or shows stale data, that's the lesson.

Then make it stick

My actual problem with hooks wasn't understanding them once. I'd read the effects docs, get it, and a month later on a different project write the same broken fetch again. The rules of the dependency array are the kind of thing you know in theory and forget in practice.

What helped was reviewing the handful of ideas that kept tripping me up: renders are snapshots, the updater form, dependencies are what the effect reads, maybe you don't need an effect. I'd look at those notes after a day, then a few days, then a couple of weeks. That's spaced repetition, and it works better for this than rereading a tutorial when you're already stuck.

I built Recl for exactly this kind of learning. You share a video, article, reel or podcast to it, say a conference talk on effects or the react.dev page itself, and it writes a summary of the key points, files it under a topic like "React", and brings it back for review on a spaced repetition schedule. A plain notes file with calendar reminders does the same job if you'd rather not use an app. What matters is seeing it again before the next bug does the reminding for you.

I build Recl, an AI learning app that saves your videos, reels, podcasts and articles, summarizes them, sorts them into topics, and uses spaced repetition so you remember what you learned.

title: Fintech Ticket Triage with Node.js RAG: PDF Upload, Semantic Search, and Citations
description:
Short answer: use Node.js for the upload workflow, pgvector for metadata-aware semantic search, and embeddings plus citations as a validated contract; choose a shared OpenAI-compatible runtime only when its breadth is more useful than provider-specific controls.

The practical answer is a small retrieval pipeline: parse the uploaded PDF, split it into overlapping chunks, embed each chunk with its filename, page, and section, retrieve the nearest chunks with pgvector, and pass those chunks and their citation metadata to the answer model. For a fintech support queue, I would make structured output correctness the release gate, not a dashboard score or a fluent demo.

At 3 a.m., the useful page is the one that says a ticket cannot be answered because its evidence is missing or malformed. A page saying “retrieval healthy” is not enough. What page fired, and can the on-call engineer reproduce the answer from the cited source?

What should the page fire on?

Imagine the support worker receives a question about a transfer limit. The user uploaded a policy PDF last week. The worker finds a semantically similar passage, generates an answer, and the UI displays a citation. The failure worth paging on is not that the prose sounds awkward; it is that the returned object has an answer with no source, a source with no page, or a citation whose chunk was not among the retrieved chunks.

Work backwards from that contract. Store each chunk with a stable document identifier, filename, page, section, and chunk position. Keep the exact text used to create the embedding. Then the retrieval result can carry evidence forward instead of asking the answer model to recreate provenance from memory.

The instrumentation change is small: count malformed structured responses, missing citation metadata, and citations that do not resolve to retrieved chunk IDs. Include a request ID and a ticket ID in logs, but never put the uploaded document or payment details into a broad operational log. For a queue handling several document revisions, I would also record the document version beside the chunk ID, because a valid page from yesterday's policy can still be the wrong answer today. The check needs to distinguish a bad model response from a stale retrieval index, then attach the distinction to the page so the responder knows where to start. A threshold that pages on every malformed response will train the team to ignore the page; a threshold that hides all failures makes the citation promise fictional.

The page is binary.

How should a Node.js RAG handle PDF upload and semantic search?

Chunking is a boundary decision, not a magic number. A chunk that is too large brings unrelated policy language into the context; one that is too small can separate a condition from its exception. Overlap helps preserve that relationship, while page and section metadata make the result inspectable. Token counting is useful here because chunk size and top-k context must fit the answer prompt.

One workable record looks like this. It is deliberately boring: the source fields travel with the text instead of being reconstructed after generation.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
