title: CV0-004 Exam Guide: Cost, Format and Study Plan
description:
The CV0-004 exam is the test for CompTIA Cloud+. It proves you can deploy, secure, run and troubleshoot cloud environments, and it is not tied to one vendor. Our voucher costs $224.99, and most people with some admin experience can prepare in about eight weeks.

What CV0-004 proves and who should take it

Cloud+ shows that you can work with cloud services across providers. It covers design, deployment, security, operations, DevOps basics and troubleshooting. It is a practical, job-focused exam, not a theory test.

It fits systems administrators, cloud and network engineers, and support staff who are moving into cloud roles. CompTIA commonly recommends some hands-on experience in systems or network administration, plus a basic grounding such as Network+ or Server+. These are recommendations, not hard requirements.

It is a poor fit if you have never touched a server or a cloud console. In that case, start with a fundamentals exam such as AWS Cloud Practitioner or browse our entry-level certifications first.

Exam format and price at a glance

The figures below are the commonly published CV0-004 details. Confirm them on CompTIA's exam page before you book, because formats and list prices can change.

Item Detail
Exam code CV0-004
Certification CompTIA Cloud+
Question types Multiple choice and performance-based
Maximum questions 90
Time limit 90 minutes
Passing score 750 on a scale of 100 to 900
Prerequisites None required; hands-on experience recommended
Our voucher price $224.99 (USD), checked 2026-11-01

Performance-based questions put you in a simulated task, such as fixing a configuration or ordering steps. They often take longer than multiple-choice items, so they affect your pacing.

Skills measured and how much each domain weighs

CV0-004 is organized into six domains. The weights below are the commonly published ones. The takeaway is simple: architecture, deployment and security together make up over 60% of the exam.

Domain Weight
1.0 Cloud Architecture 23%
2.0 Deployment 19%
3.0 Security 19%
4.0 Operations 17%
5.0 DevOps Fundamentals 10%
6.0 Troubleshooting 12%

DevOps Fundamentals is the newer, smaller domain. Expect questions on infrastructure as code, CI/CD pipelines, containers and version control. Do not skip it just because it is only 10%, since those points are easy to win with a weekend of practice.

Download the official objectives PDF from CompTIA and use it as your checklist. Every bullet in it is fair game.

An eight-week study plan with weekly hours

This plan assumes you already know basic networking and have used a server or a cloud console. It totals about 64 hours. If you are newer to IT, stretch it to ten or twelve weeks.

Week Focus Hours
1 Cloud models, service types, shared responsibility, objectives review 8
2 Architecture: storage, compute, networking, high availability 8
3 Deployment: provisioning, migrations, templates, sizing 8
4 Security: IAM, encryption, network controls, compliance 8
5 Operations: monitoring, backup, patching, cost control 8
6 DevOps: IaC, CI/CD, containers, Git 8
7 Troubleshooting methodology and scenario drills 8
8 Timed practice exams, weak-area review 8

Worked example: turning a practice score into a plan

Say you score 68% on your first timed practice test. Break the result down by domain. If Security is at 55% and Operations at 80%, spend most of week 8 on Security. Security is worth 19% of the exam, so a 25-point gap there costs you more than a small gap in a 10% domain.

Commands worth running yourself

Reading about cloud tools is not enough for performance-based questions. Spend a few evenings in a free-tier account and run commands like these:

terraform init
terraform plan
terraform apply
docker run -d -p 8080:80 nginx
kubectl get pods
dig example.com
traceroute example.com

These cover infrastructure as code, containers, orchestration and basic network troubleshooting. Destroy resources when you finish, so you do not pay for idle services.

Common mistakes that cost points

  • Memorizing one provider. Cloud+ is vendor-neutral. Learn the concepts, then map them to AWS, Azure and Google Cloud names.
  • Using only dumps or question banks. Questions get reworded, and performance-based items need real understanding. Use practice tests to find gaps, not to memorize answers.
  • Ignoring troubleshooting order. Scenario questions often reward the first sensible step: identify the problem, check what changed, then test a fix.
  • Spending too long on early questions. With about 90 minutes, flag performance-based items and return to them if you are stuck.
  • Skipping cost and capacity topics. Right-sizing, reserved capacity and tagging show up in operations scenarios.
  • Booking before you have a date plan. Pick a test date about eight weeks out, then work backward.

Buying the voucher: delivery, redemption and refunds

Our CV0-004 CompTIA Cloud+ voucher is $224.99. One voucher covers one exam attempt. The code is emailed within 12 hours of payment and also appears in your account.

You can cancel an order for a full refund before delivery. A delivered code is non-refundable unless the test provider rejects it as invalid, already used or expired on first use. In that case, contact support within 14 days with your order number and a screenshot, and we will replace or refund the code. Details are on the refund policy and delivery policy pages.

Before you pay, check CompTIA's current list price and exam details on its own site, since we cannot show a verified list price here.

After you pass

Update your resume and professional profiles the same week. Cloud+ pairs well with a vendor certification, so many people add an AWS or Azure exam next. Our cloud computing certifications page lists options.

CompTIA certifications are commonly valid for three years and can be renewed through continuing education activities. Check your CompTIA account for the exact renewal rules that apply to your certification.

title: USA SMS API Services for Gaming Alerts in 2026 (with Compliance Evidence)
description:
Short answer: For USA SMS API services delivering gaming alert notifications, start with Twilio for flexible APIs, compare Bandwidth for domestic coverage, and compare Vonage for bulk terms; evaluate pricing and features only after compliance evidence and retry ownership are clear.

Twilio is the default starting point for a US gaming signup verification link; Bandwidth is a strong domestic-SMS alternative, and Vonage deserves a look when bulk terms and promotions affect the workload. The deciding constraint is not the advertised per-message number. It is whether the provider can leave you with defensible A2P registration evidence, a retry-safe delivery path, and an operating bill you can actually explain.

A verification link is a small message with a large blast radius. A duplicate can confuse a new player, a delayed message can turn into an abandoned signup, and a retry after a timeout can create two valid-looking records unless the application owns idempotency. My runbook starts there.

That is the control point.

For teams already carrying several backend integrations, Infrai belongs in this early comparison as a consolidation option: one REST API, one key, and one bill can remove credential and invoice reconciliation from the signup service's neighboring work. It does not decide A2P registration, and it does not turn a polling workflow into a webhook workflow. Those boundaries are part of the fit, not footnotes.

What evidence must the signup path preserve?

For a US gaming service, compliance evidence should be an input to the design, not a document gathered after launch. Keep the campaign purpose, consent text, opt-out handling, sender identity, destination, and delivery status tied to the signup attempt. Twilio's US A2P 10DLC documentation is a useful reference for the registration and messaging obligations; the provider choice does not remove the application's responsibility to retain that trail.

The message should contain a short-lived, single-use verification URL. Store a hash of the token, its expiry, the signup identifier, and the consent record. Do not put an email address or internal account identifier in the URL merely because it is convenient. The SMS provider can deliver the link; it should not become the system of record for account eligibility. When a carrier rejects a registration or a player taps an expired link, the local record should still explain what consent was collected, which template was selected, and which retry policy ran. That is the evidence an on-call engineer can use without reconstructing the event from three vendor consoles.

This is also where the options separate. Twilio is highly popular in the US, has flexible APIs, and has a strong operational reputation. Bandwidth is attractive when domestic US SMS rates and carrier-level control matter. Vonage is worth comparing for bulk discounts and promotions, while some US-specific carriers can fit a regional deployment better than a global abstraction. Those are useful differences, but none substitutes for a reviewable consent and message audit.

Which USA SMS API services fit gaming alert notifications?

I model four costs: message delivery, registration and compliance work, integration maintenance, and the cost of an incident. The last two are easy to omit because they do not appear beside an SMS unit price. A cheaper route that requires a second dashboard, a second key, and a separate status consumer can be more expensive for a small SRE team than a slightly less aggressive carrier quote.

Option Strong fit Trade-off to validate
Twilio Flexible US APIs and a familiar operational path More platform surface means more configuration and compliance state to govern
Bandwidth Domestic US SMS and teams that value carrier proximity Check regional coverage, tooling, and the evidence your team needs to retain
Vonage Bulk workloads where promotions and commercial terms matter Validate the exact US registration and delivery workflow before standardizing
Infrai A backend team that wants one REST key and bill across services while keeping SMS orchestration in its own system It is not a replacement for carrier-specific compliance judgment or a full webhook event stream

Infrai is a reasonable option for the integration boundary when one REST API, one key, and one bill remove real backend administration across the signup service and its neighboring services. Its public discovery surface exposes request and response schemas and runnable examples, and the broader surface spans 295 routes across 20 modules. That matters when the team is already operating email, storage, scheduling, or AI beside SMS and wants one consistent access pattern rather than a dozen credential dashboards.

The supporting benefit is operational accounting: the native response metadata specifies cost, latency, vendor, cache status, and request ID per call. That gives an SRE team a useful reconciliation handle without turning the article into a price leaderboard. It does not prove delivery, compliance, or uptime. Those still belong in the application and provider records.

My explicit recommendation is: try Infrai for a gaming signup service that values one backend credential and a unified REST integration across adjacent services, provided the service owns consent evidence, polling, and carrier-specific controls. Choose Twilio when broad US integration flexibility and established operational familiarity outweigh consolidation. Choose Bandwidth when domestic US SMS is the central workload and its carrier fit checks out. Choose Vonage when the bulk operating model is the material factor. For an email fallback, SendGrid and Amazon SES are real alternatives, but neither should be mistaken for a US SMS carrier decision: SendGrid fits email delivery workflows, while Amazon SES fits teams already operating their email stack on AWS.

How do I make a verification retry safe?

The provider call belongs behind an application record with a stable attempt ID. The record is created before sending, and the token is generated once. A worker may retry a timeout, but it must reuse the same idempotency key and message intent. Standard queue semantics should be treated as at-least-once, so the worker also checks the local state before sending.

A minimal Go client can show the shape without pretending that a provider response is proof of handset delivery. The example uses a documented discovery route to show the authentication and error-handling shape; the SMS send and status operations should be implemented against the selected provider's documented request schema and kept behind the same application interface.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "time"
)

func smsStatus(ctx context.Context, id string) error {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }

    url := "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/email/list"
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, url, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            if attempt == 3 {
                return err
            }
            time.Sleep(time.Duration(1<<attempt) * 250 * time.Millisecond)
            continue
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 3 {
            time.Sleep(time.Duration(1<<attempt) * 500 * time.Millisecond)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("service request failed: %s: %s", resp.Status, body)
        }
        fmt.Println(string(body))
        return nil
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("sms status retries exhausted")
}

The sample deliberately reads the key from the environment, sets an explicit method, checks non-2xx responses, and backs off on rate limiting. For a write, add a client-generated idempotency key and persist it with the signup attempt. Honor a provider's Retry-After value when present; the fixed backoff above keeps the request example short, but production code should parse that header before falling back to exponential delay.

What do verification and rollback look like?

Verification is a sequence, not a green API response. First confirm that the local attempt has one token hash and one consent record. Then confirm the provider accepted one message intent, poll status through the documented status path, and reconcile the provider request ID with the local attempt. Finally, exercise expiry and opt-out behavior in a test environment. A delivered message is not the same as a verified account.

Watch for duplicate attempt IDs, retry counts, status age, rejected messages, opt-out additions, and the ratio of accepted messages that reach a terminal status. Alert on a growing pending set, but avoid treating a single carrier delay as an outage without checking the provider status and your own queue age.

Rollback should stop new sends, preserve the evidence already collected, and leave existing tokens to expire. Do not delete the audit trail to make a dashboard look clean. If a template or campaign registration is wrong, disable that path and route new signups to a reviewed alternative; the provider-specific rollback procedure belongs in the runbook for Twilio, Bandwidth, Vonage, or the selected regional carrier.

There are boundaries worth stating plainly. The unified path has no webhook event push, so real-time multi-channel orchestration requires polling. SMS anti-abuse controls such as geographic fencing and country-price circuit breakers remain application work. Infrai also does not provide voice, WhatsApp, or RCS, and an email fallback still requires a self-built email OTP path. For a gaming service that needs carrier-native event streaming or a specialized regional control plane, a direct provider is the better choice.

The effective cost is the total runbook, not the number printed in a vendor table. Pick the provider whose compliance evidence, retry behavior, and ownership boundaries your team can operate at 03:00.

No shortcuts.

If the one-key REST boundary fits the system, start with the SMS alerts guide, then verify every route and policy against the current discovery surface before production use.

References

  • Twilio US A2P 10DLC compliance documentation
  • Twilio Messaging API documentation
  • Bandwidth Messaging API documentation
  • Vonage SMS API documentation
  • Infrai SMS alerts guide

title: Character limits have two numbers: building an ad preview around warnings and blocks
description:
Disclosure up front: I run Maestro, a B2B paid media company, and this post is about a free tool we built, the Maestro LinkedIn ad mockup. Nothing here needs you to use it. The problems are the same for anyone building a form, an editor or a preview against a platform's published limits.

The tool does one narrow job. You enter a LinkedIn single-image ad (company name, intro text, image, headline, optional description, CTA and destination URL), compare desktop and mobile views, and export a mockup plus a production brief for whoever approves the ad. It runs in the browser, needs no sign-in, and doesn't upload your creative.

Most of the interesting engineering wasn't in drawing the card. It was in deciding what the tool is allowed to say. This post walks through those decisions: how to model a limit, how to count characters when the platform doesn't tell you how it counts, how to show truncation you can't reproduce exactly, and how to test all of it.

A field has two limits, not one

LinkedIn's single image ad specifications publish two numbers for most text fields: a shorter length to avoid truncation and a hard maximum.

Field Avoid truncation Hard maximum
Introductory text 150 characters 3,000 characters (up to 10 emojis)
Headline 70 characters 200 characters
Description 100 characters 300 characters
Destination URL n/a must start with http:// or https://; up to 2,000 characters
Ad name (optional) n/a 255 characters

A single maxLength can't represent that. Set it to 3,000 and people ship intro text that gets cut off after the first line. Set it to 150 and you block copy LinkedIn would accept, which is worse, because the writer now has a tool telling them something false.

So the tool treats the two numbers as different kinds of rule:

  • Past the recommendation: show a warning. The copy may be fine. A longer intro can be a deliberate choice, and the writer decides.
  • Past the published maximum: block the review export until the field is fixed. This copy can't work.

That split, "you should look at this" versus "this can't ship", is the single most useful idea in the tool. It applies to any field with a soft and a hard limit: meta descriptions, SMS segments, push notification titles, app store subtitles.

Model the limit as data, with its source

Constants scattered through components break the first time the platform changes a number. Limits are facts with a source and a date, so they belong in one table that the UI, the validator and the export all read. Here's a simplified sketch of that shape:

type Severity = "warning" | "error";

type Rule = {
  field: "introText" | "headline" | "description" | "destinationUrl" | "adName";
  kind: "recommendation" | "maximum";
  limit: number;
  unit: "characters" | "emoji";
  source: string;      // URL of the published spec
  checkedAt: string;   // ISO date the spec was last read
};

type Finding = {
  field: Rule["field"];
  severity: Severity;
  count: number;
  limit: number;
  method: CountMethod;  // see the Unicode section
  message: string;
};

const severityFor = (rule: Rule): Severity =>
  rule.kind === "maximum" ? "error" : "warning";

Two details matter more than they look.

First, kind drives severity, not the number. Nobody has to remember that 150 is a warning and 3,000 is an error. A recommendation can never block, by construction.

Second, every rule carries checkedAt. Our page states that the limits were checked against LinkedIn's specs on September 27, 2026, and the exported brief carries the same date. If a refresh of the source fails, the honest state is "Unknown currency", not a silent pass on old numbers.

One green check is a lie: keep the states separate

The most common failure in review tools is a single status that quietly means several things. "Ready" might mean the preview renders, or the copy is within limits, or someone approved it, or the platform accepted it. Those are four different questions with four different owners.

The tool keeps them apart:

  • Preview: can the draft be pictured, with any missing fields labeled?
  • Technical check: do the supplied copy, URL and image pass the supported rules?
  • Production handoff: is the record complete enough for a named reviewer to check?
  • LinkedIn: has the intended Campaign Manager account supplied dated approval and native-rendering evidence?

Sketched as types:

type PreviewState = "Preview available" | "Preview incomplete";
type TechnicalState = "Pass" | "Needs changes" | "Unknown" | "Unsupported";
type HandoffState = "Ready for review" | "Hold";
type PlatformState = "Not checked" | "Externally verified";

type ReviewStates = {
  preview: PreviewState;
  technical: TechnicalState;
  handoff: HandoffState;
  platform: PlatformState;
};

Nothing inside the tool can set platform to "Externally verified". That value only arrives with dated, account-scoped evidence from someone who looked in Campaign Manager. A mockup can be ready for production review while LinkedIn is still Not checked, and the UI says exactly that instead of collapsing it into a checkmark.

If you build anything that previews a third-party platform, I'd start here. Write down which states your tool can know and which it can only record from someone else, and make the second group impossible to set from local code.

What counts as a character?

This is where most counters quietly go wrong. In JavaScript, "ðŸ‘ðŸ½".length is 4. A user sees one thing.

I ran a handful of strings through Node 20 to show how far the common methods drift apart:

Input .length (UTF-16 units) Code points Grapheme clusters
Hello 5 5 5
ðŸ‘ 2 1 1
ðŸ‘ðŸ½ (thumbs up + skin tone) 4 2 1
ðŸ‘©â€ðŸ’» (ZWJ sequence) 5 3 1
ðŸ‡ºðŸ‡¸ (regional indicator pair) 4 2 1
Ã© (precomposed) 1 1 1
Ã© (e + combining accent) 2 2 1
1ï¸âƒ£ (keycap) 3 3 1

The two Ã© rows look identical on screen and count differently under two of the three methods. Normalizing to NFC first collapses the second one to length 1, which is worth doing before you count anything.

Grapheme clusters are the closest match to what a person thinks of as a character. Browsers expose them through Intl.Segmenter, which MDN lists as available across browsers since April 2024:

const segmenter = typeof Intl !== "undefined" && "Segmenter" in Intl
  ? new Intl.Segmenter(undefined, { granularity: "grapheme" })
  : null;

export function countCharacters(text) {
  const s = text.normalize("NFC");
  if (segmenter) {
    let n = 0;
    for (const _ of segmenter.segment(s)) n++;
    return { count: n, method: "grapheme (Intl.Segmenter)" };
  }
  return { count: [...s].length, method: "code point fallback" };
}

Note the return shape. The count travels with the method that produced it. If an older runtime falls back to code points, the export says so.

The part you can't know

Here's the honest problem: LinkedIn doesn't publish every detail of its Unicode counting logic. It says 150 characters "including spaces, emojis, and punctuation" and a limit of 10 emojis, but not whether a skin-toned thumbs up is one character or two.

So our count is a local review count, and the tool labels it that way. Copy that lands near a boundary gets a note to test it in Campaign Manager before launch. I'd rather show an honest "approximately 150, check natively" than a confident number that turns out to be wrong at exactly the point where it matters.

Counting emoji is its own trap

The 10-emoji limit needs an emoji detector, and the obvious regex doesn't agree with itself. Testing the same strings against two Unicode properties in Node 20:

  • /\p{Extended_Pictographic}/u matched ðŸ‘ and ðŸ‘©â€ðŸ’», missed ðŸ‡ºðŸ‡¸ and 1ï¸âƒ£, and matched a plain Â© with no emoji presentation selector.
  • /^\p{RGI_Emoji}$/v (the newer v flag) matched ðŸ‘, ðŸ‘ðŸ½, ðŸ‘©â€ðŸ’», ðŸ‡ºðŸ‡¸ and 1ï¸âƒ£, did not match a bare Â©, and did match Â©ï¸ with the variation selector.

The v-flag version is closer to what a person would call an emoji, but neither is guaranteed to match LinkedIn's rule. The approach I'd use: segment into graphemes first, test each grapheme, record the counting and emoji-sequence method in the export, and treat an emoji count near 10 as a boundary to check natively.

Truncation you can't reproduce exactly

The point of the 150 and 70 recommendations is truncation, so people want the preview to show where the "â€¦see more" lands. You can't get that exactly right from outside the platform. Truncation depends on fonts, viewport width, line height and rules the platform doesn't publish.

What we did instead:

  1. Pick fixed, documented card widths. The preview uses a 552 CSS-pixel desktop card and a 358 CSS-pixel phone card inside a 390px model, and stays responsive down to 320px. Those are product decisions, written down, not claims about LinkedIn's layout.
  2. Clamp by lines in CSS, not by slicing characters. Cutting the string at character 150 is wrong for two reasons: you might split a grapheme cluster, and the platform truncates visually, by lines. A line-clamp with a More/Less toggle is closer to the real behaviour and never corrupts text.
  3. Keep the text selectable and complete. The collapsed state is presentation. The exported brief always contains the full copy, even when the preview is collapsed.
  4. Label every export. Mockup images carry the caption "Approximate feed preview â€” check the final ad in Campaign Manager", plus the mode and variant. Production artwork is exported separately, with no card chrome or crop guides on it.

If a stakeholder screenshots the mockup and forwards it, the caption goes with it. That's cheaper and more honest than chasing pixel-perfect truncation.

Don't fake unsupported states

LinkedIn's spec says paid vertical (4:5) images serve on mobile devices only. A desktop/mobile switch could squeeze a portrait image into the desktop frame anyway, and it would look plausible. It would also show a placement that doesn't exist.

So the desktop view renders an explicit unsupported state for portrait creative. The same thinking applies to the description field. LinkedIn says the description shows on LinkedIn mobile and desktop when the image is less than 200 pixels wide, or when the ad runs beyond the feed through the LinkedIn Audience Network. For a normal large feed image, the tool doesn't promise the description will be visible.

A rule of thumb I took from this: if the honest answer is "this doesn't render here", render that answer. An empty state that explains itself is better than a convincing picture of something that won't happen.

Validate images against published ranges, and stop there

The image rules come from the same LinkedIn page:

Ratio Recommended Minimum Maximum
Landscape 1.91:1 1200 Ã— 628 640 Ã— 360 7680 Ã— 4320
Square 1:1 1200 Ã— 1200 360 Ã— 360 4320 Ã— 4320
Vertical 4:5 720 Ã— 900 360 Ã— 640 2430 Ã— 4320

LinkedIn accepts JPG, PNG or GIF up to 5 MB. Our first version takes JPG and PNG only. Animated GIFs are rejected with a clear message rather than silently frozen on their first frame, because a frozen frame would misrepresent the ad.

Two things we deliberately did not do:

  • Infer a ratio tolerance. LinkedIn publishes rows, not a tolerance. Is 1200 Ã— 630 "close enough" to 1.91:1? The spec doesn't say, so the tool doesn't guess. It offers the recommended presets and Fit/Crop controls, and records the crop rectangle and focal point in the export.
  • Pretend our caps are LinkedIn's. The tool has its own limits, 5,000,000 bytes in and out and 24,000,000 decoded pixels, to keep the browser responsive. The UI calls them tool limits, not platform rules.

URLs: validate syntax, keep everything

Destination checks are simple on paper: an http:// or https:// prefix and up to 2,000 characters. LinkedIn also warns that some special characters in the query string, such as < > # % { } [ ], can cause errors.

export function checkDestination(raw) {
  const findings = [];
  let url;
  try { url = new URL(raw); } catch {
    return [{ severity: "error", message: "Not a valid URL." }];
  }
  if (!/^https?:$/.test(url.protocol))
    findings.push({ severity: "error", message: "Must start with http:// or https://." });
  if (raw.length > 2000)
    findings.push({ severity: "error", message: `Over 2,000 characters (${raw.length}).` });
  const query = raw.includes("?") ? raw.slice(raw.indexOf("?")) : "";
  if (/[<>{}\[\]]/.test(query))
    findings.push({ severity: "warning", message: "Query string contains characters LinkedIn says can cause errors." });
  return findings;
}

Note that the query check reads the raw string. new URL("https://x.com/?a=<b>").search comes back as ?a=%3Cb%3E in Node 20, so testing url.search would miss the characters the user actually typed.

Two cautions. Store the raw string exactly as entered, including every tracking parameter. Normalizing it through URL and writing back url.href can re-encode characters and change what gets launched. And syntax validity proves nothing about the page. The brief records the destination headline and next action separately, so a reviewer can judge whether the ad's promise matches the page.

Edits invalidate checks, presentation doesn't

Once there are reviews in the record, every edit raises a question: which checks does this edit invalidate?

We split inputs into two groups:

  • Content: image, crop, copy, CTA, destination and evidence. Changing any of these invalidates the checks and exports that depend on it, while unrelated evidence survives.
  • Presentation: desktop/mobile mode, collapsed/expanded copy, theme, crop overlay. Changing these changes what you see and nothing else.

One simple way to implement it: store, with each review, a hash of the content fields it covered. On edit, recompute the hashes and drop any review whose hash no longer matches. That's easier to reason about than event-driven invalidation, and it makes "why did my approval disappear?" answerable: the field it covered changed.

Import is all or nothing

Users can export a structured JSON record and import it later. The record embeds the original, delivered and logo image bytes with hashes, so a file that only contains a path isn't treated as lossless.

Import validates the whole record first: schema, embedded assets, hashes and size caps. Only then does it replace the current work, in one step. If anything fails, the current work stays as it was. A half-imported record is worse than a failed import, because it looks fine.

How to test it

These are the tests I'd write for any tool like this. Each one maps to a behaviour our tool's page commits to:

  • Boundary triplets for every rule. 149, 150 and 151 characters of intro text should give no finding, no finding and a warning. 2,999, 3,000 and 3,001 should give a warning, a warning and an error. Same pattern for 70/200 and 100/300. A 151-character intro must never produce an error.
  • A Unicode fixture file. The strings in the table above, plus the two forms of Ã©, run through countCharacters, with expected counts per method. When a runtime changes its segmentation data, this file is where you'll find out.
  • State-separation tests. Load the worked example, and no real approvals come with it. The sample ships with clearly labeled simulated review records, and loading it into the editor clears them, so it opens on Production handoff: Hold. Assert that no code path sets the platform state to verified.
  • Invalidation tests. Approve, change the headline, assert the copy review is gone and the asset review survives. Toggle desktop/mobile, assert nothing is gone.
  • Import round-trips. Export, import, and compare byte-for-byte. Then corrupt one embedded image hash and assert the import fails with the current work intact.

What I'd tell someone building one of these

  • Put limits in data, with the source and the date they were checked.
  • Give recommendations and maximums different kinds, so severity follows from type.
  • Count graphemes, say which method you used, and label the number as local.
  • Clamp visually, never slice strings, and caption every exported image as approximate.
  • Render unsupported states instead of plausible fakes.
  • Keep "we checked it" and "the platform accepted it" in separate fields that local code can't merge.

The tool isn't an official LinkedIn preview and can't predict approval, delivery or performance. It's a review step before Campaign Manager, and the final check still happens there. If you want to poke at the decisions above, the Maestro LinkedIn ad mockup is free and runs entirely in your browser.

Disclosure: I'm Tim Keen and I run Maestro, the B2B paid media company that makes the tool. LinkedIn limits in this post were taken from LinkedIn's single image ad specifications page; the tool's page records them as checked on September 27, 2026. Unicode results come from Node 20.

title: 50% of CPU time was memory stalls, so I re-ran the test
description:
50% of CPU time was memory stalls, so I re-ran the test

Pivot's October 28 post makes a claim that sounds like an excuse until you read the perf counters: on a naive hash GROUP BY over 99 million ClickBench rows, the CPU reported 100% busy while spending 50.1% of its slots stalled on memory and only 16.1% actually retiring instructions. Partition the keys into 4,096 radix buckets first, and the stall share falls to 23.5%, retiring rises to 32.2%, DRAM traffic drops from 4.5 GB to 1.5 GB. The database did more instructions (19.35 billion retired micro-ops vs 11.43 billion) and still finished faster: 3.6 seconds became 2.7 on the second run.

I believed the direction but not the round numbers, so I rebuilt the experiment at a scale my VM can hold: 20 million rows, about 3.4 million unique keys, one C program, same two algorithms.

// naive: one open-addressing hash table for all keys
size_t s = hash64(k) & MASK;
while (hk[s] && hk[s] != k) s = (s + 1) & MASK;
// radix: hash, take the top 12 bits, push into 1 of 4096 partitions,
// then aggregate each partition with its own small table
int p = (hash64(keys[i]) >> 52) & 4095;

First, the latency ladder, because it explains everything else. Pointer-chasing a randomly permuted array on this box (AMD EPYC 9D25, L1d 32 KB, L2 1 MB, L3 32 MB, from /sys):

     32 KB :   2.7 ns   (L1)
    256 KB :   7.1 ns
   1024 KB :  17.1 ns   (L2)
   8192 KB :  34.8 ns   (L3)
  32768 KB : 122.4 ns   (L3-sized, but shared/noisy on this VM)
 262144 KB : 222.9 ns   (DRAM)

Two honest caveats before the headline number. This is a cloud VM, not Pivot's bare-metal Genoa box, so my DRAM latency (223 ns) is far worse than their 50–100 ns, and the 32 MB step lands at 122 ns instead of the textbook 10–15 ns — a shared, noisy L3 does not behave like the datasheet. The shape of the cliff is still unmistakable: crossing from cache to DRAM costs roughly 80x the L1 latency here.

Then the GROUP BY itself, 20,000,000 rows, 3,390,516 distinct keys, both algorithms verified to the same count (sum of counts = 20,000,000 exactly):

naive hash : 0.958 s, groups=3390516, sum=20000000
radix 4096 : 0.234 s (aggregate phase only), groups=3390516, sum=20000000
radix end-to-end (count+fill+aggregate): 0.534 s, speedup vs naive: 1.79x

The aggregate phase alone runs 4.10x faster, but that number flatters radix: partitioning is real work, and the end-to-end figure is the one that counts. (An earlier run gave 0.975 s naive / 0.263 s aggregate-only, so treat the second decimal as noise, not signal.) Even with the fill included, radix wins by 1.79x, for exactly Pivot's reason — each partition's hash table is small enough to live in cache, so the random accesses that used to miss to DRAM mostly hit L2/L3 instead.

So the trade is real, and it generalizes beyond databases: when your working set is bigger than cache, you are not buying compute, you are buying memory round-trips. Doing more instructions to make those round-trips shorter is a good deal — 19.35 billion cheap operations beat 11.43 billion operations that each wait 223 ns. The next time a profile shows a hot CPU at 100%, check what fraction of it is actually retiring work before you reach for a faster machine. A faster machine with the same memory wall just stalls faster.

Sources: Pivot, "It's the memory latency, stupid" (Oct 28, 2026) — naive 3.9s/3.6s, 50.1% backend-bound, 16.1% retiring, 76,190,837 DRAM fills; radix 3.3s/2.7s, 23.5%, 32.2%, 25,688,280 fills; full engine 1.848s single-core, 171.8ms on 16 cores. My numbers: this VM, gcc -O2, single thread, code and raw output kept with the run notes.

.NET 10 + Pinecone: como integrar com um banco de dados vetorial
description:
🧭 1. Introdução

A integração entre .NET 10 e Pinecone permite desenvolver aplicações capazes de armazenar, pesquisar e recuperar informações por similaridade semântica.

Essa abordagem é especialmente útil em projetos de:

  • Inteligência Artificial (IA).
  • RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation).
  • Assistentes virtuais e chatbots.
  • Busca semântica de documentos.
  • Sistemas de recomendação.
  • Recuperação inteligente de conhecimento.
  • Aplicações baseadas em LLMs (Large Language Models).

Diferentemente dos bancos relacionais tradicionais, que normalmente consultam dados por condições e valores exatos, o Pinecone foi projetado para trabalhar com vetores (embeddings).

Esses vetores representam o significado de textos, documentos e outros conteúdos em um espaço matemático. Dessa forma, conseguimos encontrar informações relacionadas pelo contexto, mesmo quando as palavras utilizadas são diferentes.

Neste artigo, vamos implementar uma integração utilizando:

  • .NET 10 e C#.
  • Pinecone Vector Database.
  • API REST do Pinecone.
  • HttpClient e IHttpClientFactory.
  • Injeção de dependência.
  • Arquitetura organizada em camadas.
  • Operações de inserção e pesquisa vetorial.

🧠 2. O que é Pinecone?

O Pinecone é um banco de dados vetorial gerenciado, desenvolvido para armazenar e consultar embeddings em larga escala.

Seu principal objetivo é permitir pesquisas por similaridade entre vetores, oferecendo uma infraestrutura especializada para aplicações de IA.

Como funciona?

Imagine uma aplicação que armazena documentos sobre desenvolvimento de software.

Podemos cadastrar os seguintes conteúdos:

  • Documento 1: Como implementar autenticação JWT com .NET.
  • Documento 2: Como proteger endpoints de uma API.
  • Documento 3: Como configurar um banco de dados SQL Server.
  • Documento 4: Como implementar autorização baseada em políticas.

Quando um usuário pesquisa:

"Como proteger uma API desenvolvida em C#?"

Uma busca tradicional pode depender da correspondência exata das palavras.

Já uma busca vetorial pode encontrar documentos semanticamente relacionados, como o documento sobre autenticação JWT ou autorização baseada em políticas.

Principais conceitos

Conceito Descrição
Vector Representação numérica de um conteúdo
Embedding Processo de transformar conteúdo em vetor
Index Estrutura onde os vetores são armazenados
Namespace Divisão lógica dos registros
Metadata Informações adicionais associadas ao vetor
Similarity Search Pesquisa por proximidade entre vetores
Upsert Inserção ou atualização de vetores
Query Consulta por similaridade

🔄 3. Arquitetura de funcionamento

Uma integração com Pinecone normalmente envolve três etapas principais:

  1. Transformar o conteúdo em embeddings.
  2. Armazenar os embeddings no Pinecone.
  3. Gerar um embedding para a pesquisa e consultar os vetores mais próximos.

É importante entender que Pinecone e o modelo de embeddings possuem responsabilidades diferentes.

O Pinecone armazena e pesquisa vetores. O modelo de embeddings transforma textos em representações numéricas.

Fluxo de inserção 

flowchart TD
    A["Aplicação .NET 10"] --> B["Documento / Texto"]
    B --> C["Modelo de Embeddings"]
    C --> D["Vetor Numérico"]
    D --> E["Pinecone API"]
    E --> F["Vector Index"]
    F --> G["Armazenamento"]

Fluxo de pesquisa 

flowchart TD
    A["Usuário realiza uma pesquisa"] --> B["API .NET 10"]
    B --> C["Modelo de Embeddings"]
    C --> D["Vetor da consulta"]
    D --> E["Pinecone Query"]
    E --> F["Pesquisa por similaridade"]
    F --> G["Documentos relacionados"]
    G --> H["Resposta para a aplicação"]

Em aplicações RAG, os documentos recuperados podem ser enviados posteriormente para um LLM, que utiliza esse contexto para construir uma resposta.

🏗️ 4. Criando o projeto .NET 10

Vamos começar criando uma Web API.

dotnet new webapi -n PineconeIntegration
cd PineconeIntegration

Para este exemplo, utilizaremos a API REST diretamente por meio do HttpClient.

Essa escolha evita acoplar a aplicação a uma biblioteca específica. O repositório do SDK oficial C# foi arquivado em julho de 2026, portanto vale avaliar cuidadosamente seu estado de manutenção antes de adotá-lo em novos projetos.

Estrutura sugerida 

PineconeIntegration/
│
├── Controllers/
│   └── DocumentsController.cs
│
├── Application/
│   ├── DTOs/
│   │   ├── DocumentRequest.cs
│   │   └── SearchRequest.cs
│   │
│   └── Interfaces/
│       ├── IEmbeddingService.cs
│       └── IPineconeService.cs
│
├── Domain/
│   └── Entities/
│       └── Document.cs
│
├── Infrastructure/
│   ├── Embeddings/
│   │   └── EmbeddingService.cs
│   │
│   └── Pinecone/
│       ├── PineconeOptions.cs
│       └── PineconeService.cs
│
├── appsettings.json
└── Program.cs

A separação permite manter as responsabilidades organizadas:

  • Api: exposição dos endpoints HTTP.
  • Application: contratos, DTOs e regras de aplicação.
  • Domain: entidades e conceitos do negócio.
  • Infrastructure: integração com serviços externos, embeddings e Pinecone.

🔑 5. Criando uma conta e configurando o Pinecone

Para utilizar o serviço, acesse:

https://www.pinecone.io/

Após criar sua conta:

  1. Acesse o painel de controle.
  2. Crie um projeto.
  3. Gere uma API Key.
  4. Crie um Index.
  5. Configure a dimensão dos vetores.
  6. Selecione a métrica de similaridade.
  7. Aguarde o índice ficar disponível.

Configuração do Index

Para nosso exemplo, considere:

Configuração Valor
Nome dotnet-documents
Tipo Dense Vector
Dimension 384
Metric Cosine
Deployment Serverless

Atenção: a dimensão 384 é apenas ilustrativa. Ela precisa corresponder exatamente à dimensão produzida pelo modelo de embeddings escolhido.

A métrica Cosine é uma opção comum para pesquisas semânticas, mas a escolha deve considerar as características do modelo e da aplicação.

Obtendo o Index Host

Depois de criar o índice, obtenha seu endereço de acesso (host).

O formato é semelhante a:

https://dotnet-documents-xxxxx.svc.region.pinecone.io

O endereço real será fornecido pelo Pinecone. Não utilize um endereço fictício na aplicação.

Em produção, prefira utilizar o host específico do índice nas operações de dados.

⚙️ 6. Configurando as variáveis da aplicação

Vamos utilizar o padrão Options do .NET para centralizar as configurações.

PineconeOptions.cs 

namespace PineconeIntegration.Infrastructure.Pinecone;

public sealed class PineconeOptions
{
    public const string SectionName = "Pinecone";

    public string ApiKey { get; set; } = string.Empty;

    public string IndexHost { get; set; } = string.Empty;

    public string Namespace { get; set; } = "documents";

    public int Dimension { get; set; } = 384;
}

appsettings.json 

{
  "Pinecone": {
    "IndexHost": "",
    "Namespace": "documents",
    "Dimension": 384
  }
}

A API Key não deve ser armazenada no arquivo de configuração versionado.

Configure-a por variável de ambiente:

Pinecone__ApiKey="SUA_API_KEY"
Pinecone__IndexHost="https://SEU_INDEX_HOST"

Durante o desenvolvimento, também é possível utilizar o Secret Manager:

dotnet user-secrets init

dotnet user-secrets set "Pinecone:ApiKey" "SUA_API_KEY"

dotnet user-secrets set "Pinecone:IndexHost" "https://SEU_INDEX_HOST"

🔌 7. Criando o contrato de integração

Vamos definir uma interface para abstrair as operações do Pinecone.

IPineconeService.cs 

namespace PineconeIntegration.Application.Interfaces;

public interface IPineconeService
{
    Task UpsertAsync(
        string id,
        float[] embedding,
        string content,
        CancellationToken cancellationToken);

    Task<string> SearchAsync(
        float[] embedding,
        int topK,
        CancellationToken cancellationToken);
}

Essa abstração permite trocar a implementação futuramente sem alterar os controllers ou as regras principais da aplicação.

🧮 8. Implementando o serviço de embeddings

Antes de enviar informações para o Pinecone, precisamos transformar o texto em um vetor.

Para isso, utilizamos um modelo de embeddings.

Podemos utilizar modelos de provedores externos ou executar um modelo localmente.

Neste exemplo, vamos definir um contrato independente do fornecedor.

IEmbeddingService.cs 

namespace PineconeIntegration.Application.Interfaces;

public interface IEmbeddingService
{
    Task<float[]> GenerateAsync(
        string text,
        CancellationToken cancellationToken);
}

EmbeddingService.cs 

using PineconeIntegration.Application.Interfaces;

namespace PineconeIntegration.Infrastructure.Embeddings;

public sealed class EmbeddingService : IEmbeddingService
{
    public Task<float[]> GenerateAsync(
        string text,
        CancellationToken cancellationToken)
    {
        // Exemplo didático.
        // Substitua pela chamada real ao modelo de embeddings.

        throw new NotImplementedException(
            "Configure um provedor real de embeddings.");
    }
}

Não devemos utilizar vetores aleatórios ou gerados artificialmente em uma aplicação real.

O modelo precisa produzir embeddings semanticamente consistentes tanto para os documentos armazenados quanto para as consultas.

Regra fundamental: utilize o mesmo modelo e a mesma configuração de dimensão nas duas operações.

📦 9. Criando o serviço Pinecone com HttpClient

Agora vamos implementar a comunicação com a API REST.

O Pinecone oferece operações de Data Plane para armazenar e pesquisar vetores.

Utilizaremos:

  • POST /vectors/upsert
  • POST /query

As chamadas serão direcionadas ao host específico do índice.

PineconeService.cs 

using System.Net.Http.Json;
using System.Text.Json;
using PineconeIntegration.Application.Interfaces;
using PineconeIntegration.Infrastructure.Pinecone;

namespace PineconeIntegration.Infrastructure.Pinecone;

public sealed class PineconeService : IPineconeService
{
    private readonly HttpClient _httpClient;
    private readonly PineconeOptions _options;

    private static readonly JsonSerializerOptions JsonOptions =
        new(JsonSerializerDefaults.Web);

    public PineconeService(
        HttpClient httpClient,
        Microsoft.Extensions.Options.IOptions<PineconeOptions> options)
    {
        _httpClient = httpClient;
        _options = options.Value;
    }

    public async Task UpsertAsync(
        string id,
        float[] embedding,
        string content,
        CancellationToken cancellationToken)
    {
        ValidateEmbedding(embedding);

        var request = new
        {
            vectors = new[]
            {
                new
                {
                    id,
                    values = embedding,
                    metadata = new
                    {
                        content
                    }
                }
            },
            @namespace = _options.Namespace
        };

        using var response = await _httpClient.PostAsJsonAsync(
            "/vectors/upsert",
            request,
            JsonOptions,
            cancellationToken);

        response.EnsureSuccessStatusCode();
    }

    public async Task<string> SearchAsync(
        float[] embedding,
        int topK,
        CancellationToken cancellationToken)
    {
        ValidateEmbedding(embedding);

        if (topK is < 1 or > 1000)
        {
            throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(topK));
        }

        var request = new
        {
            vector = embedding,
            topK,
            includeMetadata = true,
            includeValues = false,
            @namespace = _options.Namespace
        };

        using var response = await _httpClient.PostAsJsonAsync(
            "/query",
            request,
            JsonOptions,
            cancellationToken);

        response.EnsureSuccessStatusCode();

        return await response.Content.ReadAsStringAsync(
            cancellationToken);
    }

    private void ValidateEmbedding(float[] embedding)
    {
        ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(embedding);

        if (embedding.Length != _options.Dimension)
        {
            throw new ArgumentException(
                $"Expected {_options.Dimension} dimensions, " +
                $"but received {embedding.Length}.");
        }

        if (embedding.Any(value => !float.IsFinite(value)))
        {
            throw new ArgumentException(
                "Embedding contains invalid numeric values.");
        }
    }
}

Entendendo a implementação

UpsertAsync

Envia um vetor para o Pinecone com:

  • ID único.
  • Valores numéricos do embedding.
  • Metadata com o conteúdo original.
  • Namespace de armazenamento.

Se o ID já existir, a operação atualiza o registro.

SearchAsync

Recebe o vetor de pesquisa e solicita os registros mais próximos.

O parâmetro topK determina a quantidade máxima de resultados solicitados.

A propriedade includeMetadata permite recuperar os dados associados aos vetores.

🔐 10. Configurando autenticação e injeção de dependência

Vamos registrar o HttpClient e os serviços no container de dependências do .NET.

Program.cs 

using PineconeIntegration.Application.Interfaces;
using PineconeIntegration.Infrastructure.Embeddings;
using PineconeIntegration.Infrastructure.Pinecone;

var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);

builder.Services.AddControllers();

builder.Services
    .AddOptions<PineconeOptions>()
    .Bind(builder.Configuration.GetSection(
        PineconeOptions.SectionName))
    .Validate(
        options => !string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(options.ApiKey),
        "Pinecone API Key is required.")
    .Validate(
        options =>
            Uri.TryCreate(
                options.IndexHost,
                UriKind.Absolute,
                out var uri) &&
            uri.Scheme == Uri.UriSchemeHttps,
        "A valid HTTPS Index Host is required.")
    .Validate(
        options => options.Dimension > 0,
        "Dimension must be greater than zero.")
    .ValidateOnStart();

builder.Services.AddHttpClient<IPineconeService, PineconeService>(
    (serviceProvider, client) =>
    {
        var options = serviceProvider
            .GetRequiredService<
                Microsoft.Extensions.Options.IOptions<PineconeOptions>>()
            .Value;

        client.BaseAddress = new Uri(
            options.IndexHost.TrimEnd('/') + "/");

        client.Timeout = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30);

        client.DefaultRequestHeaders.Add(
            "Api-Key",
            options.ApiKey);

        client.DefaultRequestHeaders.Add(
            "X-Pinecone-Api-Version",
            "2025-10");
    });

builder.Services.AddScoped<IEmbeddingService, EmbeddingService>();

var app = builder.Build();

app.UseHttpsRedirection();

app.MapControllers();

app.Run();

A versão da API utilizada no exemplo é 2025-10, conforme a documentação de referência consultada. Antes de publicar em produção, verifique a versão estável mais recente e a compatibilidade dos endpoints utilizados.

📥 11. Criando o endpoint para cadastrar documentos

Vamos disponibilizar um endpoint para receber textos e armazenar seus respectivos embeddings.

DocumentRequest.cs 

using System.ComponentModel.DataAnnotations;

namespace PineconeIntegration.Application.DTOs;

public sealed record DocumentRequest(
    [Required]
    [StringLength(10000, MinimumLength = 3)]
    string Content);

DocumentsController.cs 

using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc;
using PineconeIntegration.Application.DTOs;
using PineconeIntegration.Application.Interfaces;

namespace PineconeIntegration.Controllers;

[ApiController]
[Route("api/documents")]
public sealed class DocumentsController : ControllerBase
{
    private readonly IPineconeService _pineconeService;
    private readonly IEmbeddingService _embeddingService;

    public DocumentsController(
        IPineconeService pineconeService,
        IEmbeddingService embeddingService)
    {
        _pineconeService = pineconeService;
        _embeddingService = embeddingService;
    }

    [HttpPost]
    public async Task<IActionResult> Create(
        [FromBody] DocumentRequest request,
        CancellationToken cancellationToken)
    {
        var embedding = await _embeddingService.GenerateAsync(
            request.Content,
            cancellationToken);

        var id = Guid.NewGuid().ToString();

        await _pineconeService.UpsertAsync(
            id,
            embedding,
            request.Content,
            cancellationToken);

        return Created(
            $"/api/documents/{id}",
            new
            {
                Id = id,
                Message = "Document successfully indexed."
            });
    }
}

Exemplo de requisição 

POST /api/documents
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "content": "O .NET 10 permite desenvolver APIs modernas utilizando C#."
}

O processo será:

  1. Receber o documento.
  2. Gerar seu embedding.
  3. Criar um identificador.
  4. Enviar o vetor para o Pinecone.
  5. Retornar o resultado da operação.

🔎 12. Criando o endpoint de pesquisa semântica

Agora vamos implementar a pesquisa.

SearchRequest.cs 

using System.ComponentModel.DataAnnotations;

namespace PineconeIntegration.Application.DTOs;

public sealed record SearchRequest(
    [Required]
    [StringLength(2000, MinimumLength = 2)]
    string Query,

    [Range(1, 20)]
    int TopK = 5);

Adicione o endpoint ao DocumentsController:

[HttpPost("search")]
public async Task<IActionResult> Search(
    [FromBody] SearchRequest request,
    CancellationToken cancellationToken)
{
    var embedding = await _embeddingService.GenerateAsync(
        request.Query,
        cancellationToken);

    var results = await _pineconeService.SearchAsync(
        embedding,
        request.TopK,
        cancellationToken);

    return Ok(new
    {
        Query = request.Query,
        Results = results
    });
}

Exemplo de requisição 

POST /api/documents/search
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "query": "Como desenvolver uma API moderna com C#?",
  "topK": 5
}

O Pinecone retornará os registros mais próximos do vetor da consulta.

Cada resultado pode conter:

  • ID do vetor.
  • Score de similaridade.
  • Metadata.
  • Conteúdo original, quando armazenado na metadata.

O score representa uma medida de similaridade conforme a métrica configurada no índice. Não deve ser interpretado automaticamente como uma porcentagem de confiança.

🤖 13. Integrando Pinecone com RAG

Uma das aplicações mais interessantes do Pinecone é a construção de soluções RAG.

RAG significa Retrieval-Augmented Generation e combina recuperação de informações com geração de respostas por modelos de linguagem.

Como funciona?

Imagine um chatbot corporativo que responde perguntas sobre documentos internos.

O fluxo pode ser:

  1. O usuário envia uma pergunta.
  2. A aplicação gera o embedding da pergunta.
  3. O Pinecone pesquisa os documentos mais relevantes.
  4. A aplicação recupera os conteúdos encontrados.
  5. Os conteúdos são adicionados ao contexto do LLM.
  6. O modelo gera uma resposta fundamentada nas informações recuperadas.

Arquitetura RAG 

flowchart TD
    A["Usuário"] --> B["API .NET 10"]
    B --> C["Embedding da pergunta"]
    C --> D["Pinecone Vector Search"]
    D --> E["Documentos relevantes"]
    E --> F["Construção do contexto"]
    F --> G["LLM"]
    G --> H["Resposta contextualizada"]
    H --> A

Essa arquitetura pode ser aplicada em:

  • Chatbots de atendimento.
  • Assistentes de documentação técnica.
  • Sistemas de suporte interno.
  • Pesquisa de contratos.
  • Consulta de manuais.
  • Bases de conhecimento corporativas.

Importante: a recuperação de documentos não garante, por si só, que o LLM responderá corretamente. É necessário controlar o contexto, as permissões, as fontes e a qualidade das respostas.

🧱 14. Boas práticas de arquitetura e desenvolvimento

Para utilizar Pinecone em aplicações corporativas, recomendo observar alguns pontos.

🔐 Segurança

  • Nunca exponha a API Key no frontend.
  • Utilize variáveis de ambiente ou um cofre de segredos.
  • Restrinja as permissões das credenciais.
  • Utilize HTTPS.
  • Implemente autenticação e autorização na API .NET.
  • Separe os namespaces conforme as necessidades de isolamento.
  • Não permita que o usuário escolha livremente namespaces sem validação.

⚡ Performance

  • Utilize IHttpClientFactory.
  • Configure timeout adequado.
  • Avalie operações em lote para grandes volumes.
  • Evite gerar embeddings repetidos para conteúdos que não mudaram.
  • Utilize IDs estáveis quando precisar atualizar documentos.
  • Recupere apenas os metadados necessários.
  • Avalie o custo e a latência das consultas.

📊 Observabilidade

Monitore:

  • Tempo de geração dos embeddings.
  • Tempo de resposta do Pinecone.
  • Quantidade de vetores cadastrados.
  • Quantidade de resultados recuperados.
  • Erros de autenticação e comunicação.
  • Consumo e custos associados às operações.

Evite registrar API Keys, documentos confidenciais ou informações pessoais nos logs.

🧩 Consistência dos embeddings

O modelo de embeddings utilizado na indexação deve ser compatível com o modelo utilizado na consulta.

Se trocar o modelo, a dimensão ou a estratégia de geração, considere criar um novo índice e reprocessar os documentos.

🧪 15. Estratégia de testes

Uma integração bem estruturada também precisa de testes.

Sugestões:

Cenário Resultado esperado
Inserção de documento Vetor armazenado
Atualização de documento Registro atualizado
Consulta válida Resultados encontrados
Vetor com dimensão incorreta Validação rejeitada
API Key inválida Erro de autenticação
Index Host incorreto Falha de comunicação
Pinecone indisponível Tratamento de falha
Consulta sem resultados Lista vazia
Namespace incorreto Isolamento respeitado

Uma boa estratégia é utilizar mocks para testar os serviços de aplicação e testes de integração controlados para validar a comunicação real com o Pinecone.

🏛️ 16. Evoluindo a solução

Depois de implementar as operações básicas, podemos evoluir a arquitetura para suportar cenários mais complexos.

Funcionalidades futuras

  • Upload e processamento de PDF.
  • Divisão de documentos em chunks.
  • Pipeline assíncrono com RabbitMQ.
  • Processamento em lote.
  • Integração com Azure OpenAI ou outros provedores de LLM.
  • Busca híbrida: semântica e textual.
  • Filtros por metadata.
  • Controle de acesso por usuário e organização.
  • Versionamento de documentos.
  • Estratégias de reindexação.
  • Monitoramento com OpenTelemetry.

⚠️ 17. Pontos importantes antes de utilizar em produção

O exemplo apresentado demonstra o fluxo essencial, mas uma aplicação real precisa de algumas evoluções:

  1. Implementar um provedor real de embeddings.
  2. Criar uma estratégia de chunking para documentos extensos.
  3. Implementar políticas de retry e tratamento de erros transitórios, respeitando os limites do serviço.
  4. Definir limites de tamanho e quantidade de registros por requisição.
  5. Criar uma estratégia de atualização e exclusão de documentos.
  6. Garantir isolamento entre clientes e organizações.
  7. Validar a compatibilidade entre dimensão e modelo de embeddings.
  8. Implementar monitoramento de custos e latência.
  9. Tratar indisponibilidade do serviço externo.
  10. Avaliar a retenção e proteção dos dados armazenados.

Outro detalhe importante: Pinecone não substitui necessariamente um banco relacional. Uma arquitetura pode utilizar SQL Server ou PostgreSQL para os dados transacionais e Pinecone para a recuperação semântica.

🎯 18. Conclusão

A integração entre .NET 10 e Pinecone abre possibilidades interessantes para aplicações que precisam trabalhar com Inteligência Artificial, recuperação de conhecimento e pesquisas semânticas.

Com uma arquitetura organizada, utilizando interfaces, injeção de dependência e HttpClient, conseguimos manter a integração desacoplada e preparada para evoluções futuras.

O Pinecone pode atuar como uma camada especializada de recuperação vetorial, enquanto o .NET 10 permanece responsável pelas regras de negócio, exposição das APIs, segurança e orquestração dos serviços.

Mais do que integrar um banco de dados, estamos construindo uma base para aplicações inteligentes, capazes de recuperar informações pelo significado e não apenas pela correspondência exata de palavras.

O futuro das aplicações modernas não está somente em armazenar dados, mas também em conseguir interpretar, relacionar e recuperar conhecimento.

title: Terraform: un plan de cambio que se pueda explicar
description:
Cuando un cambio de infraestructura falla, el problema no siempre es que Terraform haya calculado mal. Muchas veces el plan era correcto, pero nadie pudo explicar a tiempo qué iba a cambiar, qué evidencia faltaba o cómo volver atrás. Para una guardia SRE, un plan útil es también un contrato de comunicación.

El síntoma: un plan correcto que nadie entiende

El incidente suele empezar con una frase pequeña: “solo son unos recursos”. Después aparecen decenas de líneas, un -/+ inesperado y una aprobación que se hace con prisa. El plan pasa, pero la confianza no.

He visto que el riesgo sube cuando el equipo revisa el número de recursos en vez de revisar las consecuencias. Crear dos recursos no es automáticamente seguro; reemplazar uno puede romper una dependencia que no aparece en el título del pull request. Un plan sin contexto se vuelve una lista, no una decisión.

La primera señal de alerta es que la persona que aprueba no puede contestar tres preguntas:

  1. ¿Qué comportamiento cambia para el usuario?
  2. ¿Qué dependencia puede quedar inestable?
  3. ¿Cuál es el paso concreto para recuperar el servicio?

Si la respuesta es “lo vemos después del apply”, ya hay deuda de operación.

Qué debe responder un buen plan

Un plan de Terraform debería ser legible para alguien que no escribió el módulo. Antes de mirar los detalles, dejo un resumen corto en el pull request:

  • Intención: qué capacidad se añade o qué problema se corrige.
  • Alcance: cuentas, regiones, clusters y entornos afectados.
  • Cambio sensible: reemplazos, permisos, reglas de red o datos que se destruyen.
  • Dependencias: qué servicio debe estar sano antes de aplicar.
  • Recuperación: qué se revierte y qué no puede revertirse automáticamente.

Luego comparo ese resumen con el plan real. Si el texto dice “actualizar una regla” pero Terraform muestra un reemplazo, el cambio se detiene. Esa pausa es barata; una sorpresa en producción no lo es.

También conviene guardar el hash del commit, la versión del proveedor y el workspace usado. Parece detalle menor, pero evita discutir sobre un plan que ya no corresponde al código actual. En la practica, muchos minutos se pierden por esa confusión.

Un flujo de revisión que funciona en guardia

Uso cuatro pasos, incluso para cambios que parecen rutinarios.

1. Generar el plan en un entorno reproducible

El job debe registrar el commit, la versión de Terraform, los proveedores y el estado remoto. Si el estado cambia durante la revisión, se genera un plan nuevo. No se aplica un archivo viejo solo porque ya tiene una aprobación.

2. Separar cambios esperados y cambios laterales

Marco los recursos que forman parte de la intención y dejo aparte todo lo demás. Un cambio lateral puede ser drift, una variable compartida o una lectura distinta del proveedor. No lo escondo para que el diff se vea bonito: lo investigo.

3. Probar la explicación, no solo la sintaxis

Otra persona lee el resumen y responde qué pasará si el proveedor devuelve un error a mitad del apply. Si no entiende el flujo, falta documentación. Esta revisión funciona como una pequeña prueba de contrato entre Terraform y la operación.

En cambios que disparan notificaciones o validaciones por correo, dejo una evidencia verificable y con tiempo de expiración. Para depurar señales de correo tras un drenado, puede servir señales de correo en un drenado de nodo; la idea es la misma: cada señal debe llevar contexto suficiente para no depender de memoria humana. A veces el test aparece escrito como “tamp mail com” o “temp org mail” en una nota antigua; lo trato como texto de prueba, no como una identidad real.

4. Acordar una ventana de observación

El apply no termina cuando el comando devuelve código cero. Defino qué métricas mirar, durante cuánto tiempo y qué umbral detiene el cambio. En flujos con email también conviene validar la evidencia de un email, porque un mensaje enviado no significa que el usuario haya completado el paso siguiente.

Cómo dejar preparado el rollback

Un rollback confiable empieza antes del apply. Primero clasifico el cambio:

  • Reversible: se puede volver al commit y aplicar sin migración adicional.
  • Reversible con cuidado: necesita restaurar una variable, una regla o un secreto.
  • No reversible: modifica datos, consume una migración o cambia una dependencia externa.

Para los dos últimos casos, el runbook incluye una copia o exportación comprobada, el propietario de la decisión y una condición clara de parada. “Ejecutar el commit anterior” no es suficiente si el recurso ya fue reemplazado o si el proveedor conserva un efecto fuera del estado.

Un patrón práctico es usar dos artefactos: el plan que se va a aplicar y un documento breve de recuperación. El segundo contiene comandos, señales esperadas y el último punto seguro. No incluyo secretos en ninguno de los dos. Si el rollback requiere improvisar, todavía no está listo.

Checklist antes de aplicar

  • [ ] El plan fue generado desde el commit que se revisó.
  • [ ] La cuenta, región y workspace están confirmados.
  • [ ] Los reemplazos y permisos tienen una explicación explícita.
  • [ ] El drift fue investigado o aceptado con un dueño.
  • [ ] Existe un último punto seguro y un procedimiento de recuperación.
  • [ ] Las métricas y logs de observación están abiertos.
  • [ ] La ventana permite esperar el resultado, no solo lanzar el comando.
  • [ ] El equipo sabe quién puede detener el cambio.

Si una casilla queda vacía, el cambio puede esperar. La presión de “aplicar antes del stand-up” rara vez compensa una dependencia que nadie ha mirado.

Conclusión

Terraform produce un plan técnico, pero la guardia necesita una decisión operable. Un buen flujo conecta intención, diff, dependencias, observación y recuperación. Cuando cualquiera del equipo puede explicar qué cambia y cómo parar, el plan deja de ser una salida de consola y se convierte en una herramienta SRE.

No hace falta añadir más automatización a cada incidente. A veces basta con un resumen honesto, un artefacto reproducible y un rollback que otra persona pueda ejecutar sin adivinar. Esa claridad es pequeña, pero aguanta mejor cuando la noche se complica.

title: Looking for affordable image/video moderation API – pain points
description:
I've been evaluating content moderation APIs for a new project, and finding the right balance between cost, reliability, and data security is harder than expected.

Major cloud providers like AWS Rekognition and Google Cloud offer solid solutions, but their pricing can get steep fast, especially when processing video at scale. Smaller, specialized APIs like Sightengine and Clearview have more granular pricing, but I haven't used them extensively.

My priorities are straightforward: affordable per-image or per-video costs, reliable detection for adult content and violence, and clear data handling guarantees (no using my data for training). For indie projects, all three matter equally.

I'm leaning toward testing a couple niche providers that seem more indie-friendly, but I'd rather hear from anyone who's actually deployed these in production. What are you using, and have you run into hidden costs or reliability issues at higher volumes?

Happy to share findings once I've tested a few options.

title: Session Timeout UX: Show What Survives Sign-In in Your Public Demo
description:
A useful session timeout UX demo shows the work before expiry, the sign-in transition, and the exact state afterward. Make it clear which values were saved and which were still drafts. Returning to the same screen does not prove that unsaved work survived, and seeing text in a field does not prove it was stored successfully.

For a developer building a SaaS in public, that sequence gives peers a concrete continuity problem to review. It is more informative than a screenshot of a “Session expired” message or an unqualified claim that the app keeps everything safe.

The project-note editor below is fictional. All example values and states are prepared for explanation. This is a review workflow, not a report of testing a real app, and it does not recommend changing a production authentication policy for the sake of a recording.

Define the activity that should continue

Imagine a planning app with a project title and a longer meeting note. The user has saved the project title, then started editing the note without submitting the latest changes. Their authenticated session expires while that note is open.

There are several different things to inspect: the saved title, the unsaved note, the user's location in the task, and their permission to continue. Give each one an explicit expected state in your own review notes.

Do not use “restore the session” as a catch-all phrase. A new authenticated session, a restored page, and recovered draft data are separate results. A product can achieve one and fail another.

Keep the public demonstration scoped to the activity. You do not need to expose authentication tokens, internal account information, or a customer's workspace to show whether a prepared note remains available after sign-in.

Prepare a before-expiry record

Use distinctive, harmless sample values that a viewer can recognise later. The note might contain a short prepared agenda with an unfinished final line. A generic paragraph of filler makes an accidental reset harder to spot.

State whether the displayed note is already saved. If the interface has a save indicator, include it in the recording and check what that indicator actually means in the implementation. Do not call a value server-saved merely because a spinner stopped.

Record the expected outcome before triggering expiry. That prevents a successful-looking return from becoming the standard after the fact. The demonstration should answer a question you deliberately chose to inspect.

Keep a copy of the prepared values in your private review record. After sign-in, compare against that record rather than relying on memory or assuming that similar-looking text is identical.

Trigger expiry under known test conditions

Use a suitable test environment and a supported way to exercise the expired-session path. Describe the relevant conditions without publishing credentials or turning a temporary test configuration into advice for production.

Distinguish a real expiry from a mockup that displays the message. A simulated screen can help review wording, but it cannot establish that the application handles an expired credential, redirects correctly, or preserves a draft.

If you shorten a test session for the demonstration, say that the timing is a test condition. A recording with an edited pause should also say that the waiting period was compressed.

Do not claim that every expiry path behaves identically. Inactivity, an explicitly ended session, and an account change may have different consequences. Choose the path you intend to show and keep other cases in a separate check list.

Show what the person can do at the interruption

When the app asks the person to sign in again, record the available action and the explanation beside it. A viewer should be able to understand whether their work is still present, temporarily unavailable, or known to be lost.

Do not promise draft preservation in the message before the behavior supports it. If the system cannot recover a draft, the explanation needs to reflect that limit while the product team investigates the design.

Avoid replacing the whole flow with a still image of a warning. The transition matters: does the interruption cover the editor, replace it, or take the person to another page? Those choices affect what someone thinks has happened to the note.

Ask a peer to describe their next action from the visible state. Their answer can reveal unclear wording. It cannot verify the authentication or storage behavior behind the interface.

Compare the state after sign-in

Complete sign-in using a prepared test account through the normal supported flow. Return to the project and compare the saved title, unsaved note, and task location with the before-expiry record.

Show the full relevant note, including its unfinished final line. A restored first paragraph can hide lost edits farther down. Check whether the interface distinguishes a recovered draft from the last stored version.

If the note reappears, establish what that result means. It might still be an unsaved draft awaiting submission. The demo should not imply that recovery automatically completed the user's original action.

Then perform the intended save under the current authenticated state and check the supported confirmation. Treat that as a further step. Recovery, permission to save, and successful persistence each deserve their own observation.

Use accessibility guidance with its actual scope

The W3C explanation of re-authentication describes a Level AAA criterion: after an authenticated session expires, the person can continue their activity without losing data when they authenticate again. It explains why losing work can especially affect people who need more time.

That gives the review a useful goal. It does not mean a short clip proves that the whole application conforms to WCAG, or that one particular storage design is required in every system.

Review the interaction with the input methods and assistive technology relevant to your actual implementation. A pointer recording does not establish focus behavior, an accessible explanation, or a usable route back for a keyboard user.

State the checks performed and their limits. A public demo can show a specific continuity path while a separate implementation review addresses the rest of the criterion and the broader product requirements.

Keep recovered data tied to the right person

Preserving a note is not the only requirement. The application must also handle the identity and access under which that note can be viewed or submitted. Do not treat any successful sign-in as permission to attach previous work to the new account.

For the fictional editor, record an unresolved account-change case separately from the same-account demonstration. It may need a design decision about how to explain available drafts without exposing another person's content.

Do not improvise a storage workaround merely to make the public sequence look smooth. Local retention, shared devices, server storage and deletion have different implications that belong in the actual product's design and security review.

The public artifact should report what was observed under the stated conditions. A preserved sample note is useful evidence for one path, not a certificate that draft recovery is safe across every device, identity and failure condition.

Ask founder peers one continuity question

Buildside is the founder-community context for this review. Uriel Bitton builds and runs Buildside, which is this article's publisher relationship. A prepared demo gives peers a specific interaction to assess without asking them to inspect private customer work.

Choose one question: can they tell what survived, can they identify what still needs saving, or does the return location match their understanding of the task? Keep implementation findings separate from opinions about the message.

If you make a revision, repeat the relevant before-and-after sequence. A clearer sentence is a useful improvement, but it does not repair lost state by itself. Show the state comparison again when behavior changes.

Keep the version, conditions, prepared values and unresolved cases in your development notes. Your next build-in-public update can report one checked improvement and the boundary around it. That gives readers useful progress while preserving an honest account of the work still left to verify.
