title: CDC Schema Changes: What Breaks and How to Ship Them
description:
On Friday at 17:40, someone renamed one column in the orders table. The pipeline stayed green all weekend. On Monday, the revenue dashboard showed zero for Saturday and Sunday. Nothing failed, and that was the problem.

This is Part 5 of CDC in Production. In Part 4 the sink learned to survive duplicates, late events and deletes. This time the table itself changes. We'll follow a schema change through the pipeline, look at the registry rules that decide what's allowed, see what Snowflake and the lakehouse can absorb, and finish with a migration pattern that never breaks either side.

Prefer to watch? Here's the 7-minute video version with animated diagrams:

Video link: CDC Schema Changes: What Breaks and How to Ship Them

How a schema change travels

Postgres logical decoding (the feature that turns the write-ahead log into row changes) doesn't carry DDL. So Debezium never sees the ALTER TABLE itself. It notices the new shape on the next row change for that table and refreshes its in-memory schema. That event goes out with the new structure.

If you use Avro, the converter then registers the new structure as a new schema version in Schema Registry, a service that stores every version of each message schema. Versions are grouped under a subject; with the default naming, the value schema for topic shop.public.orders lives under shop.public.orders-value. Before accepting a new version, the registry runs a compatibility check against what's already there.

The converter is configured on the connector (or the Connect worker):

"value.converter": "io.confluent.connect.avro.AvroConverter",
"value.converter.schema.registry.url": "http://schema-registry:8081"

Registry compatibility modes

Compatibility is the rule the registry uses to decide whether a new version may be registered. The default is BACKWARD.

Mode Guarantee Upgrade first
BACKWARD (default) Consumers using the new schema can read data written with the old one Consumers
FORWARD Consumers using the old schema can read data written with the new one Producers
FULL Both directions Either side, independently

By default the check compares only against the latest version. The _TRANSITIVE variants (BACKWARD_TRANSITIVE and so on) compare against every version, which matters if a consumer might replay old data from the start of a topic.

What does that allow in practice, with Avro?

Change BACKWARD FORWARD FULL
Add an optional field (has a default) ✅ ✅ ✅
Remove an optional field ✅ ✅ ✅
Add a required field (no default) ❌ ✅ ❌
Remove a required field ✅ ❌ ❌

All of it comes from one rule in Avro's schema resolution: if the reader's schema has a field with no default, and the data was written without that field, the read fails. With Debezium, a nullable Postgres column becomes an optional field with a null default. A NOT NULL column becomes a required field, unless Debezium can carry the column's default value into the schema (it does this for many defaults; for function defaults, see mistake 4 below).

The rename, two ways

amount_cents became total_cents. To Debezium, that's one field gone and a new one added.

If the column is NOT NULL, the new field is required, with no default. Under BACKWARD, the registry rejects it. The converter throws, and with Kafka Connect's default errors.tolerance=none, the connector task fails. That's loud, and loud is good: someone gets paged on Friday.

In the real incident, the column was nullable. Both fields are optional, so the registry accepts the change and nothing turns red. Snowflake, with schema evolution switched on, adds a TOTAL_CENTS column. The old AMOUNT_CENTS column gets NULL on every new row. Every dashboard still sums AMOUNT_CENTS, so weekend revenue reads zero.

A failed connector is the good outcome. The dangerous schema changes are the ones every system accepts.

What Snowflake absorbs

Schema evolution lets a load add columns to the target table automatically. It needs three things:

ALTER TABLE analytics.orders SET ENABLE_SCHEMA_EVOLUTION = TRUE;

-- The loading role needs EVOLVE SCHEMA (or OWNERSHIP) on the table
GRANT EVOLVE SCHEMA ON TABLE analytics.orders TO ROLE loader;

and a supported loading method: COPY INTO (with MATCH_BY_COLUMN_NAME), Snowpipe, or Snowpipe Streaming. Plain INSERT can't evolve a table.

And it does only two things:

  • it adds new columns, and
  • it drops NOT NULL from columns that are missing in new data.

It never renames and never changes a type.

Type changes through ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN are stricter still:

Change Allowed?
Make a VARCHAR longer ✅
Raise a number's precision ✅
Change a number's scale ❌
Make a VARCHAR shorter ❌
Turn a number into a VARCHAR ❌

So if Postgres moves price from numeric(10,2) to numeric(12,4), Snowflake can't follow in place. The scale changed. You add a new column, backfill it, and switch readers over, which is the pattern at the end of this post.

The lakehouse: more forgiving, not magic

Apache Iceberg tracks every column by a unique field ID, not by its name. Renames and drops are metadata changes, so no data files are rewritten. A new column gets a fresh ID, so it never reads old data by mistake, even if it reuses an old name. Type changes are limited to safe widening: int to long, float to double, or a decimal with more precision and the same scale.

Delta Lake can rename and drop columns only with column mapping enabled:

ALTER TABLE orders SET TBLPROPERTIES (
  'delta.columnMapping.mode' = 'name',
  'delta.minReaderVersion'   = '2',
  'delta.minWriterVersion'   = '5'
);

That's a protocol upgrade you can't undo, and after a rename or drop it can break readers of the table's change data feed.

Here's the catch for both formats: a CDC sink still sees a rename as a dropped field and a new one, because that's what the events say. Unless you rename the table column yourself, you get the same split as in Snowflake.

Expand, then contract

The safe pattern is expand/contract: make the schema bigger first, move everything over, and only then make it smaller. A rename becomes four steps:

-- 1. Expand: add the new column as nullable (or with a constant default)
ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN total_cents bigint;

-- 2. Backfill in small batches, and have the application write both columns
UPDATE orders
SET    total_cents = amount_cents
WHERE  total_cents IS NULL
  AND  id BETWEEN 1 AND 50000;

-- 3. Move every reader (views, models, dashboards) to total_cents

-- 4. Contract, weeks later, once nothing reads the old column
ALTER TABLE orders DROP COLUMN amount_cents;

Because amount_cents was nullable, every step only adds or removes an optional field, which the registry accepts in any mode. (Dropping a NOT NULL column removes a required field, which passes BACKWARD but not FORWARD or FULL.) Two practical notes:

  • The backfill is CDC traffic. Every row it updates becomes a change event, which is why it runs in batches.
  • Snowflake won't drop the old column for you. Schema evolution never removes columns. Drop AMOUNT_CENTS in the warehouse yourself once readers have moved.

Two guardrails

Test schemas in CI. Schema Registry has a compatibility endpoint that tells you whether a schema would be accepted, without registering it:

# Wrap the new Avro schema in the request body the registry expects
python3 -c 'import json, sys; print(json.dumps({"schema": open(sys.argv[1]).read()}))' \
  orders-value.avsc > payload.json

curl -X POST \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/vnd.schemaregistry.v1+json' \
  --data @payload.json \
  'http://schema-registry:8081/compatibility/subjects/shop.public.orders-value/versions/latest?verbose=true'
# {"is_compatible":false,"messages":[...]}

Fail the build when is_compatible is false. Remember that a nullable rename passes this check, so it catches only the loud kind of break.

Watch the warehouse. Alert when a new column appears on a captured table, and when a column's null rate jumps:

SELECT DATE_TRUNC('hour', updated_at)              AS hour,
       COUNT(*)                                    AS rows_loaded,
       COUNT_IF(amount_cents IS NULL) / COUNT(*)   AS null_rate
FROM   analytics.orders
WHERE  updated_at >= DATEADD(day, -2, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP())
GROUP  BY 1
HAVING null_rate > 0.2
ORDER  BY 1;

The threshold is yours to pick. Either alert would have caught Friday's rename on Friday night.

Five common mistakes

  1. Renaming a column with a single ALTER. Use expand/contract.
  2. Changing a numeric column's scale in place. Snowflake can't follow.
  3. Setting compatibility to NONE just to get a failed connector running again. You've switched off the only alarm.
  4. Trusting function defaults. Debezium exports a default like CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(6) as a zero value (1970-01-01) in the schema.
  5. Changing a schema during an incremental snapshot. The Postgres connector doesn't support it.

Recap

  • Postgres doesn't send DDL, so the next event carries the new schema.
  • The registry checks compatibility, BACKWARD by default. Optional fields are safe to add or remove; required fields are not.
  • Snowflake adds columns, but never renames or changes types.
  • In the lakehouse, your sink still sees a rename as a drop and an add.
  • So expand, then contract.

This week, find the last schema change on a captured table and check what it did in the warehouse.

The CDC in Production series

  • Part 1: Change Data Capture (CDC) Explained (article · video)
  • Part 2: Debezium Postgres to Kafka: Every Setting Explained (video)
  • Part 3: The Silent CDC Bug: Data Loss With No Errors (video)
  • Previous, Part 4: CDC Deletes, Tombstones and the Idempotent MERGE (video)
  • Part 5: CDC Schema Changes: What Breaks and How to Ship Them (this post · video)
  • Next, Part 6: Running CDC in Production: The WAL Slot Trap (video, out November 2)

If this was useful, the video version has the animated diagrams for every step: watch it on YouTube. Subscribe to Pipeline Whiteboard for more diagram-first data engineering explainers. Next up, in the final part: the WAL slot trap, lag, heartbeats, alerting and runbooks.

title: Node.js Code for Verifying Property-Management Phone Numbers with SMS (Audit Evidence)
description:
Short answer: for a property-management portal, use a managed OTP boundary when the requirement is proving control of a resident's phone, but keep the decision, expiration, attempt count, recipient, and provider response in your own audit record. Send through /v1/sms/otp, validate the submitted code in your application, and treat resend as a new rate-limited action through /v1/sms/resend/{id}. That gives the platform a reviewable record without making the SMS vendor the system of record.

Infrai fits this boundary when one REST API and one key can cover the communications call alongside other backend capabilities, while the property application keeps its own evidence policy. Its public discovery surface is self-describing and does not require a key, so the request schema can be reviewed before implementation rather than inferred from an SDK.

The important distinction is between delivery and evidence. An SMS provider can create and deliver a challenge; it cannot, by itself, explain why your leasing workflow accepted a phone number, which policy version applied, or why a number was suppressed after repeated failures. Those are application decisions.

What should the property portal actually prove?

The login flow has two separate questions: did the service send a challenge to the claimed number, and did the person presenting the code satisfy the verification policy? A successful provider response answers only the first question. Your database must bind the challenge to the account, record an expiration policy, count failed attempts, and retain enough provider metadata for an auditor to reconstruct the decision.

This is also where bounces and invalid recipients matter. A failed delivery is not proof that the person lacks access to the phone, but it is a useful signal for pausing future sends. Keep a suppression decision separate from the OTP decision: a number may be temporarily blocked for abuse, permanently invalid, or merely awaiting a delivery-status check. Do not turn a transient delivery failure into an irreversible identity judgment.

For a platform team, the invariant is simple: no accepted login without a valid, unexpired challenge tied to the intended account; no retry that can create an accidental second accepted state; and no resend path that bypasses the same abuse controls as the first send. The audit trail is part of the feature, not logging polish added after launch.

Which architecture fits the evidence requirement?

There are two viable shapes.

The first is a specialist verification service. Twilio Verify, Vonage Verify, and Amazon Cognito's MFA features each represent a different version of this approach: the provider owns more of the challenge lifecycle, while your application integrates at a narrower boundary. Twilio Verify is a focused verification product with a mature channel and country footprint; Vonage Verify is another managed verification option with its own regional and policy constraints; Cognito fits best when the identity system already lives in AWS and the application is willing to adopt its user-pool model. The trade-off is control. A specialist can reduce the amount of OTP machinery you operate, but it may leave your property-specific evidence model, suppression policy, and cross-channel records split across systems.

The second is an application-owned policy layer over a communications API. Your service owns challenge state, account binding, expiry, attempt limits, suppression decisions, and audit exports. The API owns SMS submission and the provider-facing delivery surface. Infrai is a deliberate option in this shape: its communications capabilities sit behind one REST contract, so adding adjacent backend capabilities does not require another SDK, key, and integration boundary. Its public discovery surface also exposes request and response schemas and runnable examples, which makes an API review easier to repeat during a control assessment.

I would choose the second architecture for a property-management platform when compliance evidence must connect the phone challenge to the resident, lease context, suppression decision, and policy version in one record. I would choose Twilio Verify, Vonage Verify, or Cognito when the team explicitly values a more managed identity workflow and can accept the provider's lifecycle and evidence boundaries. There is no honest universal winner here; the right answer follows the ownership boundary.

Decision Application-owned policy over a communications API Specialist verification service
Evidence One property-specific audit record can contain the decision inputs Provider records are more central, application context may be separate
Operating load You own expiry, attempts, suppression, and reconciliation More challenge lifecycle is managed for you
Lock-in Communications contract is narrower, policy remains yours Identity and verification workflow can be more provider-shaped
Best fit Compliance review needs account and property context together The team wants a pre-shaped verification product

How should Node.js code verify a phone number with SMS?

The send operation should create a pending challenge before calling the provider, then mark it sent only after a successful response. The provider's identifier belongs in that record. Store a hash or otherwise protected representation of the one-time code, never the usable code in plaintext, and expire the challenge according to the policy your security review approved.

The sample below keeps the provider payload outside the example because the verified contract is discoverable and the exact request schema should be copied from that live capability definition, not guessed from a blog post. It still shows the important operational properties: explicit POST, bearer authentication from an environment variable, status checking, Retry-After handling, and a bounded exponential retry for 429 responses. The application should supply a request body generated from the discovered schema through OTP_REQUEST_JSON. It uses only the Go 1.22 standard library.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func sendOTP() ([]byte, error) {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    payload := os.Getenv("OTP_REQUEST_JSON")
    if key == "" || payload == "" {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_API_KEY and OTP_REQUEST_JSON are required")
    }

    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodPost, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/sms/otp", bytes.NewBufferString(payload))
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")

        resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 3 {
            wait := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if seconds, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); parseErr == nil && seconds > 0 {
                wait = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            time.Sleep(wait)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("otp request failed with HTTP %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        return body, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("otp request exhausted retries")
}

func main() {
    body, err := sendOTP()
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Println(string(body))
}

For a real create operation, add an idempotency key derived from the pending challenge before retries, using the provider's documented convention. The same key must not be reused for a separate resend. A resend is an explicit state transition, and the application should retain its own attempt and cooldown record before invoking /v1/sms/resend/{id}.

Keep it boring.

What does verification and rollback look like?

Your application endpoint should load the pending challenge, reject an expired or already-consumed record, compare the submitted code against the protected value, and atomically mark success. Rate-limit by account and phone number as well as by source address; otherwise an attacker can rotate one of those dimensions while brute-forcing the same challenge. Keep the failure response deliberately unhelpful so it does not reveal whether a phone is registered.

The rollback story deserves equal attention. If the SMS call fails, leave the challenge in a failed-send state and make the next attempt create a fresh pending record. If delivery later proves invalid, add the recipient to the appropriate suppression workflow and stop automatic sends until a reviewed action clears it. Since the relevant event surface is pull-based rather than webhook-driven, reconciliation needs a scheduled poll and a visible freshness timestamp. A dashboard that says “verified” without showing when its delivery evidence was last refreshed is not a compliance control.

Before production, test these cases explicitly: a successful first send, an expired code, a reused code, four consecutive rate-limit responses, a resend after cooldown, an invalid recipient, and a provider error with a non-2xx body. Rollback should disable new sends behind a feature flag while preserving already-created audit records. Do not delete evidence to make a failed migration look clean.

The conditional recommendation is therefore narrow: try Infrai for the communications boundary when one consistent REST surface and a discoverable, broad backend capability set reduce integration ownership, while your service remains responsible for property-specific OTP evidence and suppression policy. Choose a specialist verification product when managed identity lifecycle is more valuable than keeping that policy layer in your application. For the Infrai boundary, start with the SMS OTP guide and verify the current request schema before shipping.

References

  • RFC 4226: HOTP: An HMAC-Based One-Time Password Algorithm
  • RFC 6238: TOTP: Time-Based One-Time Password Algorithm
  • Twilio Verify documentation
  • Vonage Verify API documentation
  • Amazon Cognito MFA documentation
  • Infrai SMS OTP guide

title: Bridging Python and Rust: Building Type-Safe Data Quality Pipelines with PyO3 and JSON Schema 2020-12 #rust #python #pyo3 #jsonschema
description:
Introduction

What happens when Python's flexibility meets Rust's performance in a data engineering pipeline?

Imagine processing millions of rows of data, only to discover that a critical column contains unexpected null values, duplicate records, or an incompatible data type.

You could catch these problems after processing. But what if you could define quality rules before the data reaches your warehouse—and enforce those rules through a high-performance Rust engine?

That's the engineering challenge behind combining Python, PyO3, Rust, and JSON Schema Draft 2020-12.

In this article, we'll explore the architecture, schema design, native Rust integration, and testing strategy behind a declarative data quality gate.

The goal: Make configuration validation predictable, keep the Python–Rust boundary clean, and separate structural validation from runtime data checks.

Executive Summary

When building data profiling and data quality pipelines, engineers face a classic dilemma: Rust delivers zero-cost abstractions, fearless concurrency, and high-performance data processing, while Python provides data teams with expressiveness, rich ecosystem tooling, and declarative configuration.

In dataprof, the core profiling engine is written in Rust and exposed to Python via PyO3 native bindings. However, enterprise pipelines require declarative Quality Gate Policies to verify null thresholds, uniqueness constraints, distinct value bounds, and column data types before committing data to downstream warehouses.

This case study explores the architecture described in PR #1061 (schema architecture and test suite) and PR #863 (production error subsystem), focusing on the relationship between JSON Schema Draft 2020-12 and native Rust profiling kernels.

The central engineering principle is straightforward: validate configuration early, keep the interoperability contract explicit, and evaluate data-dependent invariants where the actual data is available.

1. The Architectural Challenge

Data profiling engines may need to inspect datasets containing millions of rows. Meanwhile, quality policies are authored by data engineers or orchestration systems in YAML or JSON.

The challenge is to translate human-readable configuration into reliable rules that a native Rust engine can evaluate.

Architecture Overview 

          DATA ENGINEER
            YAML / JSON
                 |
                 v
      +----------------------+
      | JSON Schema 2020-12  |
      | Policy Validation    |
      +----------------------+
                 |
                 v
      +----------------------+
      | Python Validation    |
      | Clear Error Messages |
      +----------------------+
                 |
                 v
      +----------------------+
      | PyO3 Boundary        |
      | Python <-> Rust      |
      +----------------------+
                 |
                 v
      +----------------------+
      | Native Rust Engine   |
      | Quality Evaluation   |
      +----------------------+
                 |
                 v
        QUALITY GATE RESULT

The Pitfalls of Naive Implementations

1. Schema Draft Incompatibilities

Older JSON Schema drafts, such as Draft 4 and Draft 7, differ from Draft 2020-12 in their supported keywords and semantics.

Modern keywords such as $defs and prefixItems require a compatible validator. Using an older validator without checking its behavior can result in unsupported keywords not being enforced as expected.

2. Wildcard Resolution

Policies often apply default rules across multiple columns while allowing column-specific overrides.

For example, a global rule might require columns to contain no null values, while a particular column may explicitly disable that restriction.

{
  "*": {
    "null_count": {
      "max": 0
    }
  },
  "user_notes": {
    "null_count": null
  }
}

The intended behavior is that the global rule applies by default, while the specific column overrides it.

Implementing this behavior requires a clear rule-resolution strategy. JSON Schema can validate the configuration's structure, but the application's policy evaluator must implement the actual wildcard matching and precedence semantics.

3. Runtime-Only Semantic Boundaries

Not every invariant belongs in JSON Schema.

For example, a schema can validate that a column name is a string. It cannot independently establish that the column actually exists in a particular Parquet or CSV dataset.

That check belongs in the runtime evaluation layer, where the dataset's metadata and profiling results are available.

Separating structural validation from runtime semantics makes the system easier to reason about and maintain.

2. Designing the JSON Schema Draft 2020-12 Policy Specification

A maintainable policy format should be explicit, modular, and strict enough to catch configuration mistakes.

JSON Schema Draft 2020-12 provides useful features for this purpose:

  • $defs allows reusable schema definitions.
  • $ref allows one schema component to reference another.
  • patternProperties applies schemas to object properties whose names match regular expressions.
  • additionalProperties: false rejects properties that are not otherwise permitted.

Example JSON Schema

The following illustrates the intended schema architecture. The referenced TableRules definition must be supplied in a complete implementation.

{
  "$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema",
  "$id": "https://github.com/AndreaBozzo/dataprof/schemas/quality_policy.json",
  "title": "DataProfQualityPolicy",
  "type": "object",
  "additionalProperties": false,
  "properties": {
    "version": {
      "type": "string",
      "enum": ["1.0"]
    },
    "global_rules": {
      "$ref": "#/$defs/TableRules"
    },
    "columns": {
      "type": "object",
      "patternProperties": {
        "^[a-zA-Z0-9_*.-]+$": {
          "$ref": "#/$defs/ColumnRuleSet"
        }
      },
      "additionalProperties": false
    }
  },
  "$defs": {
    "MetricBound": {
      "type": "object",
      "additionalProperties": false,
      "properties": {
        "min": {
          "type": ["number", "null"]
        },
        "max": {
          "type": ["number", "null"]
        }
      }
    },
    "ColumnRuleSet": {
      "type": "object",
      "additionalProperties": false,
      "properties": {
        "null_count": {
          "$ref": "#/$defs/MetricBound"
        },
        "distinct_ratio": {
          "$ref": "#/$defs/MetricBound"
        },
        "expected_type": {
          "type": ["string", "null"]
        }
      }
    }
  }
}

Key Architecture Highlights

Pattern-Based Column Matching

The patternProperties keyword allows property names matching a regular expression to be validated against a specified schema.

This can support naming conventions and wildcard-like policy keys. However, actual wildcard matching—such as interpreting prefix_* as a prefix matcher—must be implemented by the policy evaluator. A JSON Schema regular expression does not automatically provide glob-matching semantics.

Explicit Null Handling

Allowing null in a schema makes it possible to represent explicit null values in the configuration.

However, the meaning of null must be defined by the application. If null disables an inherited rule, the policy evaluator must implement that behavior explicitly.

Strict Property Validation

Using additionalProperties: false helps reject unexpected properties and catches configuration typos instead of silently accepting unknown keys.

Reusable Definitions

Using $defs and $ref avoids repeating the same rule definitions throughout the schema. This makes future changes easier to manage.

3. Bridging with PyO3 Native Rust Extensions

The next challenge is translating validated configuration into structures that Rust can process.

Serde provides serialization and deserialization support, while PyO3 allows Rust functions to interact with Python.

A practical architecture separates responsibilities:

  1. Python receives the configuration.
  2. A Draft 2020-12-compatible validator checks its structure.
  3. The validated configuration is serialized or passed across the Python–Rust boundary.
  4. Rust deserializes the configuration into typed structures.
  5. The native evaluator applies the rules to the dataset profile.
  6. The result is returned to Python.

Rust Data Structures

The following example illustrates how policy components can be represented using Serde.

use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
use std::collections::HashMap;

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Serialize, Deserialize)]
pub struct MetricBound {
    pub min: Option<f64>,
    pub max: Option<f64>,
}

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Serialize, Deserialize)]
pub struct ColumnRuleSet {
    pub null_count: Option<MetricBound>,
    pub distinct_ratio: Option<MetricBound>,
    pub expected_type: Option<String>,
}

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Serialize, Deserialize)]
pub struct QualityPolicy {
    pub version: String,
    pub columns: HashMap<String, ColumnRuleSet>,
}

These structures provide a typed representation of the policy.

The Option<T> type represents an optional Rust value. However, when configuration semantics distinguish between a missing property and an explicitly supplied null, additional deserialization logic may be required to preserve that distinction.

PyO3 Integration

A simplified PyO3 function can accept a JSON string, deserialize it, and invoke a native evaluator.

use pyo3::exceptions::PyValueError;
use pyo3::prelude::*;

#[pyfunction]
fn evaluate_quality_gate(
    policy_json_str: &str,
) -> PyResult<bool> {
    let policy: QualityPolicy =
        serde_json::from_str(policy_json_str)
            .map_err(|e| {
                PyValueError::new_err(e.to_string())
            })?;

    // Invoke the native policy evaluator here.
    // The evaluator must be implemented separately.
    let is_valid = run_policy_evaluation(&policy)
        .map_err(PyValueError::new_err)?;

    Ok(is_valid)
}

Here, run_policy_evaluation is a placeholder for the native evaluation implementation and must be defined before the example can compile.

Why This Separation Matters

Python handles configuration validation.

Python provides access to JSON Schema validators and can generate detailed validation errors for configuration authors.

Rust handles typed evaluation.

Rust can evaluate rules against native profiling structures without requiring every operation to pass through Python.

PyO3 provides interoperability.

PyO3 exposes native functionality to Python while keeping the interface explicit.

Serde provides structured deserialization.

Serde maps JSON values into Rust data structures. Ordinary JSON deserialization should not automatically be described as zero-copy; that depends on the implementation and the data being processed.

The key design objective is to keep the boundary simple and ensure that both sides agree on the policy's semantics.

4. Practical Example: Defining a Quality Gate

Consider a dataset containing customer records.

Before loading the dataset into a warehouse, a team may want to verify that customer IDs do not contain null values and that email addresses have the expected type.

A policy could look like this:

{
  "version": "1.0",
  "columns": {
    "customer_id": {
      "null_count": {
        "max": 0
      }
    },
    "email": {
      "expected_type": "string"
    }
  }
}

The schema validates the configuration's structure. The runtime evaluator then interprets the rules against the actual dataset profile.

For example, if the profile reports that customer_id contains three null values, a rule requiring a maximum null count of zero should fail.

The evaluator should return a meaningful result that identifies the violated rule rather than merely reporting that the overall policy failed.

A production implementation should also define:

  • How missing columns are handled.
  • How global rules interact with column-specific rules.
  • Whether explicit null disables a rule.
  • How conflicting rules are resolved.
  • How invalid configuration differs from failed data quality.
  • How errors are reported to Python callers.

These details are essential for predictable behavior in real data pipelines.

5. Exhaustive Parity Verification: 30 Test Cases

Schema validation and native evaluation must remain consistent as the policy format evolves.

A useful test suite should cover ordinary configurations, edge cases, invalid inputs, and serialization behavior.

The original case study reports 30 test cases distributed across four categories.

Test Suite Category Verification Invariants Reported Result
Baseline Policy Conformance Minimal versioned schema, table-level bounds, column metric boundaries 10 / 10 PASSED
Wildcard & Column Mapping Universal wildcard *, prefix patterns, column-specific rule overrides 8 / 8 PASSED
Strict Rejection & Negative Tests Unknown keys, additionalProperties: false, negative bounds, invalid types 7 / 7 PASSED
Encoding & Serialization Parity UTF-8 BOM handling, null-pointer safety, Serde deserialization parity 5 / 5 PASSED
Total 30 reported test cases 30 / 30 PASSED

Running the Tests

The case study identifies the following test command:

pytest tests/test_quality_policy_schema.py -v

Reported output:

========================= 30 passed in 0.18s =========================

These results are reproduced from the case study and have not been independently verified here.

Additional Tests Worth Considering

Beyond baseline validation, a robust implementation should consider the following cases.

1. Missing Versus Explicit Null

Verify whether an omitted rule and an explicitly supplied null have different meanings.

2. Wildcard Precedence

Verify that a specific column rule overrides a global rule according to the documented precedence rules.

3. Unknown Column References

Verify how the evaluator responds when a policy references a column that does not exist in the dataset.

4. Invalid Numeric Bounds

Test reversed minimum and maximum values, negative values where prohibited, and non-finite numeric values where relevant.

5. Schema-to-Rust Compatibility

Verify that configurations accepted by JSON Schema can be deserialized into the Rust policy structures, and that unsupported configurations are rejected with useful errors.

6. Error Reporting

Ensure configuration errors can be distinguished from runtime evaluation failures.

7. Large Policies

Measure performance and memory consumption for configurations containing many column rules.

These tests help protect the contract between configuration authors, the Python validation layer, and the native Rust evaluator.

6. Key Engineering Lessons

1. Shift Schema Validation to the Language of the Caller

Validate human-authored configuration in Python using a Draft 2020-12-compatible JSON Schema validator before passing it across the PyO3 boundary.

This makes it possible to report actionable validation errors close to where the configuration originates.

2. Keep the FFI Contract Lean

Pass JSON-serialized configurations or structured Python objects that map clearly onto Rust data structures.

The best approach depends on the size of the policy, interoperability requirements, and performance measurements.

The interface should remain explicit, predictable, and easy to test.

3. Decouple Syntax Validation from Runtime Semantics

JSON Schema validates structure and types.

The native Rust evaluator validates domain-specific conditions against the actual dataset profile.

Keeping these responsibilities separate avoids trying to solve data-dependent problems during static configuration validation.

4. Define Null and Override Semantics Explicitly

A configuration format is only reliable when its behavior is unambiguous.

If explicit null disables an inherited rule, document that behavior and implement it consistently in both validation and evaluation.

5. Test the Contract, Not Just Individual Components

Unit tests for Python validation and Rust evaluation are useful, but integration tests are equally important.

They establish whether the complete pipeline behaves consistently from configuration input to final quality-gate result.

7. Final Thoughts

Bridging Python and Rust is not just about making code faster. It is about assigning the right responsibilities to each layer.

In this architecture:

  • JSON Schema defines the structure of a quality policy.
  • Python validates human-authored configuration and produces actionable errors.
  • PyO3 provides the boundary between Python and native Rust code.
  • Serde maps JSON data into typed Rust structures.
  • Rust evaluates policy rules against dataset profiles.

The key lesson is simple: validate configuration early, keep the interoperability contract explicit, and evaluate data-dependent invariants where the actual data is available.

A well-designed Python–Rust boundary can make data quality systems easier to maintain, test, and extend.

Let's Discuss

If you were designing a production-grade Python–Rust data quality engine, how would you handle schema evolution, wildcard precedence, and error reporting across the FFI boundary?

Would you prefer JSON serialization for a simple contract, or structured Python objects for tighter integration?

I'd love to hear how other engineers approach this problem.
