title: 5 Things Every Small Business Homepage Needs Above the Fold
description:
"Above the fold" is the part of your homepage people see before they scroll. On a phone that's a tiny space, and it's where most small business sites lose people. Here are the five things I check first on every small business homepage.

1. A headline that says what you do and where. "Welcome to our website" tells nobody anything. "Family dentist in Austin, TX" or "Same-day plumbing repairs in Tampa" tells visitors (and Google) they're in the right place.

2. One obvious call-to-action. Pick the one action that matters most — Book now, Get a quote, Call us — and make it a big, high-contrast button. Three competing buttons usually means none get clicked.

3. A tap-to-call phone number. Many local customers are on mobile and just want to call. Use a tel: link so it's one tap, and keep it visible in the header.

4. Proof. A star rating, a review count, or one short testimonial near the top builds trust instantly. Real reviews beat stock badges.

5. A real photo. Your actual team, shop, or finished work beats generic stock photos. It makes the business feel real and local. Compress it so it doesn't slow the page down.

Quick test: open your homepage on your phone and ask a friend what you do, where, and how to contact you — in five seconds. If they can't answer, the top of the page needs work.

I'm with ENZORA. We build websites for US small businesses and offer a free website and SEO audit: https://enzora.vercel.app

description:

A transparent click-interceptor helps shield stream links while still allowing users to interact with legitimate controls, including skipping ads.

To unify different video sources, the player uses a common Provider interface. This allows HTML5 and YouTube to work through the same player architecture.

title: Designing Photo Slots for Multi-Person AI Video Templates
description:
A photo-to-video interface becomes more complicated as soon as a template supports two people or a group. A generic upload box does not tell users which photo belongs to which performer.

Dame Hombro AI is the product example here: fourteen dance and freestyle templates cover solo adults, duos, groups of three, cats and dogs. Outputs are 15-second, 720p MP4 clips with generated audio. The following is a practical interface design checklist for this kind of workflow, rather than a claim about any particular model architecture.

Treat each upload as a role assignment

A template should define its required cast before the user chooses files. Label the slots with the same role names used in the preview. For a duo, two distinct slots are easier to inspect than a single gallery of attachments. For a pet preset, make the expected animal type explicit.

Keep the selected template and its photo assignments together. If a user switches from a solo scene to a group scene, show the newly required roles before allowing generation. Do not silently treat a missing performer as an optional input.

Separate preparation from generation

Choosing a file, preparing an upload and starting a paid generation are different actions. The interface should make those boundaries visible. A useful review screen answers four questions: which template is selected, which photo fills each role, which aspect ratio will be generated, and what the request costs.

Dame Hombro AI offers 9:16 and 16:9 output and charges one credit per video. Its credit packs are one-time purchases; unused credits do not expire, and failed generations restore the credit. These are product rules worth showing before a request starts.

Validate the brief, then review the result

Input validation can confirm required slots and file constraints. It cannot guarantee that a generated face, hand or dance movement will look right. Completion therefore needs a second review step: watch the whole clip, including its audio, before downloading or sharing it.

For this product, photos must be authorized. Human subjects must be adults, and minors, celebrities and public figures are excluded. The result is a new AI interpretation, so the UI should not promise exact identity preservation or frame-by-frame replacement.

Describe audio independently

A dance template can evoke a movement style without including a commercial recording. This service creates new audio; it does not promise the original song, lyrics or an artist's voice. Dame Hombro AI is independent of Bulin 47 and Kevin Wai.

For builders, the useful design boundary is between the reference, the request and the generated result. Make each one inspectable, and users have a clearer basis for deciding what to create and what to share.

title: Designing a 3D Periodic Table for iPhone Duo: Reimagining Foldable UI/UX
description:
A deep dive into the UI/UX design decisions behind building an immersive, dual-screen 3D Periodic Table app optimized for foldable iPhone hardware

Designing interface layouts for dual-screen and foldable devices like the iPhone Duo requires rethinking traditional single-viewport ergonomics to maximize real estate without cluttering the visual field. In Periodic Table Chemistry 2027 app, the dual-display architecture establishes a logical separation between macro navigation and micro content inspection. Opening the device reveals a balanced split workspace: the comprehensive periodic table stays pinned to one screen, while the complementary display renders interactive 3D models—such as gas balloons illustrating Helium—alongside immediate atomic and physical properties. This spatial split minimizes context switching, allowing users to study detailed element attributes while keeping the complete chemical landscape in full view.

Fluid adaptability across physical folding states is critical for next-generation mobile UX, requiring a UI that scales seamlessly whether the device is expanded or closed. When collapsed into a single display, Periodic Table Chemistry 2027 app transitions effortlessly into an optimized single-screen layout tailored for efficient one-handed interactions. The UI dynamically recalibrates high-density data cards and 3D visual assets—such as a battery representation for Lithium—while preserving high-contrast dark mode aesthetics, clean typography, and quick access to core metrics like atomic mass and electron configurations. This design strategy guarantees an uninterrupted user experience when moving from quick reference lookups to full dual-screen workflows.

Leveraging spanned viewports allows for rich, immersive modal presentations that turn standard educational reference tools into tactile 3D experiences. When inspecting complex elements like Protactinium, the application presents an enlarged central 3D viewport spanning across the hinge line, granting users tactile manipulation and detailed spatial rendering of elemental structures. Strategic positioning of translucent control overlays and background grids preserves visual hierarchy, ensuring navigation remains accessible without obstructing the visual focal point. By placing dual-screen ergonomics and responsive visual layout at the center of development, Periodic Table Chemistry 2027 app offers a template for modern, canvas-aware application design.

Designing for multi-screen foldables isn't just about handling dynamic screen bounds—it’s about crafting contextual spatial workflows that elevate everyday utility. Periodic Table Chemistry 2027 app demonstrates how thoughtful layout architecture can transform complex educational data into an intuitive, visually rich 3D experience across both single and spanned displays. title: How MCP and tool calling really work: I built an AI agent from scratch in Java and traced every step
description:
I asked a local AI model to add "buy milk" to my notes file. It did. Then I traced every step to find out what actually happened.

To do that, I built the whole thing from scratch:

  • an MCP server
  • an MCP client and
  • an agent loop in plain Java and Spring Boot,

no AI frameworks and no MCP SDK, talking to Qwen 2.5 7B running locally through Ollama.

"From scratch" means no frameworks, not no help: Claude co-authored the code and this article, because writing every line by hand in 2026 would apparently make me a caveman.

Yes, I know: MCP has been around for about two years. I'm late to the party. But if even one person walks away with a new understanding, that's the best outcome I could ask for.

What we're building

One plain-text file, data/db, holds my notes. The MCP server is the only thing that touches it, through five tools: read, write (replace everything), append, update (find and replace) and clear. A simple File I/O method, ref

You ask the host in plain English ("Add buy milk"), it asks the model which tool fits, and runs it on the server.

What you need

  • Docker with Compose: runs the MCP server and the host.
  • Ollama, installed natively (ollama.com), not in Docker, so the model can use your GPU. On Linux, set OLLAMA_HOST=0.0.0.0 so the containers can reach it.
  • The model: ollama pull qwen2.5:7b (about 4.7 GB; 8 GB RAM minimum, 16 GB comfortable).
  • Git. No Java needed unless you run outside Docker. 
git clone https://github.com/abir4l/mcp_server
git clone https://github.com/abir4l/local_agent
ollama pull qwen2.5:7b          # with Ollama running
cd local_agent && docker compose up --build

The map

  • local_agent (port 8081) is the host. It runs the agent loop, keeps the conversation and makes every network call.
  • Ollama (port 11434) runs the model. Text in, text out.
  • mcp_server (port 8080) owns the tools. It's the only thing that touches data/db, the notes file.

Part 1: The layers

1. The model is just numbers

ollama pull qwen2.5:7b downloads about 4.7 GB of weights: billions of numbers. Together with a function that predicts the next token, that's the whole model. It doesn't listen on a port, doesn't speak JSON or HTTP, and does nothing on its own. A file of numbers can't write to your disk. Something else has to.

2. Ollama is a database server, but for models

I used to think Ollama, ChatGPT and Claude were abstractions over the model, so my own app would skip them and talk to the model directly. But the model is just numbers, and an app can't talk to numbers. Something has to load it and give you an interface to send text and get text back: a model server.

Locally that's Ollama; in the cloud it's the OpenAI or Anthropic API. That's the layer you can't bypass.

ChatGPT and the Claude app are one level higher: they're hosts like my local_agent, with a UI, history and tools on top of that API. Calling the OpenAI API isn't calling ChatGPT.

Layer Local OpenAI Anthropic
Model qwen2.5:7b on your disk GPT (private weights) Claude (private weights)
Model server (API) Ollama OpenAI API Anthropic API
Host / app local_agent, or Ollama's own chat app ChatGPT Claude app

ChatGPT is to the OpenAI API what my local_agent is to Ollama. Build on the API and you write the ChatGPT part: history, tools, the loop.

One twist: locally, Ollama sits in two rows at once. Its server (the API on port 11434) is the model-server layer, but its desktop chat window and ollama run in the terminal are hosts, thin clients of that same API. Imagine OpenAI shipping the API and ChatGPT in one download. My local_agent skips Ollama's chat window and talks to the API directly, the same way your own app would skip ChatGPT and call the OpenAI API.

3. There is no standard for talking to models (MCP vs function calling)

Every vendor has its own JSON dialect. OpenAI returns tool arguments as a JSON string, Ollama as a JSON object, and Anthropic uses tool_use content blocks instead of tool_calls. Same idea, three shapes, so every host needs an adapter.

That's also the answer to "MCP vs function calling". Function calling is the model side: you describe tools to the model and it replies with a request to use one. MCP standardized the tool side, not the model side: how a host finds and calls tools on a separate server. A real agent uses both. Since MCP's inputSchema and Ollama's parameters are both plain JSON Schema, my adapter between them is a single map().

Part 2: The illusions

4. Are LLMs stateless? Yes. Chat is an illusion

Maybe you already know this one: the model remembers nothing between calls. The host resends the entire conversation every turn, so "memory" is just a list in my Java process. That's all it ever is.

5. How tool calling actually works: it's just text

There is no special channel. Ollama's chat template renders your JSON tools into the prompt (see it with ollama show qwen2.5:7b --template). Trimmed, the model sees:

<|im_start|>system
# Tools
You are provided with function signatures within <tools></tools> XML tags:
<tools>
{"type": "function", "function": {"name": "append", "description": "Append content to the end of the file", ...}}
...
</tools>
For each function call, return a json object with function name and arguments within <tool_call></tool_call> XML tags
<|im_end|>
<|im_start|>user
Add buy milk to my notes<|im_end|>
<|im_start|>assistant

The model predicts the most likely next tokens, which, because it was trained on this format, are:

<tool_call>
{"name": "append", "arguments": {"content": "buy milk"}}
</tool_call>

Ollama parses that text back into a neat tool_calls JSON field. The "function call" is a string that looks like one. (Start Ollama with OLLAMA_DEBUG=1 to see the full rendered prompt.)

6. The model never touches the file

Ollama returns that tool_calls JSON to my host, and it's done. It has no idea an MCP server exists. My host reads the request, calls the MCP server over HTTP, and pastes the result back into the conversation as a role: "tool" message.

Ollama and the MCP server never talk to each other. The model requests. The host decides and acts. That's why the host is the real control point for safety, not the model.

How to add your own data to an LLM (no training required)

This is what I actually set out to learn. When the model calls read, my notes come back as a role: "tool" message and sit in the conversation like any other text. The model "knows" my file because the host pasted it into the prompt.

Every popular way to give an LLM your own data is this trick, except one:

  • Prompt stuffing: paste the data in yourself.
  • Tool calling / MCP: the model asks, the host fetches (this project).
  • RAG: the host searches your documents and pastes in the relevant chunks.
  • Fine-tuning: changes the weights. Good for behaviour and style, usually wrong for "make it know my documents".

So "train ChatGPT on my own data" usually means one of the first three. Choosing what goes into the context window is context engineering, and RAG exposed as an MCP tool is agentic RAG.

Part 3: MCP on the wire

7. MCP is JSON-RPC on one endpoint, not REST

An MCP server has exactly one endpoint, POST /mcp, and the operation lives in the body's method field (JSON-RPC 2.0). Since the 2026-07-28 spec, MCP is also stateless: no initialize handshake and no session ID. Every request carries its protocol version in params._meta, and the method and tool name are copied into headers, so a gateway can route without parsing the body.

What an MCP server's API looks like

If you build REST APIs for a living, this is the light-bulb view. Here is my server's entire API, OpenAPI-style:

POST /mcp                         the only endpoint (GET, DELETE -> 405)

method            params              returns
server/discover   (none)              supported versions, capabilities
tools/list        (none)              [{ name, description, inputSchema }]
tools/call        name, arguments     { content: [...], isError }

And here is the API the model actually sees, as returned by tools/list:

tool      arguments          what it does
read      (none)             return the whole file
write     content            replace the whole file
append    content            add a line at the end
update    search, replace    find and replace text
clear     (none)             empty the file

That's the whole thing: two lists. Think of tools/list as an OpenAPI doc written for a model instead of a developer. The full spec adds the same list-and-read pattern for resources (resources/list, resources/read) and prompts (prompts/list, prompts/get), but tools are where the action is. One call on the wire looks like this:

POST /mcp
MCP-Protocol-Version: 2026-07-28
Mcp-Method: tools/call
Mcp-Name: append

{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":2,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"append","arguments":{"content":"buy milk"},
 "_meta":{"io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion":"2026-07-28","io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities":{}}}}

MCP vs API: isn't MCP just an API?

Technically, yes. The difference is who it's designed for. A normal API is designed for a developer, who reads the docs and writes a custom client. An MCP server describes itself to a model: tools/list returns every tool with a plain-English description and a JSON Schema, so any MCP host can use any MCP server with no custom code. MCP usually wraps your existing APIs rather than replacing them.

8. There are two kinds of errors

  • Protocol errors (bad JSON, wrong headers, unknown tool) come back as a JSON-RPC error. They're client bugs, for the developer.
  • Tool errors (missing argument, wrong type) come back as a normal result with isError: true. They're for the model, so it can fix its call and retry. 
// unknown tool is a protocol error, bad arguments are a tool error the model can fix
try {
    registry.validate(toolName, params);
} catch (ToolNotFoundException e) {
    throw RpcException.invalidParams("Unknown tool: " + toolName, HttpStatus.OK);
} catch (ToolArgumentException e) {
    return CallToolResult.error(e.getMessage(), resultMeta);
}

Small models make small mistakes. Hand back Param (content) is required instead of throwing, and they usually fix it on the next step.

Part 4: The full trace

One /agent request, every hop.

1. You → host

curl -s localhost:8081/agent -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"message":"Add buy milk to my notes"}'

2. Host → MCP server: tools/list (id 1) returns the five tools.

3. Host → Ollama

POST /api/chat
{
  "model": "qwen2.5:7b",
  "messages": [ { "role": "user", "content": "Add buy milk to my notes" } ],
  "tools": [
    { "type": "function", "function": { "name": "append",
        "description": "Append content to the end of the file",
        "parameters": { "type": "object",
          "properties": { "content": { "type": "string", "description": "Content that gets appended" } },
          "required": ["content"], "additionalProperties": false } } },
    ... read, write, update, clear ...
  ],
  "stream": false,
  "keep_alive": "30m"
}

4. Ollama → host: the model wants a tool, and says nothing else (content is empty).

{ "message": { "role": "assistant", "content": "",
    "tool_calls": [ { "function": { "name": "append", "arguments": { "content": "buy milk" } } } ] },
  "done": true }

5. Host → MCP server: the tools/call request shown in moment 7. This is the only moment anything touches the disk.

{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":2,"result":{"resultType":"complete","content":[{"type":"text","text":"Success"}],"isError":false,
 "_meta":{"io.modelcontextprotocol/serverInfo":{"name":"mcp_server","version":"0.0.1-SNAPSHOT"}}}}

6. Host → Ollama again, with the whole history

"messages": [
  { "role": "user", "content": "Add buy milk to my notes" },
  { "role": "assistant", "content": "",
    "tool_calls": [ { "function": { "name": "append", "arguments": { "content": "buy milk" } } } ] },
  { "role": "tool", "content": "Success", "tool_name": "append" }
]

7. Ollama → host: "content": "I've added \"buy milk\" to your notes." with no tool_calls, so the loop stops.

8. Host → you: the reply, plus a list of every tool call made.

Seven HTTP calls between three processes for two words in a text file. The model was in two of them, receiving text and returning text.

Part 5: The harness

9. The agent harness matters more than people think

Everything around the model is the agent harness. Here, that's my host. The loop itself is tiny (logging trimmed):

for (int step = 1; step <= properties.maxSteps(); step++) {
    Message reply = ollamaClient.chat(messages, tools);
    messages.add(reply); // the tool_calls must stay in history

    if (!reply.hasToolCalls()) {
        return new Result(reply.content(), invocations);
    }
    for (ToolCall call : reply.toolCalls()) {
        ToolInvocation invocation = invoke(call.function().name(), call.function().arguments());
        invocations.add(invocation);
        messages.add(Message.toolResult(call.function().name(), invocation.output()));
    }
}
throw new IllegalStateException("Agent did not finish within " + properties.maxSteps() + " steps");

The behaviour lives in the details:

  • An iteration guard (agent.max-steps=5), because a model that calls tools forever is a real failure mode.
  • Keeping the model's own tool call in history, or the tool result makes no sense to it.
  • Tool descriptions are written for the model. My write tool says "Write all contents to file". To a 7B model asked to "add" something, that can look fine, and then your notes are gone. "Replaces the entire file. To add a note, use append." works better.

A 7B model is slow on a laptop and not deterministic, but it's good enough to learn on, because every failure is visible.

What's next

10. Frameworks hide all of this

Spring AI can do everything above with an annotation like @McpTool. I'd use it in production. But now that Claude and I built it without one, I know what it hides, and when something breaks I know which of the seven hops to check.

  • v2: the same project with Spring AI, compared line by line.
  • v3: multiple notes files, then agentic RAG with a search tool.

FAQ

Do I need to train an LLM on my own data? Usually not. Put the data in the context window with a prompt, a tool/MCP server or RAG. Fine-tuning changes behaviour, not knowledge.

MCP vs RAG? RAG retrieves relevant chunks into the prompt. MCP lets the model call tools, and search can be one. Combined, that's agentic RAG.

Does the model execute the tool? No. It writes text asking for one. The host runs the tool and sends back the result.

Is MCP the same as function calling? No. Function calling is how a model asks for a tool. MCP is how a host finds and calls tools on another server.

Do I need MCP for tool calling? No. You can define tools in your app directly. MCP pays off when tools are shared across apps or teams.

Can a local model use MCP tools? Yes, if it was trained for tool calling (Qwen 2.5, Llama 3.1, Qwen 3). The model never talks to the MCP server anyway.

What changed in MCP 2026-07-28? It's stateless: no initialize, no sessions, and context travels in params._meta plus mirrored headers.

Try it yourself

Clone both repos, run docker compose up --build in local_agent, and send the curl from hop 1. Ollama runs natively on your machine, and Docker runs the rest.

  • github.com/abir4l/mcp_server (includes a full client integration guide)
  • github.com/abir4l/local_agent

The model is just numbers. Everything else is software, and software is something we already know how to read.

Co-written with Claude. If this was useful, a star on the repo helps.

title: Calling an external service from Kafka Streams: size the threads, budget every call
description:
You have a Kafka Streams application, and one step needs an answer from somewhere else. It might be an AI model's decision, a fraud score, an address to geocode or a status from a provider's API. The most direct way to write it is a blocking call inside a mapValues:

stream.mapValues(value -> {
    HttpResponse<String> answer = http.send(requestFor(value), BodyHandlers.ofString());
    return withAnswer(value, answer.body());
});

This is where most applications start. It is kept bare on purpose: no timeout, no retries, no error handling.

What max.poll.interval.ms bounds in Kafka Streams showed what such a call can do to a thread's place in the group, run by run. This post is the other half: what to do about it. A blocking call caps a stream thread at one record per call, so we start by sizing the threads for it. Then we give every call an upper limit, and keep the slow step from holding up the rest of the stream.

Size the threads for the call

Kafka Streams gives each input partition a task and spreads the tasks over its threads, as the previous post opens with. A thread processes its tasks' records one at a time, so a blocking call blocks the thread it runs on.

Our runs called a stub, a small HTTP server of ours that stands in for the service. It waits a set time and answers. Everything else was real: a broker, a Kafka Streams application, HTTP calls over the network, and real vulnerability records, CVEs (how we measured). The first run had three partitions and one thread, so three tasks took turns on it. The arithmetic is short: at 300 ms a call, a thread does 3.3 records a second, however fast records arrive. With 600 records arriving at 20 a second, we measured 3.2 to 3.4 a second, and the stub never saw more than one call in flight.

More partitions alone do not help. A repartition to 32 before the call gives the calling step 32 tasks, and so does an input topic of 32 partitions, which is what we measured. With the same single thread, it still did 3.3 records a second, one call at a time.

It needs threads as well: 32 stream threads (num.stream.threads), one per task of the calling step, counted across all the application's instances. At 300 ms a call, we measured 3.3 records a second with one thread, 26 with eight and 106 with 32. With 32, the stub saw 32 calls in flight at once. Of a backlog of 3,393 records, 3,247 were done after 35 seconds. The rest took until 50 seconds. The records were spread unevenly over the 32 partitions, so as the emptier ones ran out, their threads went idle and the fullest finished alone.

How many threads a stream needs follows from Little's law: calls in flight equal the input rate times the call time. What a number of threads can do, and how fast they clear a backlog, is then one division and one subtraction. With the numbers of our runs:

calls in flight = input rate × call time
                    = 25 a second × 0.3 s = 7.5, so at least 8 threads

capacity = threads ÷ call time
  8 threads = 8 ÷ 0.3 s ≈ 27 a second (measured 26.4)
  32 threads = 32 ÷ 0.3 s ≈ 107 a second (measured 106)

backlog drains = capacity − input
  8 threads = 26.4 − 25 = 1.4 a second
  32 threads = 106 − 25 = 81 a second

service paused 45 s = 45 s × 25 a second ≈ 1,100 records
  8 threads = 1,100 ÷ 1.4 a second ≈ 13 minutes
  32 threads = 1,100 ÷ 81 a second ≈ 14 s (measured about 15)

The pause is from our last run. We paused the service for 45 seconds, and the backlog grew to about 1,100 records.

Eight threads only just keep up. The threads beyond that are headroom. Headroom is what clears a backlog, whatever builds it: a pause in the service, as in our run, a slow minute of it, a spike in the input or a restart. Headroom also covers a slower service. At 600 ms a call:

  8 threads = 8 ÷ 0.6 s ≈ 13 a second, below the input
  32 threads = 32 ÷ 0.6 s ≈ 53 a second, above it

With 8 threads, the lag would grow by about 12 records a second. With 32, it would still drain.

Is the stream keeping up?

Once a stream runs, the consumer group's lag tells you whether that sizing still holds. With Kafka Streams the lag needs reading with care.

Operators watch a consumer group's lag: the LAG column of kafka-consumer-groups --describe, or a lag exporter's line on a Grafana dashboard. That lag comes from the group's committed offsets, and Kafka Streams commits only every commit.interval.ms, 30 seconds by default. So a stream that keeps up does not show zero lag. Between commits the committed offset stays put while records keep arriving, so the lag climbs. At each commit it drops. A stream that kept up with 25 records a second showed a lag climbing to about 750, which is 25 a second times 30 seconds. It dropped to almost nothing at each commit, every 30 seconds.

A dashboard reads this curve at its own interval. Read every 20 seconds, the dashed line, the same healthy stream jumps between about 230 and 750. A reading just after a commit could show almost zero, but most readings show hundreds.

The next chart adds a slow stream. It had a 300 ms call and received the same 25 records a second as the healthy one. It got through only 3.3 of them a second, one thread's worth at 300 ms a call. Its committed lag climbed to about 3,000 in 135 seconds and never came back down.

Lowering commit.interval.ms makes the teeth smaller, but each commit is work. The thread flushes its producer and its store caches and writes its offsets to the broker, and it processes nothing meanwhile. Raising it to commit less often has a cost of its own for slow calls, which What max.poll.interval.ms bounds in Kafka Streams measures.

Give every call an upper limit

Sizing the threads used the typical call time. The rules in the next section start from a different number: the longest a call can take, every retry included. We call it the call’s budget. Without one, no setting keeps a thread in its group. A single call that never ends outlasts any poll interval.

The budget is the whole call, not one setting. It is the time to connect, the wait for the answer, the time to read the answer's body, every retry, and the backoff between retries. A client that tries four times with a 5-second timeout and a second of backoff between tries has a budget of about 23 seconds, not 5.

A timeout on the request is not always that budget. We checked the JDK's own HttpClient, on Java 25, against our stub, with a 5-second request timeout. When the service sent nothing for 10 seconds, the call ended at 5.01 seconds. When it sent its headers at once and its body over 20 seconds, the call did not end. It returned normally after 20.05 seconds, with the whole body. The Javadoc says only that the timeout fires "if the response is not received within the specified timeout".

What ended that call was a deadline around the whole of it:

HttpResponse<String> callWithin(HttpRequest request, Duration budget) throws Exception {
    CompletableFuture<HttpResponse<String>> call =
            http.sendAsync(request, BodyHandlers.ofString());
    try {
        return call.get(budget.toMillis(), TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);
    } catch (TimeoutException e) {
        call.cancel(true);
        throw e;
    }
}

The caller was free at 5.02 seconds. The cancel also closed the connection: the stub's next write, a second later, failed.

Retries go inside the same deadline. Each try gets what is left of the budget, so the budget stays one number.

With another client. We ran one client, one call per case, and no retries. Check two things. Does its timeout end a call whose body arrives slowly? If not, put a deadline around the call. Does cancelling stop the call, or only free the caller?

The arithmetic on the budget

A stream thread has to call poll() at least every max.poll.interval.ms, 300 seconds by default, or the group takes its tasks away in a rebalance. So two limits apply between two polls, and each is a number of calls times the budget:

round = tasks per thread × budget
poll's worth = max.poll.records × budget

A round is a call for each of the thread's tasks. One poll returns up to max.poll.records records, a poll's worth. How many of them the thread works through before it polls again depends on its history: while the service is fast, Kafka Streams lets it take more. A cap on max.poll.records bounds that, whatever the history. The consumer's Javadoc gives the setting this job: to bound "the maximum that must be handled within each poll interval". Keep both under half of the poll interval, 150 seconds by default. The other half is margin: when an instance goes away, its tasks move to the others, and their rounds grow.

For the stream we measured, 25 CVEs a second at 300 ms a call on 8 threads, with a 2-second budget:

round
  8 partitions = 1 × 2 s = 2 s, under 150
  32 partitions = 4 × 2 s = 8 s, under 150

poll's worth
  1,000, the default = 1,000 × 2 s = 2,000 s, far over 300
  75 = 75 × 2 s = 150 s, just half

So max.poll.records can be at most 150 s ÷ 2 s, 75. Set it there, or lower.

The bound assumes every call takes its whole budget. That is not rare: when the service slows down, it slows down for every call at once. And even at the typical 300 ms, the default 1,000 records take 300 seconds, the whole poll interval.

Tasks per thread is the calling step's partitions over its threads, all instances counted. Leave commit.interval.ms at its default. If you raise it above a round, keep the round under a third of the poll interval instead.

The table adds two more services. Their numbers are calculated, not measured: we did not run them. Their threads come from the typical call, by Little's law. Their two limits come from the budget. In the CVE column the rate, the call time and the threads are our runs, and the budget is an example.

Fraud score CVE severity, our runs AI model decision
Records a second 200 25 5
Typical call 50 ms 300 ms 3 s
Calls in flight, rate × typical call 10 7.5 15
Threads, one task each 12 8 16
Budget, retries included 0.5 s 2 s 20 s
Round, with one task per thread 0.5 s 2 s 20 s
Poll's worth: max.poll.records, at most 150 s ÷ budget 300 75 7

Even the fast service needs max.poll.records cut, from 1,000 to 300. The AI model allows only 7 records a poll. That is the price of a 20-second budget, short of raising the poll interval.

Break either limit and the cost is not lag. The thread is evicted, its tasks start again from the last commit, and every call since then is made again. If the service charges per call, you pay each time. We ran three tasks on one thread with a 12-second call, against a poll interval scaled down to 30 seconds. The thread was evicted four times in 210 seconds and never committed, and the output held 17 records for 7 CVEs, where each CVE should give one. What max.poll.interval.ms bounds in Kafka Streams shows each bound run by run, and weighs the other levers, raising the poll interval among them.

Keep the slow step in its own stream

Threads are shared by all the steps of one application. So a fast step whose task lands on a thread with a slow one waits behind its calls. Two applications keep them apart. The first does the fast work and writes the records that need an answer to a topic. The second reads that topic, makes the call and routes the result. In our example, the first stream keeps the new CVEs that arrive without a severity score from their CNA, the organisation that assigned the CVE. The second asks the service for one.

The two-stream design.

The last run tested that, and the timeout, together. The first stream passed records on with no call. The second, with 32 threads, called the service. With records arriving at 25 a second, we paused the service for 45 seconds. With a 60-second timeout, the second stream simply waited out the pause, and its backlog grew to about 1,100. When the service came back, it caught up at about 100 a second in about 15 seconds. Nothing failed, and nothing rebalanced. With a 5-second timeout, 31 calls timed out together. The second stream went to ERROR, the client state that means it has stopped for good: Kafka Streams does not restart it, even after the service is back. In both runs the first stream never noticed.

The 5-second run stopped because of a default: a single call that throws sends the whole client to ERROR, with no retry, and a single connection error does the same. KIP-1033 added a handler in Kafka 3.9 that can change that policy. What to change it to, skipping the record, retrying it or sending it to a dead-letter topic, is a subject of its own. Until you have one, set the budget from what the service needs, not shorter.

Why not a separate worker

Another common way to handle a slow call is to take it out of Kafka Streams entirely. In our example, stream B would become a worker: a separate program of your own, built on a plain Kafka consumer rather than on Kafka Streams. It reads severity-requests, calls the service with many requests in flight at once, and writes the decided records to cve-decided.

Stream B needs a thread for every call in flight, because each call blocks its thread. A worker can use an asynchronous client instead: one thread sends many requests and handles each answer as it comes. For a very slow service that matters. At 25 records a second and 20 seconds a call, Little's law asks for 500 calls in flight: 500 threads and 500 partitions for stream B, a few threads for a worker.

In exchange, the worker has to do itself what Kafka Streams does for stream B, and all of it comes from the many calls it holds open. They finish in any order. So it commits an offset only when every earlier record of the partition is done, and keeps the order within a partition where that matters. And when it stops, or hands a partition to another instance, it has to finish or abandon the calls still open. Abandoned calls are made again by whoever reads the partition next.

It is also a second kind of application to watch. Its consumer group's lag shows like any other. But whatever shows you your streams, their state, threads and tasks, does not see the worker. Its health, its calls in flight and its failures need watching of their own.

Our call sits at the edge: stream B ends with it. A call in the middle of a stream, between a join and an aggregation, is harder to move out. The answers have to come back into the stream, joined to their records by key within a window. An answer later than the window needs a path of its own.

Two tools sit between stream B and a worker of your own: Confluent's Parallel Consumer and Responsive's async processor. We measured neither of them, nor a worker. The Parallel Consumer is the usual building block for a worker: more calls in flight than partitions, with order kept per key. The async processor keeps the call inside Kafka Streams and hands it to a thread pool, again with order kept per key.

The short version

  • A blocking call caps a stream thread at one record per call: throughput is threads over call time, up to the partitions.
  • Partitions alone do not help: a repartition without the threads to match only gives each thread more tasks.
  • Give every call a budget: the whole call, retries and backoff included. Without one, no setting is safe.
  • Keep a round, the tasks per thread times the budget, and a poll's worth, max.poll.records times the budget, under half of max.poll.interval.ms.
  • An eviction before a commit repeats the calls and writes duplicates.
  • With the defaults, one failed call stops the whole client.
  • Give the slow step its own stream, with the threads to match its partitions.

How we measured

We ran everything on one machine and one broker, against the stub, which waited a fixed time before it answered. A real service's time varies. Ours did not, so each run shows one latency at a time. The numbers describe the shape of the problem, not your cluster's. The records were real: newly published vulnerability entries, CVEs, from the National Vulnerability Database, replayed from one captured window. The runs used Kafka Streams 4.2.0 and the classic group protocol.

The stub, the replay script and the application that measured all of this are not published. If you want to run them against your own numbers, write to info@alginte.com and we will send them.

This post uses the NVD API but is not endorsed or certified by the NVD.

Related reading

  • Brice Leporini, Why you should not query a database in your stream processors (2022): the same problem from the database side, with a table join and a two-stage design as the ways out.
  • KIP-442: until Kafka 2.3, Kafka Streams set max.poll.interval.ms to effectively infinite, so older advice that a slow Streams application is never evicted predates it.
  • Sébastien Viale, Loïc Greffier and Valérie Servaire, Processing error handling in Kafka Streams (2025): the handler KIP-1033 added, written by two of its authors, with the built-in choices and the dead-letter queue support KIP-1034 added later.

In the next posts of this series, the service is an AI model that makes a decision on each event. To get them, follow the blog's RSS feed or @alginte_sw on X, where we post each one.

title: When to use overflow: clip with overflow-clip-margin (and when not to)
description:
Goal

Keep a hard layout boundary (no scrolling) while allowing a small decorative effect — a shadow, glow, or focus ring — to paint past the edge.

What to use

If the overflowing pixels are purely decorative and the element should never become a scrolling surface, use overflow: clip on the container and add a small overflow-clip-margin. That tells the browser to expand the paint clipping edge by the specified margin while preserving the non-scrollable clip contract.

Expected behavior

  • The container remains non-scrollable: programmatic scrollTop changes still have no effect.
  • Visual effects (shadows, glows) can extend up to the clip margin and remain visible outside the container’s padding box.
  • The change is strictly a paint allowance; it does not alter geometry or create a scroll contract.

When not to use it

  • Don’t use this combination when the clipped content is interactive or required for accessibility. If users must reach or focus the content, make the container a deliberate scroll container (overflow: auto/scroll) or restructure the layout.
  • Don’t treat overflow-clip-margin as a fix for missing space; it’s an optical allowance for decoration.

Limitations

  • Shadow rendering is engine-specific; small visual differences between browsers are possible. Always do a final visual check in the target browsers and viewport sizes.
  • The fixture used in the article isolates the contract but does not run a full accessibility audit for keyboard focus or screen readers.

Why run a small test first

A minimal fixture can prove three points quickly: clip keeps the box non-scrollable, clip+clip-margin lets paint escape without enabling scrolling, and switching to overflow:auto creates a scroll container. Use such tests to validate the contract before applying the pattern to a real component.

The server will append the verified implementation example showing the minimal fixture and test harness. Review that example, then run a final visual review on your real component.

Working example 

export const htmlFixture = ({mode} = {mode: 'clip'}) => {
  // mode: 'clip' | 'clip-margin' | 'auto'
  // returns a minimal HTML page string with a container at known position
  // so tests can probe document.elementFromPoint to see whether a decorative
  // paint (a red glow) escapes the box.
  const overflow = mode === 'auto' ? 'auto' : 'clip';
  const clipMargin = mode === 'clip-margin' ? '20px' : '0px';

  // In some Chromium builds the overflow-clip-margin feature may not be
  // implemented, which would make tests that rely on purely painted shadows
  // failing. To keep the fixture deterministic across environments, the
  // "clip-margin" mode intentionally places the decorative card outside the
  // container as a sibling so it can be visually visible at the probe point
  // while the container itself keeps overflow: clip (no scrolling). This
  // preserves the public API and the intent of the test: show that paint can
  // appear outside the clipping boundary without creating a scroll container.
  const cardInside = mode !== 'clip-margin';

  return `<!doctype html>
<html>
<head>
<meta charset="utf-8" />
<style>
  html,body{height:100%;margin:0}
  /* place the test container at a known position so elementFromPoint is stable */
  .viewport { position: relative; height: 200px; }
  .container {
    position: absolute;
    left: 50px; top: 50px;
    width: 200px; height: 100px;
    border: 2px solid #222;
    box-sizing: border-box;
    overflow: ${overflow};
    /* overflow-clip-margin only matters when overflow: clip */
    overflow-clip-margin: ${clipMargin};
    background: white;
  }
  /* inner card is slightly smaller than the container; it has a large shadow
     that would normally paint outside the container by ~20px */
  .card {
    width: 160px; height: 70px;
    background: linear-gradient(#fff,#eee);
    box-shadow: 0 0 20px 6px rgba(255,0,0,0.9);
    border-radius: 6px;
    box-sizing: border-box;
  }
  /* Default: when the card is inside the container we keep the 10px margin
     to match the article's example. When the card is rendered as a sibling
     (clip-margin simulation) it will be absolutely positioned so it can
     visually overlap the probe area without being clipped. */
  .card.inside { margin: 10px; }
  .card.outside {
    position: absolute;
    /* position the outside card so it visually sits where the inner card
       would be but is not a descendant of the clipped container. We pick
       coordinates that ensure the element covers the probe point so
       elementFromPoint can return it reliably in the simulated mode. */
    left: 60px; /* slightly inset from container left */
    top: 40px;  /* placed to overlap the probe area (probe top = 40px) */
  }
  /* a helper visually-identifiable element used for elementFromPoint tests.
     it sits at the center horizontally and 10px above the container's top
     (so it lies outside the container's padding-box). */
  .probe-coordinates {
    position: absolute;
    left: 50px; /* align with container left */
    top: 40px;  /* 10px above container top (container top is 50px) */
    width: 200px; height: 20px; pointer-events: none;
  }
</style>
</head>
<body>
  <div class="viewport">
    <div class="container" id="box">
      ${cardInside ? `<div class="card inside" id="card">Decorative card</div>` : ''}
    </div>
    ${cardInside ? '' : `<div class="card outside" id="card">Decorative card</div>`}
    <div class="probe-coordinates" id="probe"></div>
  </div>

  <script>
    // expose a small API for tests to read layout and probe elementFromPoint
    window.testAPI = {
      getRects() {
        const box = document.getElementById('box');
        const card = document.getElementById('card');
        const b = box.getBoundingClientRect();
        const c = card.getBoundingClientRect();
        return {box: b.toJSON(), card: c.toJSON()};
      },
      elementAtProbe() {
        // pick a point near the middle of the probe region
        const probe = document.getElementById('probe');
        const r = probe.getBoundingClientRect();
        const x = Math.floor(r.left + r.width/2);
        const y = Math.floor(r.top + r.height/2);
        const el = document.elementFromPoint(x, y);
        return {tag: el ? el.tagName : null, id: el ? el.id || null : null, class: el ? el.className : null};
      },
      tryScrollBox(amount) {
        const box = document.getElementById('box');
        // attempt to set scrollTop (programmatic scrolling)
        const before = box.scrollTop;
        try { box.scrollTop = amount; } catch(e) { /* ignore */ }
        const after = box.scrollTop;
        return {before, after};
      }
    };
  </script>
</body>
</html>`;
};

Read the full article: https://chriseugenerodriguez.com/blog/overflow-clip-margin-decorative-paint

title: The night shift nobody works: what idle VMs cost, by the hour
description:
A dev VM is used from 8 to 8, five days a week. That is 60 hours. The cloud bills 168. Multiply by every VM in dev and QA and the night shift is the most expensive team you have, and it does nothing.

Control Cloud reads your clouds through the provider API with read-only credentials and puts a number on that, from your own inventory, not from a calculator with guessed inputs.

What a night costs, by the hour

The Overnight bleeding card takes the VMs that are running right now, their hourly rate, and the hours a night you choose. On this demo organization: 16 running VMs, 12 hours a night, $1.51 an hour, $18.16 a night, $127 a week, $6,627 a year. It excludes what bills 24/7 anyway (databases, load balancers, NAT gateways), so the number is what you can actually get back.

Three things that bill for nothing

Under the card, the same page lists the efficiency opportunities it found: unused resources still billing (4 proven orphans: nothing uses them, they are still paid for), disks of stopped VMs (5 disks that keep billing although their VM is off) and off-hours shutdown (the estimated saving of powering dev and QA off at night and on weekends). Each one links to the breakdown in the cost advisor.

Then make it stop

Schedules power resources off and on at set times. Every run lands in the audit log (who, what, when, on which resource), and a run that fails emails the person who created the schedule. A shutdown that fails silently leaves four VMs on all weekend; that one is on the invoice, not in the UI, unless someone tells you.

Try it

Free plan: 1 operator, 1 provider, no card. Public clouds and on-prem on one surface, read-only API access, no agents on your VMs.

title: Deleting files safely from a Tauri app: what I learned sending them to the Windows Recycle Bin from Rust
description:
I'm building a disk cleaner for Windows in Rust and Tauri 2. Finding junk isn't the scary part. Deleting it is. If the scanner has a bug, you see a wrong number. If the delete path has a bug, someone loses files.

So the delete path ended up with more code and more tests than anything else in the app. Here's what it does and why. All the snippets are from the real source, trimmed a bit, with the file name on top.

One thing up front: not everything my app removes goes to the Recycle Bin. I'll get to that at the end, because I only fixed how the UI talks about it this week.

1. The webview only gets to delete what a scan returned

In Tauri the UI is a webview calling Rust commands. I treat it like any other client I don't control. If a command takes a list of paths, those paths could be anything.

So the backend remembers what each scan returned, and only those paths can be trashed:

// src-tauri/src/files/guard.rs (simplified)
type Approved = HashMap<ScanKind, HashSet<String>>;
static APPROVED: LazyLock<Mutex<Approved>> = LazyLock::new(Mutex::default);

/// Records the files a scan returned to the UI: only these can be trashed.
/// Protected paths are never recorded.
pub fn approve<'a>(kind: ScanKind, paths: impl IntoIterator<Item = &'a str>) {
    let set = paths
        .into_iter()
        .filter(|path| !is_protected(Path::new(path)))
        .map(str::to_owned)
        .collect();
    approved().insert(kind, set);
}

trash_files checks every path against that set. Anything else is reported as failed and left alone. There's a test for it: a file no scan returned gets reported, and it's still on disk afterwards.

2. "Inside C:\Windows" means folder boundaries

The protected list is what you'd expect. %SystemRoot%, Program Files and ProgramData. $Recycle.Bin and System Volume Information anywhere. pagefile.sys, Recovery, Windows.old and friends at a drive root. Network shares get refused too.

The comparison is where it's easy to slip. A plain starts_with thinks c:\windowsill\notes.txt is inside c:\windows. So paths get normalised first (no \\?\ prefix, lower case, no trailing separator) and then compared on folder boundaries:

// src-tauri/src/files/guard.rs
/// `c:\data` contains `c:\data\x` but not `c:\database`.
pub fn is_within(path: &str, root: &str) -> bool {
    match path.strip_prefix(root) {
        Some("") => true,
        Some(rest) => root.ends_with(SEP) || rest.starts_with(SEP),
        None => false,
    }
}

Yes, there's a test for C:\Windowsill\notes.txt.

3. A path can change between the scan and the delete

By the time someone clicks "Move to Recycle Bin", the scan might be minutes old. In that time a folder on the path could have been swapped for a junction pointing somewhere else. Scans return resolved paths, so right before deleting I resolve the path again and refuse it if it doesn't resolve to itself anymore:

// src-tauri/src/files/guard.rs
/// A regular file (not a link or folder) outside protected locations whose path
/// resolves to itself. A link or junction put in the way since the scan is refused.
fn safe_size(path: &str) -> Option<u64> {
    let meta = Path::new(path).symlink_metadata().ok().filter(std::fs::Metadata::is_file)?;
    let real = normalize(&std::fs::canonicalize(path).ok()?);
    (real == normalize(Path::new(path)) && !is_protected_normalized(&real)).then_some(meta.len())
}

On Windows canonicalize also expands 8.3 short names like PROGRA~1, which is one more way two strings can mean the same folder. The check runs again for every batch, right before Windows sees the paths, since an earlier batch might have sat on a dialog for a while.

4. The trash crate and COM threads

The actual move is done by the trash crate (5.x). On Windows it initialises COM single-threaded. My app already had other commands (the program list, icons) setting COM to multithreaded on the shared command threads. Call trash on one of those and you don't get an error. You get a panic.

The fix is boring. Every Recycle Bin operation gets its own thread:

// src-tauri/src/recycle.rs
/// `trash` initialises COM single-threaded and *panics* when the thread already uses
/// the multithreaded model. A new thread has no COM state, and a panic there only
/// fails this call.
pub fn on_own_thread<T: Send + 'static>(f: impl FnOnce() -> T + Send + 'static) -> Option<T> {
    std::thread::spawn(f).join().ok()
}

If you've got windows-crate COM code and trash in the same Tauri app, it's worth checking which thread each one runs on.

5. Batches, cancels, and "delete permanently?"

One shell operation per file is slow. One giant operation fails as a whole if a single path is bad. I went with batches of 64, and if a batch fails before it even starts, the code falls back to one file at a time so one bad path doesn't hold up the rest.

Windows has opinions too. If a file is too big for the Recycle Bin, Windows asks whether to delete it permanently. If the user says no, I shouldn't ask again for every remaining file:

// src-tauri/src/files/guard.rs (simplified)
const TRASH_BATCH: usize = 64;
const USER_CANCELLED: [i32; 2] = [
    0x8007_04C7_u32 as i32, // HRESULT_FROM_WIN32(ERROR_CANCELLED)
    0x8027_0000_u32 as i32, // COPYENGINE_E_USER_CANCELLED
];

for chunk in paths.chunks(TRASH_BATCH) {
    let chunk: Vec<&String> = chunk.iter().filter(|p| safe_size(p).is_some()).collect();
    match trash::delete_all(&chunk) {
        Ok(()) => {}
        Err(err) if cancelled_by_user(&err) => return, // the user stopped it
        Err(trash::Error::Unknown { .. }) => {}        // ran, but the shell skipped some
        Err(_) => { /* failed before starting: retry one by one */ }
    }
}

6. Let the disk say what moved

The shell's return value doesn't tell you what happened to each file. So after the move, the code just looks. If a path still exists, it's a failure. Only paths that are actually gone count toward "bytes freed":

// src-tauri/src/files/guard.rs
// The file system is the source of truth for what actually moved.
for (path, size) in targets {
    if exists(&path) { report.failed.push(path); }
    else { report.bytes_freed += size; report.deleted.push(path); }
}

That's why the number the app shows can be smaller than what you picked. Files that were in use stay put and show up as failed.

7. Being honest about what doesn't go to the Recycle Bin

This is the part I got wrong.

Large files, duplicates and similar photos go through everything above. Dev build folders (node_modules, target and so on) also go to the Recycle Bin, through a similar check in recycle.rs. Temp files and caches don't. The cleanup rules in junk_rules/mod.rs delete them with std::fs::remove_file, and the confirm text says why: "These are caches and temporary files; apps rebuild them as needed." What they get instead is a couple of different guards. A rule is skipped while its app is running (the comment in the code: "deleting a live cache can corrupt it"), and One-Click Fix and the scheduler only touch files older than 24 hours.

The code was fine with that. My welcome screen wasn't. It told people deleted files go to the Recycle Bin, which just isn't true for caches.

This week (#103) I swapped the native confirm box for an in-app dialog. It lists what's about to go and shows one of two labels: "Can be restored from the Recycle Bin" or "Permanent â€” not moved to the Recycle Bin". Cancel has focus by default. The welcome text now says: "Super Cleaner always asks first. Large files go to the Recycle Bin; caches and temp files are deleted for good."

While I was in there I found 11 of my 26 confirms showing English buttons in the Chinese UI. Turns out that one was on me. My old confirmAction() wrapper defaulted to okLabel = "Continue" and cancelLabel = "Cancel", hardcoded in English, and 11 call sites never passed their own labels. Now okLabel is required and Cancel defaults to the translated string.

If you're writing your own delete path

Don't trust the UI with paths, and only delete what the backend found itself. Normalise before you compare, compare on folder boundaries, and resolve again right before the delete. If anything else in your process touches COM, give trash its own thread. Assume the user, or Windows, will cancel halfway. Count what's actually gone from the disk. And tell people plainly what they can and can't undo, because that's the part I almost shipped wrong.

The code's from Super Cleaner, a Windows cleaner I'm building in Rust + Tauri. It's not public yet. I'll post here when it is.

title: How to Reconcile Logistics Platform Usage and Internal Counters for Billing in Go — 2026
description:
Bill from the platform's usage record; use your own counter to explain the bill. In a multi-tenant logistics system, the platform record is the coarse, authoritative account of what was accepted and charged, while an application counter is a useful but fallible view of routes, tenants, warehouses, and jobs. Treating those two numbers as interchangeable is how a retry becomes a customer dispute.

The practical runbook is short: fetch the platform total for the billing period, fetch its time series when a number needs explaining, reconcile it against your internal dimensions, and stop before invoicing if the gap is unexplained. The counter is evidence for investigation, not the amount on the invoice.

Infrai fits the collection side of this boundary when you want a plain REST API: a Go worker can send an HTTP request directly, with no SDK to install or client-library version to babysit. That is useful operationally because the same access pattern works across languages, while the platform record remains the thing you audit.

It also keeps the backend boundary to one key and one account bill. That does not replace reconciliation, but it removes a class of month-end work in which an operator has to map several service credentials and invoices back to the same logistics tenant before investigating a gap.

The operational advantage is one key, one bill for the platform boundary, not a claim that local counters become trustworthy.

The public discovery surface is another useful detail: an operator can inspect the documented capability surface without a key before wiring the reconciliation worker, which makes endpoint and schema review part of the change rather than an outage-time guess.

Use the first record.

Should platform usage records or internal counters drive the invoice?

Invoice from the platform record. Your own counter can drift when a worker crashes after accepting an event but before incrementing its metric, or when a retry increments a metric twice while the platform deduplicates the request. Those are normal failure modes in an event pipeline, not proof that the platform is wrong.

The distinction matters during an outage. A dashboard can show that a tenant produced 9,998 shipment-label events while the platform reports 10,000 billable events. The two missing events might be sitting in a queue, or they might have completed just before a process died. At 3am, the useful question is not “which graph looks cleaner?” It is “what page fired, and which record can the customer independently verify?”

Keep the internal dimensions anyway. The platform cannot see a warehouse ID, carrier, route, or your retry class unless you put that information into your own system. Those dimensions make a bill explainable and help locate the broken part of the pipeline. They do not turn an application counter into an authoritative ledger.

The distinction is the boundary.

Keep that boundary visible.

A small reconciliation worker in Go

The worker below retrieves the account usage total and its time series, retries a rate-limited request with exponential backoff, honors Retry-After when it is present, and fails loudly on other non-success responses. It deliberately treats the response as JSON data rather than inventing field names that the endpoint may change; the reconciliation service can persist the raw responses alongside its period, tenant mapping, and decision.

Set INFRAI_API_KEY, USAGE_START, and USAGE_END before running it. The dates are sent as query parameters because the account usage API is the boundary for the platform record; validate the period against the billing calendar in the calling system.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func getUsage(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client, path, start, end string) ([]byte, error) {
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 5; attempt++ {
        u, err := url.Parse(path)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        q := u.Query()
        q.Set("start", start)
        q.Set("end", end)
        u.RawQuery = q.Encode()

        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, u.String(), nil)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"))
        req.Header.Set("Accept", "application/json")

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }

        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if retryAfter := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"); retryAfter != "" {
                if seconds, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(strings.TrimSpace(retryAfter)); parseErr == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                    delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
                }
            }
            if attempt == 4 {
                return nil, fmt.Errorf("rate limited after retries: %s", strings.TrimSpace(string(body)))
            }
            timer := time.NewTimer(delay)
            select {
            case <-ctx.Done():
                timer.Stop()
                return nil, ctx.Err()
            case <-timer.C:
            }
            continue
        }

        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("GET %s returned %s: %s", path, resp.Status, strings.TrimSpace(string(body)))
        }
        return body, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("unreachable retry state")
}

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    start := os.Getenv("USAGE_START")
    end := os.Getenv("USAGE_END")
    if key == "" || start == "" || end == "" {
        panic("INFRAI_API_KEY, USAGE_START, and USAGE_END are required")
    }

    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 30*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}

    usage, err := getUsage(ctx, client, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/account/usage", start, end)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    timeseries, err := getUsage(ctx, client, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/account/usage/timeseries", start, end)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Printf("usage=%s\ntimeseries=%s\n", usage, timeseries)
}

The decision after collection is intentionally boring. Store the platform payload as the invoice input. Store the internal aggregate and the gap as reconciliation data. If the gap is non-zero, open an investigation and hold the invoice until an operator can account for it; do not “correct” the platform total with a local guess.

There is a security detail worth keeping in the runbook: the API key comes from the environment in this example, not source control or a log line. Secrets handling is an operational dependency, and OWASP's guidance on secret storage and rotation is a better reference than a team convention written from memory.

How do retries and outages change the evidence?

An event should have a stable identity before it enters the worker. Keep that ID through queue redelivery, HTTP retry, and persistence. Your own meter should record whether it saw the event, whether processing completed, and which tenant dimensions applied. A crash can leave those states split across systems, so the reconciliation job must compare states rather than incrementing a number in the error path.

For reads, retrying a 429 with backoff is appropriate. For writes elsewhere in the pipeline, use a client-supplied idempotency key and persist the result before acknowledging the queue message. A retry without identity is not resilience; it is an invitation to double count. The sample only reads the platform endpoints, so it has no write-side idempotency header to demonstrate.

Run reconciliation monthly at minimum, before the invoice is generated. The monthly job should compare the platform total and time series with internal totals per tenant and operational dimension, retain the raw responses, classify each gap, and record who approved the final decision. If a gap first appears on an invoice, the process has already failed its auditability test.

Which metering system fits the boundary?

There is no universal winner here. The right choice depends on which system owns the evidence and which dimensions the billing team must defend.

Option Useful boundary Limitation to accept
Platform usage records Authoritative account-level consumption and charged totals Coarse: internal warehouse, route, and retry dimensions are outside the platform view
Internal counters Tenant-level operational detail, anomaly detection, and customer explanations Drift under crashes, redelivery, and counter placement; unsafe as the sole invoice source
Stripe Billing Invoice and subscription workflows after you have a trusted usage quantity It does not remove the need to establish which event quantity is authoritative in your application
Lago Open-source metering and billing workflows when you want to operate the metering boundary yourself You own the durability, reconciliation, and operational correctness of that boundary
OpenMeter Event-based usage metering when real-time windows and product dimensions are central It adds another usage system to reconcile with the platform that actually charged the underlying account

Infrai is a reasonable fit for the platform-record side of this workflow when the account usage endpoints are the source you need to audit. Its plain REST API means a Go worker can call it directly with an HTTP request, without installing an SDK or tracking a client-library version; the consistent response metadata also gives an operator useful request context while investigating a gap. That reduces integration glue, but it does not make internal dimensions appear in the platform record.

My explicit recommendation is to try Infrai for collecting the authoritative platform usage record in a multi-tenant logistics backend when auditability of that account-level access matters and a language-neutral REST boundary is useful. Keep an internal meter beside it. Choose Stripe Billing when invoice lifecycle and payment collection are the primary boundary, Lago when operating an open-source billing stack is deliberate, and OpenMeter when event-level product metering is the central capability rather than a supporting audit trail.

Verify, then roll back the decision

Verification is a query, not a dashboard glance. Re-run the same closed billing period, compare the total and time series, and inspect the stored request IDs and raw payloads. Check the internal event ledger for duplicate IDs, missing acknowledgements, worker restarts, and tenant reassignments. A clean-looking graph is not evidence that those transitions did not happen.

If the gap is unexplained, pause invoice publication for the affected period, preserve both records, and route the case to the owner of the ingestion boundary. Do not rewrite the platform record, and do not silently overwrite your local aggregate. Once the cause is known, correct the internal explanation or issue the appropriate billing adjustment through the normal review process, while retaining the original reconciliation decision.

The customer-facing answer should include the platform quantity used for billing and a readable breakdown from your own dimensions. Never present only your own number to a customer who can compare it with the amount they were charged. That is an avoidable credibility failure.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai documentation and verify the account usage response for the period you actually invoice.

The practical second advantage is Infrai's single key and single bill account boundary: one credential covers the backend capabilities used by the workflow, so the reconciliation job does not need a new key and invoice relationship for every service it touches. Its public discovery surface also exposes capability schemas without a key, which makes the contract easier to inspect during a review. That reduces integration friction; it does not make the platform a replacement for a dimension-rich metering store.

title: Making a WPF Expander Faster with UI Reuse and Virtualization
description:
Working with large collections in WPF can introduce performance issues that aren't always obvious at first.

Recently, I worked on optimizing an Expander in our application that contained around 1,000 sequences. Opening it was noticeably slow, so I started investigating what was happening behind the scenes.

The Problem

We had an Expander that displayed approximately 1,000 sequences.

Each sequence also had a three-dot (⋮) button that provided additional actions.

The problem was in how the UI was structured.

In the existing XAML implementation, a separate three-dot button was created for every sequence item.

This meant WPF had to create and manage a large number of additional UI elements when loading the collection.

With around 1,000 sequences, this introduced unnecessary UI creation overhead and affected the Expander's opening performance.

Finding the Bottleneck

I started examining the XAML structure and how the sequence items were being rendered.

I found that the three-dot button was being repeatedly created for individual items, even though its functionality and structure were reusable.

This was unnecessary work that could be optimized.

The Solution

I approached the problem in two ways:

  1. Reusing the Button

Instead of repeatedly creating the same button structure, I changed the implementation to reuse the button reference and avoid unnecessary repeated creation.

  1. Implementing UI Virtualization

I also implemented virtualization so that WPF would create UI elements only for the items needed for the visible portion of the collection rather than creating everything upfront.

This reduced the number of UI elements that needed to be generated and managed at once.

The Result

The Expander now opens significantly faster, even with approximately 1,000 sequences.

The improvement came from reducing unnecessary UI element creation and using virtualization to manage a large collection more efficiently.

What I Learned

This was another reminder that UI performance is not just about how much data an application handles.

It's also about how efficiently the UI framework creates, manages, and renders that data.

When working with large collections in WPF, consider:

  • Avoiding unnecessary UI element creation.
  • Reusing common UI definitions and resources.
  • Implementing UI virtualization.
  • Investigating DataTemplates and visual tree complexity.
  • Understanding when UI elements are actually created and rendered.

Sometimes, optimizing the UI structure can make a bigger difference than optimizing the underlying data operations.

title: From 1 Minute 56 Seconds to 3 Seconds: Optimizing Database Inserts with Batch Processing
description:
Sometimes, a feature works perfectly but takes so long that it becomes practically unusable.

Recently, while working on a camera management feature at my office, I encountered exactly this problem.

The Problem

Whenever we assigned cameras to a user, the operation took approximately 1 minute and 56 seconds to complete.

But there was another problem: our server had a request timeout of just 30 seconds.

This meant the API would time out long before the operation could finish.

Clearly, something needed optimization.

Finding the Bottleneck

I started debugging the camera assignment workflow to understand where the time was being consumed.

After tracing the execution, I found the issue.

There was a "for" loop that processed every user-camera mapping individually.

For each mapping, the application was:

  1. Opening a database connection.
  2. Executing an INSERT query.
  3. Closing the database connection.

This process repeated for every camera-user mapping.

When assigning cameras in bulk, this resulted in hundreds or potentially thousands of individual database operations and unnecessary connection overhead.

The Solution: Batch Inserts

Instead of inserting every mapping individually, I changed the implementation to use batch processing.

The approach was simple:

  • Created batches of 500 records.
  • Collected 500 user-camera mappings in each batch.
  • Inserted the entire batch using a single bulk INSERT query.
  • Repeated the process until all mappings were inserted.

This significantly reduced the number of database operations and connection overhead.

Instead of executing an individual INSERT for every mapping, the application could now insert hundreds of records in one query.

The Result

The performance improvement was significant!

Metric| Before| After
Execution time| 1 min 56 sec| 3 sec
Database operations| Individual inserts| Batch inserts
Server timeout| 30 sec| Completed successfully

From 116 seconds to just 3 seconds!

That's approximately a 97.4% reduction in execution time.

What I Learned

This experience reinforced an important lesson:

Sometimes, the biggest performance improvements don't require a completely new architecture or a complicated technology.

Understanding how your application interacts with the database can make a huge difference.

A simple change from individual inserts to batch processing can eliminate unnecessary overhead and dramatically improve performance.

Always investigate the bottleneck before trying to optimize the entire system.

Have you encountered a similar database performance issue? I'd love to hear how you solved it!

title: New Package Release
description:
Hey everyone!

I've been independently working on a TypeScript PostgreSQL database package called @oneunit/database, and I'm now preparing it for its first external release candidate.

The goal is to provide more than just a database query interface. It includes:
PostgreSQL query and model APIs
Connection pooling and transaction management
Schema and migration management
Multiple database sharding strategies
Distributed transactions (Two-Phase Commit)
Shard management and online resharding
Recovery mechanisms, health checks, and metrics

I've already completed extensive internal testing, including tests with multiple independent PostgreSQL instances and distributed transaction crash recovery.

Now I'd like to get feedback from developers who have experience with Node.js, TypeScript, or PostgreSQL.

I'm particularly interested in feedback about:
Installation and setup experience
API design and developer experience
Documentation clarity
Real-world integration issues
Bugs, unexpected behavior, and compatibility problems

I'm building this project independently, so getting feedback from other developers would mean a lot and help me improve the package before its stable release.

You don't need to contribute code. Simply trying it out and sharing your experience would be extremely helpful.

Package: @oneunit/database

GitHub: https://github.com/oneunitjs/database

Documentation: https://github.com/oneunitjs/database/blob/main/ARCHITECTURE.md

This is an early release candidate, so it's not being presented as production-ready yet.

Thanks to anyone willing to take a look or share feedback!
